questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of secondary immunodeficiency in children? I. Diphenylhydantoin II. Severe malnutrition III. Post-varicella state IV. Nephrotic syndrome Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. I, II and IV

Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency results from non-genetic conditions that impair the immune system. In children, common causes include malnutrition, immunosuppressive drugs, protein-losing states (e.g., nephrotic syndrome), malignancy, HIV infection, and chronic systemic diseases.

• I. Diphenylhydantoin (Phenytoin) ✔

• Phenytoin can cause secondary immunodeficiency, including hypogammaglobulinemia and impaired lymphocyte function.

• II. Severe malnutrition ✔

• Protein-energy malnutrition is the most common cause of secondary immunodeficiency worldwide, leading to impaired T-cell function, reduced complement levels, and decreased antibody production.

• III. Post-varicella state ✘

• Varicella infection causes temporary immune suppression, but it is not considered a common cause of persistent secondary immunodeficiency.

• IV. Nephrotic syndrome ✔

• Urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement proteins predisposes children to recurrent bacterial infections, particularly with encapsulated organisms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which artery is used for arteriovenous shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis, and is located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior tibial artery

The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

The posterior tibial artery is situated behind the medial malleolus and approximately 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, making it a suitable site for creating an AV fistula with the great saphenous vein. This location allows for optimal access and ensures that the shunt can handle the necessary blood flow for effective dialysis with the great saphenous vein. However, they are not commonly used for AV shunting in common practices.

Arteries used for AV shunting include the radial artery and the brachial artery in the upper arm, which are frequently employed for hemodialysis access. In the lower leg, the anterior tibial artery and the peroneal (fibular) artery are less commonly used for this procedure.

Other options:

Option A: In comparison, the anterior tibial artery is located on the anterior aspect of the leg and runs down the front of the tibia, not behind the medial malleolus.

Option C: The peroneal (fibular) artery is situated on the lateral side of the leg, travelling alongside the fibula, and is also not located behind the medial malleolus.

Option D: The fibular circumflex artery is a small artery and is not commonly used for hemodialysis access. It is not a standard choice and does not fit the anatomical location described, as it is a branch of the anterior tibial artery.
questions.learning: Posterior tibial artery — The posterior tibial artery, located behind the medial malleolus and 2.5 cm in front of the tendocalcaneus, that is used for arteriovenous (AV) shunting with the great saphenous vein for hemodialysis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following subunit is associated with inspiratory stridor?
questions.explanation: Stridor is a harsh sound produced by turbulent airflow in a partially obstructed airway. Inspiratory stridor occurs when the obstruction is located at or above the level of the vocal cords (the supraglottic region). This is because the subatmospheric pressure generated during inspiration causes floppy supraglottic tissues, such as the epiglottis or aryepiglottic folds, to collapse inward. Obstruction at the glottic level (Option A) or subglottic level (Option C) typically produces biphasic stridor (both inspiratory and expiratory) because these sites have fixed, narrow diameters. Tracheal obstruction (Option D) most often results in expiratory stridor or wheezing. Therefore, the specific finding of isolated inspiratory stridor strongly points toward supraglottic pathology like laryngomalacia or epiglottitis
questions.learning: Stridor is a harsh sound produced by turbulent airflow in a partially obstructed airway. Inspiratory stridor occurs when the obstruction is located at or above the level of the vocal cords (the supraglottic region).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Modified shock index is calculated using?

HR: Heart rate

MAP: Mean arterial pressure

SBP: Systolic blood pressure

DBP: Diastolic blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HR/MAP

• Modified shock index = HR/MAP
• Original shock index = HR/SBP

The shock index is a hemodynamic stability indicator. In patients with shock, it is a better predictor of mortality than blood pressure or heart rate alone. A shock index >0.9 is indicative of higher mortality.

The modified shock index is a more sensitive indicator of tissue perfusion than the original shock index. In critically ill patients, the DBP decreases earlier than SBP, hence, the modified shock index using MAP is better suited to assess the severity of shock.
questions.learning: HR/MAP • Modified shock index = HR/MAP • Original shock index = HR/SBP The shock index is a hemodynamic stability indicator. In patients with shock, it is a better predictor of mortality than blood pressure or heart rate alone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following ovarian structures is responsible for the following finding?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Corpus luteum

The ovarian structure responsible for the following finding is the corpus luteum.

The histological image shows a corkscrew appearance of the glands, and this is characteristic of the secretory phase of the endometrium in the menstrual cycle. This phase is stimulated by progesterone, which is secreted by the corpus luteum.

Endometrial Biopsy of the various stages of the ovarian cycle:

1. Proliferative phase: The glands are simple, straight, and tubular glands. The lining of the glands shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium with mitotic figures, indicating active cell proliferation. The stroma is dense and compact, with numerous cells undergoing mitosis.

2. Early secretory phase: The initially straight glands begin to coil as the endometrium transitions into the secretory phase. Subnuclear Vacuolation is seen in the epithelial cells of the endometrial glands, caused by the accumulation of glycogen at the base of the cells.
3. Late secretory phase: The glands become maximally tortuous and assume a distinctive "saw-tooth" appearance due to extreme coiling. They are filled with secretions rich in glycogen and glycoproteins, essential for supporting a potential embryo. The stroma is edematous.

Other Options:

Option A: Secondary follicle

The secondary follicle is a more advanced stage of follicular development following the primary follicle. It contains a  fluid-filled cavity (antrum) surrounded by two layers: theca interna and theca externa.

Option B and C: Theca interna and Granulosa cell

The theca interna is a layer of stromal cells just outside the basal lamina of the granulosa cells. They are composed of cuboidal endocrine cells with lipid droplets and abundant smooth endoplasmic reticulum, reflecting its role in steroidogenesis.

Granulosa cells line the interior of the follicle. Cells are organized in layers, initially single-layered in primary follicles and multilayered in secondary follicles.
questions.learning: Corpus luteum — The ovarian structure responsible for the following finding is the corpus luteum. The histological image shows a corkscrew appearance of the glands, and this is characteristic of the secretory phase of the endometrium in the menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents to you at 36 weeks of gestation with complaints of breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension. Fetal movements are normal. On examination, fetal parts are not easily felt and fetal heartbeat is heard but it is muffled. Her symphysis fundal height is 41 cm. Her abdomen is tense but not tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Polyhydramnios

The diagnosis in this case in which symphysis fundal height (SFH) is 41 cm at 36 weeks of gestation and the woman presents with breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension is most likely polyhydramnios.

Polyhydramnios can be defined as the presence of excessive amniotic fluid, which exceeds 2,000 mL.

The sonographic diagnosis of polyhydramnios can be given as

• AFI ≥25 cm
• Deepest vertical pocket (DVP) measuring >8 cm

Causes of polyhydramnios can be due to maternal and fetal conditions-

• Maternal causes include chorioangioma of the placenta, multiple pregnancies commonly in monozygotic twins, disorders of the cardiac or the renal system, and diabetes mellitus.
• Fetal causes include anencephaly, spina bifida, atretic esophagus or duodenum, facial clefts, and neck masses that lead to abnormal swallowing or hydrops fetalis.

Patients may present with dyspnea, palpitations, and pedal edema.

On examination, the following findings can be elicited:

• Markedly enlarged abdomen with flank fullness
• Tense, shiny skin with striae
• Fundal height more than the appropriate gestational age: The SFH measured in cm after 24 weeks is equivalent to the number of weeks up to 36 weeks. A variance of 2 cm is regarded as typical. The SFH in 36 weeks of gestation should have been 36±2 cms, which is less than in this patient.
• Fetal parts and the presentation cannot be well-defined
• Fluid thrill will be present

On per vaginal examination, tensed bulging membranes can be felt. Investigations to confirm the diagnosis include an ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis and an evaluation of possible causes.

Other options:

Option A - Placental abruption classically presents with sudden onset of abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and uterine tenderness. Frequent contractions and persistent hypertonus are the other findings. When the placenta is completely detached from the uterine wall, except at the margin, blood may collect behind the placenta. This kind of presentation is known as concealed type. In another type, blood can escape via the cervix by dissecting downward between the membranes and the uterine wall. It is called the revealed type, which is the most common type.

Option B - Hydrocephalus of the fetus: Hydrocephalus is a condition where there is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the brain, leading to increased head circumference in the fetus. Although it may lead to an increased symphysis fundal height, the clinical presentation of breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension in the mother is not typical of this condition.

Option D - Fetal-maternal ascites can present as Mirror syndrome. There is a connection between fetal hydrops and the onset of maternal edema, in which the mother exhibits the same symptoms as the fetus. Because the mother, the placenta, and the fetus all develop edema, the condition is also called triple edema. At least 20% of cases of hydrops have been observed to be complicated by mirror syndrome. Women most commonly present with edema. Other symptoms may include proteinuria, hypertension, the elevation of liver enzymes, and headache.
questions.learning: Polyhydramnios — The diagnosis in this case in which symphysis fundal height (SFH) is 41 cm at 36 weeks of gestation and the woman presents with breathlessness and excessive abdominal distension is most likely polyhydramnios.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All the following are true about acute cholecystitis, except _______.
options: Gall bladder thickness >3 mm on USG
Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan

Preferential visualization of the gall bladder in a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan is not a feature of acute cholecystitis. On a HIDA scan, non-visualization of the gall bladder even after 3 hours of radioisotope administration suggests the diagnosis of acute cholecystitis.

Acute cholecystitis usually occurs due to the presence of gallstones (90%) leading obstruction of the cystic duct. This leads to inflammation, distension, and edema of the gallbladder. Acalculous cholecystitis and tumor obstructing the cystic duct are rare causes.

Clinical features of acute calculous cholecystitis: Fever, pain and right upper quadrant tenderness. A positive Murphy's sign (Option B) is right upper quadrant tenderness on palpation.

Diagnosis: An ultrasound scan is sensitive in acute cholecystitis and demonstrates a distended gallbladder with a thickened wall of >3 mm (Option A), pericholecystic fluid, the presence of gallstone(s), and the sonographic Murphy's sign. CT scan findings are similar to USG. CBC will show leukocytosis (Option C).

The following image depicts the confirmatory HIDA (Technetium-99m radioisotope) scan in which the gallbladder is not visualized even after 4 hours.

Management: Patients with acute cholecystitis are kept NPO and started on parenteral antibiotics. Cholecystectomy is the treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis. Treatment including cholecystectomy done within 72 hours has better outcomes that interval surgery.
questions.learning: Preferential visualization of gall bladder in HIDA scan Preferential visualization of the gall bladder in a hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid (HIDA) scan is not a feature of acute cholecystitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the tachycardia depicted in the given ECG.
questions.explanation: The ECG shows classic features of Atrial Flutter — characteristic sawtooth/flutter waves (F waves) visible at a rate of approximately 300 bpm with regular ventricular response, most prominent in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Key ECG Features visible: 1. Classic sawtooth pattern of flutter waves 2. Regular atrial activity at ~300 bpm 3. Consistent 2:1 or 4:1 AV conduction ratio 4. Narrow QRS complexes 5. No isoelectric baseline between atrial deflections Why other options are wrong: (A) Atrial fibrillation is incorrect because AF shows irregularly irregular rhythm with chaotic, disorganized fibrillatory waves and no identifiable P waves — completely unlike the regular sawtooth pattern seen here. (C) Ventricular tachycardia is incorrect because VT shows wide, bizarre QRS complexes at 100–250 bpm with no discernible P waves. The QRS complexes here are narrow, ruling out ventricular origin. (D) Ventricular fibrillation is incorrect because VF shows completely chaotic, irregular, disorganized electrical activity with no identifiable waveforms — incompatible with the organized regular pattern visible in this ECG
questions.learning: The ECG shows classic features of Atrial Flutter — characteristic sawtooth/flutter waves (F waves) visible at a rate of approximately 300 bpm with regular ventricular response, most prominent in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presented with redness and extreme pain in the eye. There is also diminution of vision and discharge after the use of contact lenses. Which organism can be the causative agent here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acanthamoeba

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a severe, vision-threatening corneal infection classically associated with contact lens use, especially with poor hygiene or exposure to contaminated water.

• Severe pain disproportionate to clinical findings (hallmark)
• Redness, photophobia, ↓ vision
• Ring-shaped corneal infiltrate (late sign)
• History of contact lens use / water exposure

Pathogenesis:

• Free-living protozoa (Acanthamoeba) invade cornea
• Often introduced via contaminated lens solutions or water

Why not others:

• Staphylococcus / Streptococcus: Cause bacterial keratitis but pain is not disproportionately severe
• Listeria: Rare ocular infection, not typical in contact lens users

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: This is the graph depicting the filterability of dextran through the kidney, 1 representing complete filtration and 0 representing no filtration. Choose the substance A, B, C respectively.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic

In the given graph, the order of filterability is A>B>C, which likely indicates that the substances are Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic.

The glomerular filtration barrier is negatively charged, which will repel most of the negative charged (anionic substances). Whereas, the cationic substances are easily filtered.

Hence, the order of filterability would be: Polycationic > Neutral > Polyanionic, represented by A, B, and C in the graph shown.

The glomerular filtration barrier consists of:

• Endothelium of the capillary
• Basement membrane:

• Lamina densa - electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen
• Lamina rara interna - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge
• Lamina rara externa - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge

• Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane

The capillary endothelium is perforated by thousands of small holes called fenestrae, which measure from 4 nm up to 8nm. Therefore, neutral substances with molecular diameters of less than 4 nm are freely filtered, and filtration of those with diameters of more than 8 nm approaches zero.

However, in addition to the size of the particles, the filtration also depends mainly on the charge of the particle being filtered. The glomerular capillary wall consists of highly negatively charged proteins called sialoproteins, which repel the negatively charged substances (anions). The property can be studied by using charged dextran.

When the filtration of the negatively and positively charged dextrans was studied, the results indicated that the negatively charged dextrans in the blood are repelled, with the result that filtration of anionic substances 4 nm in diameter is less than half that of neutral substances of the same size.

This explains, why albumin despite having an effective molecular diameter of approximately 7 nm, has a very low filtration rate.
questions.learning: Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic — In the given graph, the order of filterability is A>B>C, which likely indicates that the substances are Polycationic, Neutral, Polyanionic.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: After sustaining trauma to the anatomical snuff box—a triangular depression on the lateral aspect of the wrist just below the thumb—a patient is assessed for an underlying fracture. Given the anatomical importance of this region and its association with specific carpal bones, which bone is most likely to be fractured in such an injury?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the bone most commonly fractured in the carpal region, especially following trauma where tenderness is localized in the anatomical snuff box. The scaphoid forms the floor of this triangular space, making it directly accessible to palpation. A fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH) is the typical mechanism of injury that leads to this fracture. The lunate (Option B, often called lunar) is frequently involved in dislocations but less commonly fractured in the snuff box. The cuboid (Option C) is a tarsal bone in the foot, not the hand. While the trapezius (Option D, referring to the trapezium bone) also contributes to the floor of the snuff box distally, the scaphoid is significantly more prone to clinical fractures. Recognition of snuff box tenderness is vital because scaphoid fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis due to their retrograde blood supply
questions.learning: The scaphoid is the bone most commonly fractured in the carpal region, especially following trauma where tenderness is localized in the anatomical snuff box.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old patient presents with persistent flank pain, fatigue, and episodes of red-colored urine, with no prior history of urinary or renal disease. Laboratory tests show more than 20 red blood cells per high-power field in the urine, and microscopic examination reveals these RBCs to be dysmorphic. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of "dysmorphic RBCs" (such as acanthocytes) in the urine is a critical diagnostic clue indicating that the hematuria is of glomerular origin. As RBCs pass through the damaged glomerular basement membrane and navigate the osmotic changes of the renal tubules, they become distorted. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a classic cause of nephritic syndrome presenting with hematuria, flank pain, and systemic symptoms like fatigue. Minimal Change Disease (Option A) is a nephrotic syndrome characterized by massive proteinuria rather than significant hematuria or dysmorphic RBCs. Urinary Tract Infections (UTI, Option C) and Bladder Calculi (Option D) are causes of "extra-glomerular" or post-renal hematuria. In these cases, the RBCs do not pass through the glomerulus and therefore maintain their normal, uniform, biconcave shape. Since this patient's RBCs are specifically described as dysmorphic, a glomerular disease like PSGN is the only plausible diagnosis among the choices provided
questions.learning: The presence of "dysmorphic RBCs" (such as acanthocytes) in the urine is a critical diagnostic clue indicating that the hematuria is of glomerular origin.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the procedure shown in the image: ERCP- Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography CBD- Common bile duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ERCP+CBD stenting

The image shown is of ERCP and CBD stenting.

This is an invasive procedure similar to Upper GI endoscopy. Ampulla of Vater is cannulated and then a contrast-filled dye is injected for evaluation of the biliary and pancreatic tree. After a pathology has been diagnosed in CBD, a CBD stent can be placed.
CBD stenting is useful in indicated in cases of

* CBD stones

* CBD strictures

* management of mild bile duct injury leaks

* palliative drainage of malignant bile duct obstructions.

* ERCP shows filling of the main pancreatic duct (MPD), and CBD. The MPD and CBD drain into the major papillary.

* The most common significant complication is acute pancreatitis.

Other options:

(Option A) The pancreatic duct is seen below.

Option B: PTBD is a form of external biliary drainage where either biliary ductal systems are drained outside percutaneously. It is not done endoscopically.

Option D: PEG is a minimally invasive procedure used for enteral feeding. Endoscopically, a light source is placed in the stomach and a percutaneous puncture is made. A tube is entered through the ostomy and secured to the skin. Enteral feeding can be through nasogastric and nasojejunal tubes. Surgically, tube gastrostomy and feeding jejunostomy can be done.
questions.learning: ERCP+CBD stenting — The image shown is of ERCP and CBD stenting. This is an invasive procedure similar to Upper GI endoscopy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense eye itching and marked photophobia. His parents also report the presence of thick ocular discharge. Based on these symptoms, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a young boy with severe itching, photophobia (light sensitivity), and a thick ropy discharge is pathognomonic for Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). VKC is a seasonal, bilateral allergic inflammation common in young males living in warm, dry climates. Hallmark signs include "cobblestone" papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva or Horner-Trantas dots at the limbus. Trachoma (Option A) involves chronic scarring and is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option C) presents with a localized nodule (phlycten) usually due to hypersensitivity to TB or staphylococcal proteins. Xerophthalmia (Option D) is caused by Vitamin A deficiency and presents with dryness and Bitot's spots, not intense itching and thick discharge. VKC is managed with topical mast cell stabilizers and antihistamines. Therefore, based on the specific allergic symptoms and demographic, VKC is the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a young boy with severe itching, photophobia (light sensitivity), and a thick ropy discharge is pathognomonic for Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 60-year-old hypertensive patient presents with epistaxis unresponsive to nasal packing. Which artery should be ablated for relief?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Sphenopalatine artery

Severe epistaxis that is unresponsive to nasal packing is most commonly due to posterior nasal bleeding, which arises from branches of the sphenopalatine artery.

• The sphenopalatine artery is the terminal branch of the maxillary artery and the main blood supply to the posterior nasal cavity
• It is the most common source of significant posterior epistaxis

Management principle:

• If conservative measures (packing) fail, endoscopic ligation or cauterization of the sphenopalatine artery is the treatment of choice

Posterior epistaxis is more common in elderly hypertensive patients. Bleeding is often profuse and difficult to control

Why other options are incorrect:

• Greater palatine artery: minor contribution to nasal cavity
• Maxillary artery: proximal vessel; ligation is more invasive and not first-line
• External carotid artery: rarely ligated due to high morbidity

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an acute infection with hepatitis B virus. The preferred regimen in the management of HIV-1 and hepatitis B co-infection is tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir.

This regimen is also the first-line management in adults, adolescents, pregnant women, and HIV-TB co-infection.

Antivirals that are effective against hepatitis C infection are sofosbuvir, grazoprevir and glecaprevir.

ART regimen

First-line for:

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir

• Those with HIV-TB and HIV hepatitis co-infections

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Viral infection causing transient aplastic anemia is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parvovirus B-19

Parvovirus B19

• Common, most prevalent are the rash illness of erythema infectiosum and transient aplastic crisis.
• Transmission by respiratory route but also transmissible in blood and blood products.
• Shows erythrotropism – it specifically targets the erythroid cell line, especially the pronormoblast stage. Viral infection produces cell lysis, leading to depletion of erythroid precursors and a transient arrest of erythropoiesis. This may lead to a precipitous fall in haemoglobin which may even require blood transfusion.

Clinical manifestations of Parvovirus B19 infection

• Erythema infectiosum/Fifth disease (slapped cheek appearance)
• Transient aplastic anemia
• Petechial/ purpuric skin eruptions: Papular purpuric “gloves and socks” syndrome
• Arthritis and arthralgia
• Chronic anemia in immunocompromised persons
• Primary maternal infection is associated with non-immune fetal hydrops and intrauterine fetal demise.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A truck driver came with complaints of a painless indurated genital ulcer after unsafe intercourse. Motility of the most likely causative organism can be detected by which of the following microscopes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark field microscope

The clinical vignette of a painless, indurated genital ulcer in a truck driver is most likely suggestive of syphilitic chancre / hard chancre caused by Treponema pallidum. The motility of the organism can be demonstrated by dark ground/ field microscopy.

Dark ground microscopy can be used to diagnose syphilis when an active chancre or condyloma lata is present to visualize Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy images have a dark background with a refractile organism. The dark ground microscope has an optical system that enhances the contrast of unstained bodies. It is generally less sensitive.

Various types of Spirochetes and their appearances under a dark ground microscope:

• Treponemes generally are short, slender with regular and sharp spirals.
• Leptospira have a large number of closely wound spirals and characteristic hooked ends.
• Borrelia is large with irregular and wide open coils.

The image given below shows Treponema pallidum demonstrated by dark ground microscopy and the various appearances of other spirochetes respectively.

Other options:

Electron microscopy (Option-B) is not commonly used for diagnostics in laboratories. It generally helps in appreciating viral structures.

Light microscopes (Option-C) are commonly used in the labs to visualize the stained smears of various bacteria, fungi in 100x magnification. They are also used during the examination of stool specimens for identifying ova, eggs, or larvae.

Fluorescent microscope (Option-D) uses fluorescent dyes like auramine-rhodamine to appreciate Mycobacterial species and malarial parasites.

Syphilis:

Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirochete bacillus.

It shows corkscrew motility which can be demonstrated by darkfield microscopy. Smear specimens are stained using Fontana stain and pathological tissues are stained using Levaditi stain.

Serologic tests for syphilis recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC):

1. Screening or diagnosis (RPR or VDRL),
2. Quantitative measurement of antibody to assess clinical syphilis activity or to monitor response to therapy (RPR or VDRL)
3. Confirmation of a syphilis diagnosis in a patient with a reactive RPR or VDRL test (FTA-ABS, TPHA, EIA/CIA)

Treatment of syphilis is with 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin IM.

Note:

VDRL- Venereal disease Research Laboratory test

RPR- Rapid Plasma Reagin test

TA-ABS- Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption test

TPI-Treponema pallidum immobilization test

TPPA-Treponema pallidum particle agglutination assay

TPHA-Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test

EIA-Enzyme-linked ImmunoAssay

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 16-year-old female presents with multiple episodes of abdominal pain and a history of passing blood in stools. On examination, she has dark pigmented spots on her lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

The clinical scenario of passage of blood in stools with mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark pigmented spots on lips and oral mucosa) and the presence of hamartomatous polyps in the small intestines in endoscopy is highly suggestive of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation. Due to germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the gene STK11. The hyperpigmentation typically appears as dark blue to brown macules on the lips, nostrils, buccal mucosa, palmar surfaces of the hands, genitalia, and perianal region.

Complications:

* Intussusception

* Risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers.

Treatment of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome mainly involves resection of polyps when there is heavy, persistent, or recurrent bleeding, or if intussusception develops. Polyps may be removed surgically by enterotomy or laparotomy, or endoscopically using a colonoscope introduced via an enterotomy. In severe cases where large segments of the small intestine are involved, resection of the affected portion may be required.

Other options:

Option A: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) is an inherited disorder presenting with numerous colorectal adenomatous polyps. It is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the APC gene, which is a regulator in the Wnt signaling pathway. At least 100 polyps are required to make a diagnosis of FAP.

Option C: Juvenile polyposis (JPS) is an autosomal dominant inherited condition that presents with hamartomatous polyps due to mutations in the BMPR1A, SMAD4 or ENG genes. Pigmentation is not present.

Option D: Cowden disease is characterised by polyps of stomach or colon with mucocutaneous lesions, thyroid adenomas and goitre, fibroadenomas and fibrocystic disease of the breast, Uterine leiomyomas, macrocephaly.

Pearl PF0932: Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

* Autosomal-dominant disease

* Germline defects in the tumor suppressor serine-threonine kinase 11 (STK11) gene on chromosome 19.

Features:

* Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, and digits

* Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract

* Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum.

* Increased risk for extraintestinal malignant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles.

Screening: Baseline colonoscopy and upper endoscopy at age 20 years, followed by annual flexible sigmoidoscopy thereafter.

Pearl PF0293: Features of Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

Gastrointestinal manifestations:

* Colon and rectum: Multiple adenomatous polyp usually >100

* Gastric and duodenal polyps are present in 50% cases.

* Gastric polyp: fundal gland polyp, gastric adenoma.

* Duodenal polyp usually in the ampullary region: Adenomatous and premalignant

Extraintestinal manifestations

* Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) seen in 75% of cases; it is detected by indirect ophthalmoscopy.

* Epidermoid cysts

* Desmoid tumors in the abdomen

* Osteoma: In the skull, mandible, and tibia

* Brain tumors

* Tumors of the thyroid, adrenal, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, and bile duct

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young child with congenital hydrocephalus was treated with a successful ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt. Four months post surgical repair, the child presented with fever, nuchal rigidity, and irritability. You suspect meningitis. What is the next best step?
options: Check shunt patency by nuclear study
Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap
Blood culture and take CSF sample by lumbar puncture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Blood culture and take CSF sample from shunt tap

In a child with suspected shunt-associated meningitis, the next best step useful in confirming the diagnosis is by taking a blood culture and a CSF sample from a shunt tap is preferable to a lumbar puncture (LP) (option D).

Shunt aspiration allows for better detection of microbes and avoids the need for a separate procedure, reducing the risk of contamination. VP shunt fluid is obtained from a subcutaneous reservoir using a 25-gauge needle.

Bacterial meningitis may be caused due to meningococcus, streptococcus pneumoniae, or Haemophilus influenzae type b. The clinical presentation of meningitis in children with VP shunts is similar to acute bacterial meningitis in other children. These include fever, rash, vomiting, and refusal to feed. Clinical signs of meningeal irritation (Kernig and Brudzinski signs) are not usually seen in infants.

Blood cultures should be done in all cases of suspected meningitis. Treatment is aggressive with systemic antibiotics. Third-generation cephalosporins along with vancomycin can be used. Wait and watch policy is not followed (option A).

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is used to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to an obstruction in the normal outflow or there is a decreased absorption of the fluid. A silicone rubber device with a proximal portion inserted into the ventricle, a unidirectional valve, and a distal segment is commonly used for shunt placement.

Complications of the shunting procedure include infection due to skin flora entering the shunt (Staphylococcus epidermidis), intracerebral or intraventricular hemorrhage, shunt over drainage, shunt nephritis, shunt disconnection, obstruction, inguinal hernia, and seizures.

Shunt patency studies are performed to determine whether shunt revision surgery is needed in the malfunctioned ventriculoperitoneal shunt. This is done using radionucleotides (option B)

Hydrocephalus represents a group of conditions that result from impaired circulation or absorption of CSF.

Causes of communicating hydrocephalus (increased production or reduced absorption) includes choroid plexus papilloma, meningeal malignancy, and meningitis. Causes of noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus include aqueductal stenosis, infectious (toxoplasmosis, mumps), Chiari malformation, Dandy-Walker malformation, and mass lesions.

In infants, signs include rapid head enlargement, bulging fontanel, and downward eye deviation. Long-tract signs and dilated scalp veins may also be observed. Older children may experience irritability, lethargy, poor appetite, vomiting, and headaches. Diagnosis can be done using MRI, ultrasound, and measurement of ICP.

Medical management with medications like acetazolamide and furosemide can provide temporary relief, but long-term outcomes are often unsatisfactory. Most cases require surgical intervention, such as ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 20-year-old presented with gradual loss of vision at night and a fundoscopy image is shown. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinitis pigmentosa

The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules along with gradual loss of vision which implies that it is case of retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a dystrophy of rods and cones, with rods being primarily affected. It is a genetic disease. The non-hereditary/sporadic type is most common. Among the hereditary type, it can occur in an autosomal dominant (AD), autosomal recessive (AR), or X-linked recessive (XLR) pattern. AD disease generally has the best prognosis.

The presenting feature is night blindness.

Investigations:

• Perimetry- the initial stage will have ring scotoma, which further develops into tunnel vision.
• Electroretinography- reveals a decreased amplitude of both "a" and "b" waves.

Atypical types of RP are as follows:

• Sectoral RP
• Pericentric/Inverse RP
• RP sine pigmento
• RP punctata albescens

There is no effective treatment for RP.
questions.learning: Retinitis pigmentosa — The fundus shows a pale waxy disc, attenuated arteries, and bony spicules along with gradual loss of vision which implies that it is case of retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young girl presents with the complaints of continuous dribbling of urine. However, she also voids normally. Her parents tell you that she had never been totally dry since her birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ectopic ureter

The clinical presentation of a young girl with continuous dribbling of urine, despite normal voiding, strongly suggests the diagnosis of an ectopic ureter.

An ectopic ureter refers to a condition where the ureter drains outside the bladder. It is more common in females and opens either into the urethra below the sphincter or into the vagina. Hence, they present with constant urinary dripping all day, even though the child voids regularly (paradoxical incontinence).

The terminal part of the ureter is frequently narrowed, leading to hydroureteronephrosis. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are common due to urinary stasis.

In males, ectopic ureters usually enter the posterior urethra above the external sphincter, hence they are usually continent and most patients present with UTI or epididymitis.

Investigations include renal ultrasound (USG), voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG), and renal scan to assess function. USG shows a hydronephrotic kidney or dilated upper pole and ureter. If there is a satisfactory function, the recommended treatment options are ureteral reimplantation into the bladder or ureteroureterostomy. The poor function may require partial or total nephrectomy.

Other options:

Option B: A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the terminal ureter, typically obstructive due to a small ureteral opening. In childhood, they commonly present with infections. Larger ureteroceles can cause obstruction at the bladder neck.

Option C: Congenital megaureter (dilated ureter) presents UTI, urinary stones, hematuria, and flank pain because of urinary stasis.

Option D: Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is characterized by the retrograde flow of urine from the bladder to the ureter and kidney. They usually present with recurrent attacks of UTI.
questions.learning: Ectopic ureter — The clinical presentation of a young girl with continuous dribbling of urine, despite normal voiding, strongly suggests the diagnosis of an ectopic ureter.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young woman experiences recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting. Which acid–base disturbance is she most likely to develop?
questions.explanation: Recurrent self-induced vomiting, as seen in bulimia nervosa, results in a characteristic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), which contains hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻). Loss of H⁺ directly raises blood pH, producing metabolic alkalosis. The associated loss of chloride further impairs renal bicarbonate excretion, allowing bicarbonate to accumulate and perpetuate the alkalosis. In addition, volume depletion from vomiting activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, leading to increased potassium and hydrogen ion loss in urine, which contributes to hypokalemia and sustains the alkalotic state. Respiratory acidosis (Option A) and respiratory alkalosis (Option B) are caused by abnormalities in ventilation and are not primary consequences of vomiting. Metabolic acidosis (Option C) occurs in conditions such as diarrhea (bicarbonate loss) or diabetic ketoacidosis, which are physiologically opposite to the acid loss seen with vomiting. Therefore, the most likely acid–base disturbance in this patient is metabolic alkalosis
questions.learning: Recurrent self-induced vomiting, as seen in bulimia nervosa, results in a characteristic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Vomiting leads to the loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), which contains hydrogen ions (H⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which of the following is an adverse effect associated with the long-term use of intermittent teriparatide for the treatment of osteoporosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Osteosarcoma

What is Teriparatide?

Recombinant PTH (1–34) — the only anabolic (bone-building) osteoporosis drug, as opposed to antiresorptives like bisphosphonates.

The Critical Dosing Paradox of PTH

| Dosing Pattern | Effect on Bone | Mechanism

| -------------- | -------------- | ---------

| Intermittent (daily SC injection) | ↑ Bone formation | Osteoblast stimulation > osteoclast activation

| Continuous (constant exposure) | ↑ Bone resorption | Osteoclast activation dominates

This is why it's given as a once-daily injection, not an infusion.

Why Osteosarcoma?

• In rat studies, long-term teriparatide caused dose-dependent osteosarcomas
• Mechanism: sustained PTH receptor (PTH1R) signaling → uncontrolled osteoblast proliferation → malignant transformation
• Note: This has NOT been conclusively demonstrated in humans, but the black box warning stands

Practical Consequences

• Use is limited to 2 years lifetime maximum
• Contraindicated in: Paget's disease, prior radiation to bone, unexplained elevated ALP, pediatric patients (open growth plates), pre-existing bone malignancy
•

Why Not the Others?

| Option | Actually associated with:

| ------ | --------------------------

| A Osteonecrosis of jaw | Bisphosphonates

| C Subtrochanteric fracture | Long-term bisphosphonates (atypical femoral fracture)

| D Loss of bone mass | Teriparatide does the opposite — it's anabolic

questions.text: A patient from a military background presented with rash, fever, and altered sensorium. There is also a deficiency of the membrane attacking complex. The likely cause can be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Neisseria meningitides

Neisseria meningitidis causes meningococcemia ± meningitis, presenting with fever, rash, and altered sensorium.

| Defect / Deficiency | Organism Susceptibility | Mechanism

| ------------------- | ----------------------- | ---------

| C5–C9 (MAC)
(terminal) | Neisseria spp. (especially N. meningitidis) | Failure of complement-mediated lysis

| C3 deficiency | Pyogenic infections (Strep, Staph, H. influenzae) | Impaired opsonization

| C1, C2, C4 (early) deficiency | SLE-like disease | Immune complex deposition

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old female presents with pain in her back of recent onset, which has become severe of late. During the course of investigations, she was found to have lytic lesions in the vertebrae and ribs. Which of the following organs should be carefully screened now for detecting the primary cause of these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breast

In an older woman presenting with multiple osteolytic lesions involving the vertebrae and ribs, metastatic carcinoma should be strongly suspected. Among women, the breast is the most common primary site causing skeletal metastases, particularly to the axial skeleton (vertebrae, ribs, pelvis, skull, and proximal femur). Can present initially with back pain, pathological fractures, or hypercalcemia before the primary tumor is diagnosed.

Therefore, the breast should be carefully screened to identify the primary malignancy.

Why not the other options?

• A. Small intestine: Primary malignancies are uncommon and rarely present with isolated lytic bone metastases.
• B. Large intestine: Colorectal cancer more commonly metastasizes to the liver and lungs before bone.
• C. Adrenal: Primary adrenal malignancies are rare and are not a common source of multiple lytic bone lesions.
questions.learning: Breast — In an older woman presenting with multiple osteolytic lesions involving the vertebrae and ribs, metastatic carcinoma should be strongly suspected.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following can be responsible for Bezold-Jarisch reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serotonin

Serotonin can be responsible for Bezold–Jarisch reflex.

Activation of chemosensitive vagal C fibers located in the cardiopulmonary region (ex: ventricles, atria, great veins, pulmonary artery, juxtacapillary region of alveoli) causes profound bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea followed by rapid shallow breathing. This response is called Bezold-Jarisch reflex.

Other substances that can cause Bezold–Jarisch reflex are capsaicin, phenyl biguanide, and veratridine.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Consider the following regarding the human hair growth cycle: I. Anagen is a phase of active hair growth II. Telogen is a transitional phase III. Catagen is a resting phase Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I only

Human hair growth occurs in a cyclical pattern consisting of three main phases:

1. Anagen (Growth Phase)

• Phase of active hair growth
• Lasts 2–7 years on the scalp
• About 85–90% of scalp hairs are normally in this phase

2. Catagen (Transitional Phase)

• Short involution/regression phase
• Lasts about 2–3 weeks
• Hair follicle shrinks and detaches from the dermal papilla

3. Telogen (Resting Phase)

• Resting phase of the hair cycle
• Lasts about 2–3 months
• Followed by shedding of the hair (exogen phase)

Evaluation of Statements

• I. Anagen is a phase of active hair growth → Correct
• II. Telogen is a transitional phase → Incorrect (Telogen is the resting phase)
• III. Catagen is a resting phase → Incorrect (Catagen is the transitional/regression phase)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 40-year-old woman presented with jaundice, fever, and abdominal pain. She is suspected to have cholangitis. Which of the following apart from abdominal pain makes up Reynold's pentad?

1. Fever
2. Jaundice
3. Hypotension
4. Altered sensorium
5. Hematemesis
6. Melena
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1,2,3,4

Apart from abdominal pain, 1, 2, 3, and 4 form the Reynold's pentad which is seen in severe cholangitis.

The components of Reynold's pentad are:

• Right upper quadrant abdominal pain
• Fever
• Jaundice
• Hypotension
• Altered sensorium

Cholangitis is the infection of the common bile duct (CBD) secondary to obstruction and increased intraluminal pressure due to CBD stones. Cholangitis presents with the classical triad of fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice, referred to as Charcot's triad. It is a medical emergency and if left untreated, it may progress in severity and presents with Reynold's pentad - Charcot's triad with hypotension and altered mental status due to sepsis.

Abdominal ultrasound is performed to check for the presence of biliary stones and bile duct dilatations. The patient should be started immediately on a first-line broad-spectrum antibiotic and rehydration, along with biliary drainage. Biliary drainage is done using endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). Biliary stones are the cause of cholangitis the majority of the time, which can be removed by endoscopic sphincterotomy during ERCP.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old male recently diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, with imaging indicating a tumor size less than 4 cm, what would be the most suitable initial treatment approach for this patient's condition among the following options?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Partial nephrectomy

For localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with a tumor size <4 cm (clinical stage T1a), partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred initial treatment whenever technically feasible. This approach provides equivalent cancer-specific survival to radical nephrectomy while preserving renal function and reducing the risk of chronic kidney disease.

• Complete tumor excision with negative margins
• Preserves maximal functioning renal parenchyma
• Lower risk of long-term renal insufficiency
• Recommended for most T1a renal masses (<4 cm)

Why the Other Options Are Incorrect?

B. Partial nephrectomy + neoadjuvant chemotherapy

• RCC is generally resistant to conventional chemotherapy.
• Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not standard treatment for localized RCC.

C. Radical nephrectomy

• Usually reserved for larger tumors, centrally located masses not amenable to nephron-sparing surgery, or when partial nephrectomy is technically impossible.

D. Radical nephrectomy + postoperative radiotherapy

• Adjuvant radiotherapy has no established role in localized RCC after complete surgical resection.
questions.learning: Partial nephrectomy For localized renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with a tumor size <4 cm (clinical stage T1a), partial nephrectomy (nephron-sparing surgery) is the preferred initial treatment whenever technically feasible.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a warty cutaneous growth on his foot. Histopathological image of the growth is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chromoblastomycosis

This patient is likely a case of chromoblastomycosis.

It is a subcutaneous infection caused by fungi belonging to the genera fonsecaea. It enters the skin by traumatic inoculation. Hence, seen in woodcutter and farmers. It appears as sclerotic bodies on histopathology examination and copper penny bodies on KOH mount. Treatment with antifungals are given.

Other options:

Mycetoma:

* It is caused by various types of Fungi (Eumycetoma) or filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).

* It presents with a painless nodule but with time, papules and pustules may form which breaks down to form draining sinuses, with the discharge of granules.

Image: Mycetoma of Foot.

Sporotrichosis: Nodules generally develop along the draining lymphatics.

Phaeohyphomycosis : it is a chronic fungal infection involving the skin and subcutaneous tissue. The lesions maybe plaques which are verrucous, hypertkeratotis or ulcerated. The fungi implicated are usually of the class Phialophora or Cladophora or other demetacious fungi.
questions.learning: Chromoblastomycosis — This patient is likely a case of chromoblastomycosis. It is a subcutaneous infection caused by fungi belonging to the genera fonsecaea.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 34-year-old woman who works as a housemaid presents with knee pain and swelling, a condition commonly linked to repetitive kneeling and prolonged pressure. In housemaid’s knee, which specific area of the knee is typically affected?
questions.explanation: The condition known as "Housemaid's knee" refers to prepatellar bursitis. This clinical entity is an inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, which is located superficially between the skin and the patella. It is caused by repetitive friction or direct pressure from frequent kneeling, which is common in occupations such as house cleaning. This leads to localized swelling and tenderness directly over the kneecap. Suprapatellar bursa (Option A) is an extension of the knee joint cavity above the patella and is usually affected by joint effusions. Infrapatellar bursa (Option C) is located below the patella and is associated with "Clergyman’s knee," often seen in individuals who kneel more upright. The Pes Anserine bursa (Option D) is located on the medial side of the proximal tibia and is usually associated with runners or those with osteoarthritis. Therefore, label B identifies the specific area damaged in this patient
questions.learning: The condition known as "Housemaid's knee" refers to prepatellar bursitis. This clinical entity is an inflammation of the prepatellar bursa, which is located superficially between the skin and the patella.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38 year old male presents to the OPD with complaints of excessive stress and difficulty maintaining a work life balance .On examination BP is 150/100 and FBS is 150 mg/dl. He has no significant history and is not on any medications. Physical examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient?
options: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Start Telmisartan

The above clinical scenario of a 38-year-old male, with  BP: 150/100 and FBS is 150 mg/dl, is consistent with the diagnosis of Stage 2 Hypertension according to the AHA 2017 guidelines. The next step would then be to start Anti-Hypertensive medications like Telmisartan (Angiotensin Receptor Blocker) considering the sugar levels..

Drugs used in Hypertension: The first-line drug classes include

* Diuretics (Chlorthalidone, Indapamide): Side effects - Hypokalemia, impaired glucose, impaired lipid, increased uric acid.

* Calcium Channel Blockers (Amlodipine): Side effects - Hypotension

* ACE inhibitors (Lisinopril): Side effects: Dry cough, angioedema

* ARBs (Losartan): Generally well tolerated, with rare hyperkalemia

Diuretics are preferred for their long half-life and proven cardiovascular benefit. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are particularly useful in patients with diabetes and chronic kidney disease because of their nephroprotective properties. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together, as combination therapy raises the risk of hyperkalemia without offering extra cardiovascular benefits.

Other options:

Option A: Pharmacologic treatment is indicated for stage 2 hypertension

Option B: Tirzepatide is a GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist used to treat Type 2 Diabetes.

Option C: Glucocorticoids are not indicated and may worsen hypertension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following in IgA vasculitis warrants the use of corticosteroids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GI bleeding

IgA vasculitis is a small vessel vasculitis with IgA immune complex deposition.

Classic tetrad:

• Palpable purpura (skin)
• Arthralgia/arthritis
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement

Usually self-limiting, especially in children

Corticosteroids in IgA vasculitis are indicated for severe gastrointestinal involvement, especially GI bleeding, due to risk of complications like intussusception and perforation.

Skin rash, arthritis, and mild abdominal pain are usually self-limiting and managed with supportive care.

Steroids are reserved for organ-threatening disease, not routine symptoms.

| Feature | Management

| ------- | ----------

| Skin rash only | Supportive

| Arthritis | NSAIDs

| Mild abdominal pain | Supportive

| GI bleeding | Steroids

| Renal involvement | Steroids ± immunosuppressants

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old child presents to the paediatric OPD with complaints of a low-grade fever, poor appetite, and a sore throat for the past two days. Upon examination, the palms, soles, and oral mucosa show numerous vesicular lesions. The child attends daycare, and several other children have similar complaints. The neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coxsackievirus A16

The presence of vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity and the images showing the characteristic lesions are suggestive of hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), which is commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16.

Hand-foot-and-mouth disease:

It is commonly caused by Coxsackievirus A16, which is a subgroup of enteroviruses. In large outbreaks, it is also caused by enterovirus 71, coxsackie A viruses 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10, and coxsackie B viruses 2 and 5.

Clinical features:

* Usually, a mild illness

* Vesicular lesions may be seen on the tongue, posterior pharynx, buccal mucosa, palate, lips, etc.

* Maculopapular, vesicular, or pustular lesions may be present on the hands and fingers, buttocks, and groin.

* Lesions are more commonly seen in the hands than in the feet.

* These vesicles resolve in 1 week.

* Infections with enterovirus 71 are more severe and are associated with neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations.

* Infections with coxsackievirus A16 can occasionally produce complications like encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, myocarditis, pericarditis, and shock.

* Coxsackievirus A6 produces atypical HFMD, which is a severe form.

Diagnosis:

* HFMD is usually diagnosed clinically by the characteristic lesions.

* Viral culture can be done to confirm the presence of an enterovirus. Blood, CSF, urine, and mucosal swabs can be cultured.

* RT-PCR testing to detect the viral genome is more sensitive and specific. PCR testing of CSF in children with meningitis is frequently positive even when the cultures are negative.

Treatment:

* No specific antiviral agent is a proven agent for enteroviruses. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.

* Milrinone is suggested as an effective agent for enterovirus 71 cardiopulmonary disease.

* Immunoglobulins have been used to manage severe cases, but with varying outcomes.

Other options:

Option A: Roseola infantum, also known as sixth disease, caused by human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), is associated with a non-pruritic, pink, morbilliform rash on the trunk and back, which appears after the fever has subsided and disappears after two days. It is also typically associated with ulcers at the uvulo-palatoglossal junction called Nagayama spots.

Option B: Fifth disease, or erythema infectiosum, is an exanthematous fever caused by parvovirus B19 in children, which is also self-limiting and generally requires supportive care only. Its symptoms include a classical slapped cheek rash, which can evolve into a papular purpuric glove and stocking syndrome. There is usually no prodrome or minimal symptoms before the abrupt onset of rash. The virus is known to cause transient myelosuppression and anemia. In very severe disease, IVIG has been tried in some cases.

Option D: Adenovirus is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus. They are associated with infections of the respiratory tract, eye, and intestines.
questions.learning: Coxsackievirus A16 — The presence of vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral cavity and the images showing the characteristic lesions are suggestive of hand-foot-and-mouth disease (HFMD), which is commonly caused by coxsackievirus A16.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?
options: Inhibits acetylcholine release from the presynaptic terminal
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin prevents muscle contraction by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine (ACh) at the neuromuscular junction. It achieves this by cleaving SNARE proteins, such as SNAP-25, synaptobrevin, and syntaxin, which are essential for the fusion of neurotransmitter vesicles with the presynaptic membrane. This blockade leads to flaccid paralysis. Inhibiting ACh reuptake (Option B) is incorrect because ACh is typically degraded in the synapse, not reuptaken. Blocking postsynaptic receptors (Option C) describes the action of neuromuscular blockers like curare. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase (Option D) is the mechanism for organophosphates and neostigmine, which increase ACh levels. Botulinum toxin is clinically used for treating dystonias and for cosmetic purposes (Botox) to relax muscles. Severe toxicity causes botulism, which can result in respiratory failure

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the most likely cause when a patient under general anaesthesia develops left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side during auscultation? PPV-Positive pressure ventillation
options: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube
Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Right endobronchial intubation

The most likely cause of left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side, is endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

Endobronchial intubation is first indicated by a sudden rise in peak inspiratory pressure.
Capnography and detection of end-tidal CO2 is the confirmation for an advanced airway placement, but it does not differentiate endotracheal from endobronchial intubation.

Signs of endobronchial intubation:

* Elevated peak inspiratory pressure (first sign)

* Asymmetric chest expansion

* Unilateral breath sounds

* Drop in oxygen saturation (hypoxemia)

Other options:

Option A: Mucus secretions obstructing the endotracheal tube- will lead to diminished breath on both sides.

Option B: Pneumothorax on the left side due to PPV- less likely to occur immediately after intubation. It may be seen after prolonged PPV, post-intubation. It is a serious complication of mechanical ventilation. It is rare in intubated patients with normal lungs and most patients with pneumothorax related to mechanical ventilation (PRMV) have underlying lung diseases that range from primary obstructive lung disease to secondary pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Excessive airway pressure during mechanical ventilation can rupture alveoli, leading to air leakage into the pleural space → pneumothorax.

Option C: Intraoperative bronchospasm is usually manifested as wheezing, increasing peak airway pressure, and a slowly rising waveform on the capnograph.
questions.learning: Right endobronchial intubation — The most likely cause of left lung collapse after intubation, with breath sounds heard only on the right side, is endobronchial intubation of the right main bronchus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is the best method to assess the degree of muscle relaxation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Train of four

Train of four protocol is the best method to clinically assess neuromuscular blockade.

Train of four protocol is one of the methods used in the clinical assessment of neuromuscular blockade. It is done by stimulating the ulnar nerve with a stimulus and watching the contractile responses in the adductor pollicis muscle. Four successive stimuli of 2Hz strength are given at fixed time intervals and the response achieved is plotted as a graph.

Tetanic stimulation (Option A): It consists of a series of extremely rapid electrical stimuli typically applied over 5 seconds. This method has only 70% sensitivity to detect residual paralysis and its specificity is only about 50%, and is painful. Hence, this test is of limited value for assessing residual neuromuscular blockade.

Double-burst stimulation (Option B): Here two short bursts of 50 Hz tetanic stimuli is delivered, which are separated by 750 ms.

Electromyography (Option D) has been used to measure abdominal and thoracic motor function but is neither practical nor specific.
questions.learning: Train of four Train of four protocol is the best method to clinically assess neuromuscular blockade. Train of four protocol is one of the methods used in the clinical assessment of neuromuscular blockade.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A group of students who were mainly consuming khesari dal and rice water developed weakness in their legs. On examination, their legs moved in a crossed manner while walking, and some were seen walking on their toes. Which of the following vitamin prophylaxis could have prevented this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism. Vitamin C in doses of 500-1000mg can be used for the prevention and treatment of lathyrism.

Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals. It is due to the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus or its variants such as sweet pea(Lathyrus odoratus). It is mostly consumed by agricultural labourers of poor economic status because it is relatively cheap. It can present as skeletal, vascular, or neural manifestations.

It usually affects young males aged 15-45 years and it is manifested in stages:

* Latent stage: The individual is apparently healthy, but when subjected to a physical ungainly gait. if the pulse is withdrawn from the diet, it will result in complete remission of the disease.

* No-stick stage: the patient walks with short, jerky steps without the aid of a stick.

* One-stick stage: The patient walks with a crossed gait and a tendency to walk on toes. stick is used for balance due to muscular stiffness.

* Two-stick stage: Due to excessive bending of knees and crossed legs, the patient needs two crutches for support. The gait is slow and clumsy and the patient gets tired easily after walking a short distance.

* Crawler stage: Finally, the erect posture becomes impossible as the knee joints cannot support the weight of the body. The patient is reduced to crawling by throwing his weight on his hands.

The patient is initially able to walk with short jerky steps without any aids, but the progressive spastic paralysis causes a crossed gait, and the patient has to use sticks to maintain his balance. Eventually, the knee joints are unable to support the weight of the body and the patient cannot stand erect at all. Long-term consumption of khesari dal leads to neurolathyrism. It is characterized by gradual spastic paralysis of the lower limbs.

The interventions that can be used to prevent lathyrism include:

* Vitamin C prophylaxis.

* Limiting the proportion of the dal to less than a quarter of the total cereals and pulses consumed in a day.

* Removal of the toxin by parboiling and steeping method.
questions.learning: Vitamin C — The clinical scenario of students consuming mainly khesari dal and rice water and later presenting with weakness of legs and scissor-like walking(crossed legs) gait is suggestive of neurolathyrism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 40 year old female with no comorbidities complaints of swelling in both her legs which was acute in onset . She also gives a history of loose stools. Her family members too has similar symptoms. On examination there was no signs of inflammation in both the legs. Detailed history revealed that mustard oil is a staple part of their diet . Which of the following substance is responsible for her condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sanguinarine

The clinical presentation is suggestive of epidemic dropsy and Sanguinarine is the toxic compound responsible for this.

Epidemic Dropsy: Contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil.

* Toxic compound: Sanguinarine

* Mechanism of action : Sanguinarine interfers with the oxidation of pyruvic acid which inturn accumulates in the blood and causes symptoms.

* Clinical presentation :The patient presents with sudden onset, non inflammatory swelling of bilateral legs which is often associated with diarrhoea. Some patients can develop glaucoma. Dyspnea, cardiac failure and death can occur in later stages.

* Mortality rate - 5-50%

Tests to detect argemone oil:

* Nitric acid test

* Paper chromatography: most sensitive(can detect very low concentration of argemone oil)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after being sexually assaulted by a neighbor. On evaluation, the police confirm that the accused was entrusted with the child's care while her parents were away. Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, this incident is classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aggravated sexual assault

Aggravated sexual assault under the POCSO Act, 2012 refers to sexual assault committed under specific aggravating circumstances, such as when the offender:

• Is a person in a position of trust or authority (e.g., relative, teacher, guardian, caregiver).
• Is a police officer, member of the armed forces, or public servant.
• Is a staff member of a hospital, educational institution, or child care institution.
• Causes grievous hurt, disability, or life-threatening injury to the child.
• Commits the offence during communal violence, natural disasters, or similar situations of vulnerability.

In this case, the accused was entrusted with the child's care, making it an aggravated sexual assault.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structures marked in the image below are found in the epithelial lining of all of the following sites, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epididymis

The image shows an arrow mark pointing towards the cilia. All the structures given in the options have a ciliated lining epithelium except epididymis, which is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.

The given image is a histological section of the epididymis showing the pseudostratified columnar epithelium with stereocilia.

Cilia are minute hair-like projections, while stereocilia are very long, thick microvilli measuring about 5–10 μm in length.

Ciliated epithelium:

• The epithelium bears cilia, which moves in a coordinated fashion, and help in the movement of the mucus, or propel the movement of any other structures such as ova or spermatozoa.
• The ciliated columnar epithelium is found in most of the respiratory tract, the uterus, and the uterine tube (oviduct), efferent ductules of the testis, parts of the middle ear and auditory tube; the ependyma lining the central canal of the spinal cord and the ventricles of the brain.
• The pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is seen in the trachea and in large bronchi.

Abrasion collar: Gyroscopic movement of the bullet, the skin's elasticity, and the grease and dirt particles on the bullet's surface are the major causative factors of abrasion and grease collar. They are seen on the skin around the wound of entry at all ranges. Depending on the angle of entry made by the bullet, i.e.

• A perpendicular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of rounded shape.
• An acute angular entry of the bullet develops the abrasion collar of an oblique or oval shape.
• Some contusion present in the abraded collar is known as contusion collar

Grease collar: Mostly seen on the clothing and is seen as a black deposit, sharply outlined as if printed (better-seen on light color clothes and on fair-skinned individuals).

Medicolegal importance: Helpful in deriving information such as wound of entry and direction of firing

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child presents with progressive pallor and bone pain, and HPLC analysis shows elevated HbS levels. What is the best treatment to reduce hemolysis in this patient?
questions.explanation: High-Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) showing elevated HbS confirms a diagnosis of Sickle Cell Disease (SCD). SCD results from a mutation in the beta-globin gene, causing hemoglobin to polymerize in low-oxygen states, leading to RBC sickling and chronic hemolysis. Voxelotor is a novel HbS polymerization inhibitor that increases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen. By stabilizing the oxygenated state, it directly reduces sickling and, consequently, the rate of hemolysis. Hydroxyurea (Option A) is widely used in SCD to increase fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which reduces the frequency of painful vaso-occlusive crises, but it has a less direct effect on preventing active hemolysis compared to Voxelotor. Azacytidine (Option B) is used for myelodysplastic syndromes. Bortezomib (Option D) is a proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma. Therefore, Voxelotor is the most effective pharmacotherapy specifically targeted at mitigating the hemolytic process in SCD patients

questions.text: Which is the condition shown below in the image:
questions.explanation: The image shows inward turning of the eyelid margin (lower eyelid), causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea and conjunctiva — this is the classic presentation of entropion. Key features visible: 1. 1. Lid margin rolled inward 2. 2. Periocular skin changes/irritation 3. 3. Lashes directed toward the globe Why other options are wrong: (B) Ectropion : This is the outward turning of the eyelid margin away from the globe, causing exposure of the conjunctiva (red, everted lid). The image shows the opposite : inward turning. (C) Trichiasis : In trichiasis, the eyelid position is normal, but only the lashes are misdirected inward. Here, the entire lid margin is inverted, distinguishing it from trichiasis. (D) Ptosis : Ptosis refers to drooping of the upper eyelid due to levator muscle weakness, covering the pupil. The image shows lid margin malposition, not drooping

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Function of utricle and saccule?
questions.explanation: The utricle and saccule are the two otolith organs located within the vestibule of the inner ear. Their primary physiological function is the detection of linear acceleration and deceleration, as well as the position of the head relative to gravity (static equilibrium). The utricle primarily detects horizontal movement, while the saccule is more sensitive to vertical movement. Angular acceleration (Option C) is the function of the semicircular canals, which detect rotational movements of the head. Hearing (Options A and D) is exclusively the function of the cochlea. Inside the utricle and saccule, specialized sensory areas called maculae contain hair cells embedded in a gelatinous membrane covered with calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths). When the head moves linearly, the inertia of these crystals bends the hair cells, sending signals to the brain via the vestibular nerve. Understanding these distinct vestibular roles is essential for diagnosing different types of vertigo and balance disorders in clinical practice

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Gastric lavage can be performed in case of poisoning by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Carbolic acid

Gastric lavage can be performed in case of carbolic poisoning.

In carbolic acid poisoning, if the patient survives for 48 hrs, there will be carboluria followed by anuria. The victim will pass dark, smoky urine which soon turns olive green on standing due to oxidation of hydroquinone and pyrocatechol.

It is a corrosive acid, however, it hardens the GI mucosa producing a leather bottle stomach and anesthetizes the nerve endings. This allows for gastric lavage.

Contraindications of gastric lavage:

• Corrosives poisoning (except carbolic acid)
• Convulsants/CNS stimulants
• Comatose patients
• Volatile poison
• Upper GI pathology (eg. esophageal varices)
• Hypothermic patient
• Severe heart disease
• Advanced pregnancy

Sulphuric acid and kerosene are corrosives and strychnine is a convulsant. Hence gastric lavage is not done in these poisonings.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Anterior relations of the third part of the duodenum are all except:
options: Fundus and body of Gall bladder
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fundus and body of Gall bladder

Anterior relations of the third part of the duodenum include the Superior mesenteric vessels, the Root of the mesentery, and Loops of the jejunum.

Relations of the 3rd part of duodenum:

• Posterior relations of 3rd part of duodenum include right ureter, right psoas major, right gonadal vessels, inferior vena cava and abdominal aorta (at the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery).
• Anterior relations: Loops of jejunum, Root of mesentery and Superior mesenteric vessels.
• Superiorly related to head of the pancreas and Inferiorly to loops of jejunum.

Note: Root of mesentery (containing Superior mesenteric vessels) lies anterior to the 3rd part of Duodenum. Hence, posterior relations of 3rd part of duodenum are the same as structures crossed by root of mesentery.

questions.text: A 40-year-old man had a RTA and was admitted to a hospital. After a few days, he had an exaggerated right-sided extensor plantar reflex and knee jerk. What other finding would be seen?

Loss of proprioception in the left leg

Sudden stretch (ankle dorsiflexion)

↓

↓

↓

Clonus

Hence, ankle clonus in the right foot is an expected finding.
