questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Afferent fibers from baroreceptors for blood pressure control goes to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nucleus Tractus Solitarius

Afferent fiber for blood pressure control goes to the Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS).

Increased BP stimulates the baroreceptors which provide negative feedback in response to the increase in blood pressure.

Baroreceptor reflex:

• Increased BP → stimulation of baroreceptors → stimulation of NTS → excitation of CVLM → inhibition of RVLM → inhibition of sympathetic system
• Stimulation of NTS also stimulates CVC → parasympathetic stimulation
• Net effect = sympathetic inhibition and parasympathetic stimulation → decreased HR and BP

NTS - Nucleus tractus solitarius

CVC - Cardiovagal centre

CVLM - Caudal ventrolateral medulla

RVLM - Rostral ventrolateral medulla

HR - Heart rate

BP - Blood pressure

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under IDSP, which diseases are included under sentinel surveillance?
questions.explanation: The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) utilizes different levels of surveillance, including sentinel surveillance for specific chronic or complex conditions. Sentinel surveillance focuses on designated sites to track trends and prevalence in high-risk populations for diseases like HIV and Hepatitis B (HBV). Tuberculosis (Option B), while highly prevalent, is primarily monitored through the specialized NTEP program using routine surveillance. Malaria and Dengue (Option C) are vector-borne diseases that fall under active and passive surveillance protocols to capture outbreaks quickly. Measles and Diphtheria (Option D) are vaccine-preventable diseases monitored through routine reporting to detect immunization gaps. Therefore, HIV and HBV are the primary examples of diseases where sentinel sites are used to gather detailed longitudinal data that might be missed by standard clinical reporting systems
questions.learning: The Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) utilizes different levels of surveillance, including sentinel surveillance for specific chronic or complex conditions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following can be used to calculate the cardiac output?

A. ECHO.
B. Ventilation-perfusion scan.
C. Thermodilution.
D. Fick's principle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A, C, D

Fick principle, thermodilution, and ECHO can be used to measure cardiac output.

Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart into the aorta every minute. The average cardiac output is 5L/min and can be measured by various indirect methods.

Fick's principle uses the total amount of oxygen absorbed from the air by the lungs and the arteriovenous oxygen difference of blood to calculate the cardiac output using the following formula:

Cardiac output (L/min) = (O2 absorbed per minute by the lungs (mL/min))  /  (Arterio-venous O2 difference(mL/L of blood))

Thermodilution method employs cold saline which is infused into the right atrium through a double-lumen Swan–Ganz thermodilution catheter and the temperature change is measured at the pulmonary artery using a thermistor at the end of the catheter. The mean decrease in the temperature of blood is inversely proportional to the cardiac output.

An ECHO uses ultrasound waves from a transducer placed on the chest wall to measure the velocity of blood flowing from the left ventricle into the aorta. Stroke volume can be calculated from this. Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.

The other methods that can be used to measure cardiac output include impedance cardiography a.k.a. thoracic electrical bioimpedance, electromagnetic or ultrasonic flowmeter,and  indicator dilution method.

Ventilation-perfusion scan is not a method of cardiac output measurement. It is used to assess pulmonary circulation.
questions.learning: A, C, D Fick principle, thermodilution, and ECHO can be used to measure cardiac output. Cardiac output is the amount of blood pumped by the heart into the aorta every minute.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with severe photosensitivity, freckling over sun-exposed areas, and recurrent skin lesions since early childhood. There is a history of progressive neurological decline. On examination, multiple hyperpigmented macules and areas of skin atrophy are noted on the face and arms. The underlying defect involves impaired repair of UV-induced thymine dimers. Which DNA repair mechanism is primarily affected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nucleotide excision repair

UV radiation causes DNA damage in the form of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers, which distort the DNA helix. These lesions are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.

1.      Recognition of DNA distortion (thymine dimers)

2.      Excision of the damaged DNA segment

3.      DNA polymerase fills the gap

4.      DNA ligase seals the strand

Clinical relevance:

• Defect in NER → Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP)
• Presents with photosensitivity, exaggerated skin rash on sun exposure, and early skin cancers

Why other options are incorrect:

• Base excision repair: Repairs small base changes (oxidation, deamination)
• Double-strand break repair: Repairs DNA breaks (HR, NHEJ)
• Mismatch repair: Corrects replication errors (base mismatches)
questions.learning: Nucleotide excision repair UV radiation causes DNA damage in the form of pyrimidine (thymine) dimers, which distort the DNA helix. These lesions are repaired by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) pathway.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 31-year-old female with a history of a recent divorce presents to emergency with complaints of palpitations, sweating, heaviness, and pain in the chest. She has had multiple similar episodes in the last few weeks. The blood investigations and ECG are normal. In the past too, investigations revealed no abnormality. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Use benzodiazepines for symptom relief

This clinical vignette describes a classic acute panic attack and the next best step is to use benzodiazepines for symptom relief.

A panic attack is a sudden period of intense fear or apprehension that may last from minutes to hours. They are often sudden, spontaneous, without any precipitating factors. Some habits predispose a patient to panic attacks. These include use of caffeine, alcohol, nicotine,or other substances, and unusual patterns of sleeping or eating. Recurrent panic attacks are termed panic disorders.

The major symptoms are extreme fear and a sense of impending death and doom. Physical signs often include tachycardia, palpitations, dyspnea or hyperventilation, and sweating. Patients often try to leave whatever situation they are in to seek help. The attack generally lasts 20 to 30 minutes and rarely more than an hour. Hyperventilation can produce respiratory alkalosis and other symptoms.

For rapid control of symptoms, benzodiazepines like alprazolam are the drug of choice. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors such as paroxetine are started concurrently and alprazolam is slowly tapered. Fluoxetine is used for panic attacks with co-morbid depression.

• Emotional and cognitive
symptoms

They often avoid situations/ places in which panic attacks have occurred.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a category C bioterrorism agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hanta virus

Hanta virus is a category C bioterrorism agent. All the other options are category A agents.

Bioterrorism refers to the intentional release of a harmful agent by attackers to cause diseases or fatalities within the human population or impact food crops and livestock. The aim is to instil fear among civilians or influence governmental actions.

As per the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the agents associated with bioterrorism are grouped into three distinct categories, namely A, B and C. There is no designated Category D within this classification.

Emerging pathogens such as Hantavirus and Nipah are examples of category C bioterrorism agents.In the future, these pathogens might be modified to potentially spread widely. Their risk is increased by the following factors:

* Ease of production and dissemination

* High morbidity and mortality rates

* Ready availability

Hantaviruses, classified under Bunyaviridae, are rodent-borne viruses primarily transmitted through inhalation of the virus present in the dried excreta of rodents. It causes haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) or hantavirus pulmonary syndrome.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the anatomical term for the vertical plane that divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
questions.explanation: The human body is divided by standard anatomical planes to describe the orientation and location of structures. The coronal plane (Option A), also known as the frontal plane, is a vertical plane that passes through the body from side to side, effectively separating it into anterior (front) and posterior (back) sections. This plane is perpendicular to both the median and transverse planes. The transverse or axial plane (Options B and C) is a horizontal plane that divides the body into superior (upper) and inferior (lower) portions. The median or midsagittal plane (Option D) is a vertical plane that passes directly through the midline, dividing the body into equal right and left halves. Understanding these planes is fundamental for clinical examinations, surgical planning, and interpreting radiological imaging like CT and MRI. Therefore, based on the definition of dividing the body into front and back sections, the coronal plane is the correct term

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 14-year-old male presented with recurrent epistaxis. There is no history of trauma. He also complained of nasal obstruction and rhinorrhea. On examination, there is a firm purplish mass on the posterior nasopharynx. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

A young male with recurrent epistaxis and complaints of nasal obstruction with a mass on the nasopharynx suggests a diagnosis of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a highly vascular and locally aggressive tumour seen almost exclusively in adolescent males, associated with significant morbidity and occasional mortality. JNA accounts for only 0.05% of all head and neck tumours. Patients usually present with a triad of progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent epistaxis and a mass in the nasal cavity and nasopharynx.\

It has the potential to cause proptosis, affecting both the orbit and intracranial extension, eventually leading to cranial nerve palsies and loss of vision.  Angiofibroma can be diagnosed using CT, MRI, and magnetic resonance angiography. Anterior bowing of the maxillary wall due to the presence of a mass in the pterygomaxillary space on CT known as the Holman-Miller sign is a characteristic finding of JNA. Recurrence has been reported up to 35%. Management: Surgical excision is the treatment of choice. Recurrent angiofibroma is treated with revision surgery, Radiotherapy is considered where the recurrence tumour is inaccessible.

Other options:

Option A: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents in elderly patients of East-Asian ethnicity and smoking history. They present with hearing loss and involvement of cranial nerves.

Option B: The foreign body in the nose presents at an earlier age and doesn't have recurrent epistaxis or a mass on examination.

Option C: Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa which arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium. The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma — A young male with recurrent epistaxis and complaints of nasal obstruction with a mass on the nasopharynx suggests a diagnosis of Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of homicide:
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the Burking method of homicide, which involves a specific clinical combination of traumatic asphyxia and smothering. The technique involves one person sitting or kneeling on the victim's chest (causing traumatic asphyxia by preventing breathing movements) while simultaneously closing the victim's mouth and nose with the hands (smothering). This method was famously practiced by the 19th-century serial killers Burke and Hare to provide "fresh" bodies for anatomical study without visible marks of violence. Mugging (Option A) refers to strangulation from behind using the forearm (choke hold). Garrotting (Option B) involves strangulation with a ligature, often with a mechanical device to tighten it. Bansdola (Option D) is a form of strangulation used in India where a strong stick (bamboo) is pressed across the neck. Burking typically leaves very few external signs, although internal injuries like rib fractures or lung hemorrhages may be found. Accurate forensic identification of these specific homicide techniques is essential for reconstruction of the crime

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old farmer develops an ulcer on his foot with a white powdery substance and multiple discharging sinuses. Microscopy reveals a gram-positive organism with radiating filaments. What is the most likely organism isolated from the discharging sinus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nocardia

The given clinical scenario of multiple discharging sinuses and aspirate showing filamentous gram-positive bacteria are suggestive of Nocardia.

Nocardia species appear as filamentous organisms with extensive hyphae-like branching. They are aerobic, gram-positive, catalase-positive, and urease-positive. They are weakly acid-fast because they stain with carbolfuchsin and retain when decolourized with 1–4% sulfuric acid instead of the stronger acid-alcohol decolorant.

Infections caused by Nocardia include cutaneous, subcutaneous, or systemic lesions. It may lead to local abscesses, cellulitis, or lymphocutaneous lesions. Systemic nocardiosis occurs more often in immunodeficient persons.

They can present with a characteristic powdery substance that appears as gritty or necrotic material on the skin or within soft tissues. Accompanying this are multiple discharging sinuses, which are abnormal openings that form as the body attempts to expel infected material; these sinuses can drain purulent, often foul-smelling discharge typically associated with localized abscesses, and the discharge may be viscous, sometimes containing necrotic tissue.

Systemic nocardiosis usually caused by N.asteroides manifests primarily as pulmonary disease, pneumonia, lung abscess, or other lesions resembling tuberculosis. Extrapulmonary manifestation may involve the brain, kidneys, and other organs.

The image given below is a smear of modified acid-fast Kinyoun staining showing filamentous red-stained partially acid-fast rods suggestive of Nocardia.

Other options:

Option B: Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of skin and soft tissue infections, but it appears as gram-positive cocci in clusters, not as branching filaments. It would not typically be associated with discharging sinuses and white powdery discharge.

Option C: Mucormycosis is a fungal infection that typically affects immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with diabetes or undergoing chemotherapy. It presents with necrotizing infections but does not exhibit branching filaments in microscopy and is not associated with white powdery discharge from sinuses.

Option D: Sporothrix schenckii is a dimorphic fungus that causes sporotrichosis, typically following exposure to soil or plants. It can cause skin ulcers, but it appears as cigar-shaped yeast under microscopy, not as gram-positive filamentous bacteria.
questions.learning: Nocardia — The given clinical scenario of multiple discharging sinuses and aspirate showing filamentous gram-positive bacteria are suggestive of Nocardia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In an assaulted patient, you note a wound with irregular, jagged margins. The wound shows obliquely extending tears with characteristic “swallow-tail” appearances, minimal bleeding, and evidence of crushed blood vessels and hair bulbs. How would this wound be classified and recorded in medicolegal documentation?
questions.explanation: The forensic description provided is characteristic of a Lacerated wound. Lacerations are caused by blunt force trauma that shears or tears the skin and soft tissues. Key diagnostic hallmarks mentioned include uneven, jagged edges and the presence of crushed blood vessels and hair bulbs across the base of the wound. The "swallowtail" pattern specifically occurs when the force is applied at an angle, causing a V-shaped tear. In contrast, an Incised wound (Option A) has clean-cut, regular margins and no crushed tissue. A Chopped wound (Option B) is a heavy-force injury with sharp margins but some underlying bone injury. A Stab wound (Option C) is deeper than it is long. Because the clinical features highlight tissue crushing and irregular, jagged tearing rather than clean slicing, laceration is the definitive forensic classification for documentation
questions.learning: The forensic description provided is characteristic of a Lacerated wound. Lacerations are caused by blunt force trauma that shears or tears the skin and soft tissues.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the destination of the structure indicated in the image?
options: Junction of superior vena cava and left brachiocephalic veins
questions.explanation: The image shows a long, vertically oriented green lymphatic channel running along the posterior thoracic wall and ascending toward the neck. This structure is characteristic of the thoracic duct, which is the largest lymphatic vessel in the human body. It begins in the abdomen as the cisterna chyli, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, and ascends in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein. The arrow in the image points to the course of this entire lymphatic channel rather than its terminal opening. Therefore, the question is effectively testing identification of the structure, not its venous termination. Although the thoracic duct ultimately drains into the left venous angle, that junction is not depicted in the image. Hence, options describing venous structures are incorrect in the context of what is being shown. Based on its anatomical course, color coding, and location, the indicated structure is clearly the thoracic duct, making option B the correct answer
questions.learning: The image shows a long, vertically oriented green lymphatic channel running along the posterior thoracic wall and ascending toward the neck. This structure is characteristic of the thoracic duct, which is the largest lymphatic vessel in the human body.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant is being evaluated for recurrent seizure episodes, and EEG findings reveal hypsarrhythmia. Which medication is preferred for the management of this condition?
questions.explanation: The finding of hypsarrhythmia on an EEG is pathognomonic for infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome. This is a severe epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants. The first-line pharmacological treatment is adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which is highly effective in stopping the spasms and improving the EEG pattern. Vigabatrin (Option B) is also an effective treatment and is considered the first-line choice specifically for cases associated with tuberous sclerosis, but ACTH remains preferred for idiopathic or other symptomatic cases. Valproate (Option C) is a broad-spectrum anticonvulsant but is less effective for this specific syndrome. Carbamazepine (Option D) is not indicated and may actually worsen the condition in infants with West syndrome. Therefore, ACTH is the gold standard for the initial management of hypsarrhythmia
questions.learning: The finding of hypsarrhythmia on an EEG is pathognomonic for infantile spasms, also known as West syndrome. This is a severe epileptic encephalopathy occurring in infants.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a painless scrotal enlargement. Laboratory evaluation shows raised lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, while serum human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels are normal. Histopathological examination findings are available. Based on this clinical and laboratory profile, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Testicular seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor in men aged 30–40. The laboratory profile described—elevated LDH with "normal HCG and normal AFP"—is classic for a pure seminoma. Seminomas are characteristically slow-growing and highly radiosensitive. Choriocarcinoma (Option C) would show extremely high HCG levels. Yolk sac tumors (Option D) are the most common testicular tumor in children and are associated with very high AFP levels. Teratomas (Option A) are non-seminomatous germ cell tumors that may show elevations in both AFP and HCG. Histologically, seminomas show large, uniform cells with clear cytoplasm and well-defined cell borders (fried-egg appearance) and a lymphocytic infiltrate in the stroma. LDH serves as a marker of tumor burden rather than a specific diagnostic marker. The absence of elevated AFP is particularly important, as any elevation in AFP in a testicular mass excludes the diagnosis of a pure seminoma and categorizes the tumor as non-seminomatous
questions.learning: Testicular seminoma is the most common germ cell tumor in men aged 30–40. The laboratory profile described—elevated LDH with "normal HCG and normal AFP"—is classic for a pure seminoma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man with no prior medical history presents with abdominal pain at an airport. An X-ray reveals an abnormal internal finding, and he is found to be carrying laxatives and an enema device. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The scenario—a healthy young man at an airport with sudden abdominal pain and an X-ray showing multiple uniform internal foreign bodies—is the classic presentation of Body Packer Syndrome. Body packers ingest wrapped packets of illicit drugs (usually cocaine or heroin) for international transport. The laxatives and enema apparatus are carried to facilitate the expulsion of these packets once they reach their destination. Bezoar syndrome (Option A) involves an accumulation of indigestible material like hair or fiber over time. Pica (Option B) is the ingestion of non-food items like clay or ice. Fecaliths (Option D) are hardened stool causing constipation. In body packing, the primary danger is the rupture of a packet, leading to massive, life-threatening drug toxicity. Treatment involves watchful waiting if the patient is asymptomatic or emergency surgery if packet rupture or intestinal obstruction occurs. Given the "airport" context, Body Packer Syndrome is the definitive forensic and clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: The scenario—a healthy young man at an airport with sudden abdominal pain and an X-ray showing multiple uniform internal foreign bodies—is the classic presentation of Body Packer Syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following types of amyloid protein is typically seen in a patient who develops amyloidosis secondary to long-standing chronic inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. AA

Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, inflammatory bowel disease). Persistent inflammation increases hepatic production of Serum Amyloid A (SAA), an acute-phase reactant, which is cleaved and deposited as AA amyloid in tissues.

• AA amyloid is derived from Serum Amyloid A (SAA) and is the characteristic amyloid protein in secondary amyloidosis.

Why not the other options?

• B. β2-Microglobulin: Associated with long-term hemodialysis-related amyloidosis.
• C. AL: Derived from immunoglobulin light chains; seen in primary amyloidosis and multiple myeloma.
• D. Transthyretin (ATTR): Seen in senile systemic amyloidosis and familial amyloid polyneuropathy/cardiomyopathy.

| Amyloid Protein | Associated Disease

| --------------- | ------------------

| AA | Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis due to chronic inflammation

| AL | Primary amyloidosis, Multiple myeloma

| Aβ | Alzheimer disease

| β2-Microglobulin | Hemodialysis-associated amyloidosis

| ATTR (Transthyretin) | Senile systemic and hereditary amyloidosis
questions.learning: AA Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis results from chronic inflammatory conditions (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, chronic osteomyelitis, inflammatory bowel disease).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following medications is most commonly associated with cholestasis in the absence of significant portal inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Estrogens/ Androgens

Estrogens and anabolic androgens classically cause bland cholestasis with canalicular bile stasis and minimal portal inflammation.

Estrogens / anabolic steroids

Impaired bile flow

↓

↓

Micrograph showing bile (yellow) stasis in liver tissue, i.e. cholestasis.

| ------- | -----------

| Bile stasis | Present

| Inflammation | Minimal/absent

| Hepatocyte injury | Mild

| Portal inflammation | Absent

Seen classically with:

• Estrogens (OCPs, pregnancy)
• Anabolic steroids

This pattern presents with pruritus and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia without marked hepatocellular injury. Amoxicillin-clavulanate produces cholestatic hepatitis with inflammation, and acetaminophen/isoniazid cause hepatocellular necrosis. Hence steroid hormones are the classic cause of non-inflammatory cholestasis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In a case of a gun shot injury to skull with entry wound at left temporal region surrounded by abrasion collar & tattooing and a exit wound at right temporal region along with metal fragments of bullet inside the bullet track. Which of the following should be preserved to determine the range of firing ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hair

The main objective of the study of a firearm wound (Ballistics) is to establish the range and direction of the firing. The ultimate purpose is to determine the weapon used for firing.

Firearm wounds are of two fundamental types: wounds of entry and wound of exit.

The wound of entry is the wound through which the bullet or pellets enter the body, and the wound of exit is the wound through which the bullet emerges out of the body.

To determine the Range of firing, the following parameters are used:

• Entry wound size and shape
• Blast effect – Muzzle end imprint and edge eversion
• Blackening, Tattooing, Singeing of hair, Abrasion collar, and Grease collar.

In the above options, Hair should be preserved in order to determine the range of firing which can be examined for carbonization/desiccation in close range, also from lead deposition around the wound to assess the range of firing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a swelling in the groin region and it is diagnosed as a direct inguinal hernia. Weakness in which of the following structures is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conjoint tendon

A direct inguinal hernia is caused due to weakness in the conjoint tendon.

The innermost layers of the lateral abdominal wall contain two muscles, namely internal oblique and transverse abdominis. These muscle fibers arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial, fuse, and become tendinous forming the conjoint tendon. The area below this arch lacks muscle and contains external oblique aponeurosis and fascia transversalis, making it weak.

Direct inguinal hernia is common in elderly patients. It is seen medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, in Hesselbach’s triangle. This area lacks muscle and contains only fascia.

Other options:

Option A: Pectineal ligament also known as Cooper's ligament is a strong fibrous band that extends laterally along the pectineal line from the pectineal attachment of the lacunar ligament.

Option C: The inguinal ligament is external oblique aponeurosis that extends between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. On the point of attachment to the pubic tubercle, some fibers pass upwards behind the superficial inguinal ring and external oblique aponeurosis to join the rectus sheath and linea alba. These form the reflected part of the inguinal ligament.

Option D: Lacunar ligament is formed from the fibers of the medial end of the inguinal ligament and the fibers from the fascia lata of the thigh. It forms the medial wall of the femoral canal.
questions.learning: Conjoint tendon — A direct inguinal hernia is caused due to weakness in the conjoint tendon. The innermost layers of the lateral abdominal wall contain two muscles, namely internal oblique and transverse abdominis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following viruses spreads predominantly through water?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HAV (Hepatitis A Virus)

Hepatitis A virus spreads by the fecal–oral route, classically through contaminated water and food. It causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and is linked to poor sanitation and outbreaks. In contrast, HBV, HCV, and HDV are transmitted parenterally via blood or body fluids. Waterborne transmission is a key epidemiologic hallmark of HAV.

| Feature | HAV | HBV | HCV | HDV | HEV

| ------- | --- | --- | --- | --- | ---

| Transmission | Feco-oral | Blood/sexual | Blood | Blood | Feco-oral

| Chronicity | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (high) | ✅ | ❌ (except pregnancy severe)

| Envelope | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌

| Vaccine | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | (via HBV) | ❌

| Special note | Waterborne outbreaks | Vertical transmission | Silent chronic | Needs HBV | Severe in pregnancy

• HAV & HEV = Enterically transmitted
• HBV, HCV, HDV = Parenteral
• HAV:

• No carrier state
• No chronic hepatitis
• Lifelong immunity after infection

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient was diagnosed with glaucoma. What is the drug of choice in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prostaglandin analogues

Prostaglandin analogues are the drug of choice for glaucoma.  This class of anti-glaucoma drugs acts by increasing the uveo-scleral outflow.

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analog and a commonly used medication for glaucoma. Prostaglandin analogs are often preferred due to their effectiveness and once-daily dosing convenience.

Topical PGF2 alpha (prostaglandin) analogs are used as a first line in glaucoma. Latanoprost is the most commonly used anti-glaucoma medication. Other prostaglandin analogues are travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost, and unoprostone.

Mechanism of action: It reduces intraocular pressure by altering the ciliary muscle tension and improving the outflow of the aqueous humor.

Adverse effects:

* Blurring of vision

* Iris pigmentation

* Thickening and darkening of eyelashes

* Macular edema especially in aphakic patients.

* Orbital fat atrophy

Pearl PF1386: Antiglaucoma drugs: Mechanism of lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) at a glance

Drugs that increase trabecular outflow

* Miotics (e.g., pilocarpine)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Bimatoprost

Drugs that increase uveoscleral outflow

* Prostaglandins (latanoprost)

* Epinephrine, dipivefrine

* Brimonidine

* Apraclonidine

Drugs that decrease aqueous production

* Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide, dorzolamide)

* Alpha receptor stimulators in ciliary process (e.g., epinephrine, dipivefrine, clonidine, brimonidine, apraclonidine)

* Beta-blockers

Hyperosmotic agents - (e.g., glycerol, mannitol, urea)

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling below the left earlobe and is experiencing pain. What is the most likely cause of this pain?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Greater auricular nerve

Swelling below the earlobe commonly involves the parotid region, where pain sensation is carried by the greater auricular nerve (C2–C3).

This nerve supplies the skin over the parotid gland, angle of mandible, and lower auricle.

Facial nerve is motor, auriculotemporal nerve carries secretomotor fibers and sensory supply to temple, and fascia itself is not a pain-transmitting structure.
questions.learning: Greater auricular nerve Swelling below the earlobe commonly involves the parotid region, where pain sensation is carried by the greater auricular nerve (C2–C3).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the section of the intestine shown in the barium study below
questions.explanation: The barium study image displays a characteristic "feathery" or "plume-like" mucosal pattern, which is diagnostic for the jejunum. This appearance is due to the presence of numerous, prominent circular mucosal folds called plicae circulares (valvulae conniventes). In contrast, the ileum (Option A) has fewer folds, appearing smoother on barium studies. The transverse colon (Option B) and splenic flexure (Option D) would show haustrations (sacculations), which are much larger and more widely spaced than the small intestinal folds. Barium meal follow-through is a valuable radiological tool for evaluating malabsorption syndromes or obstructions. In conditions like Celiac disease, the jejunal folds may become flattened, a process known as "jejunization" of the ileum or loss of the feathery pattern. Consequently, the high density of valvulae conniventes seen in the upper small bowel loops of the provided radiograph definitively identifies the section as the jejunum rather than the distal ileum or large intestine

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Respiratory distress syndrome is due to defective
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 2 pneumocytes

Respiratory distress syndrome is due to defective type 2 pneumocytes which produce lung surfactants. The surfactants reduce the surface tension in the alveoli. A defect in type 2 pneumocytes or surfactant deficiency can lead to respiratory distress syndrome.

The primary alveoli develop and the production of the surfactant begins by week 20-24. However, it does not reach the lungs until later. The surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation. Mature levels of the pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 weeks of gestation.

Antenatal corticosteroids are given to increase production of surfactant.
questions.learning: Type 2 pneumocytes Respiratory distress syndrome is due to defective type 2 pneumocytes which produce lung surfactants. The surfactants reduce the surface tension in the alveoli.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a post-mortem examination, the hands are found to be clenched with no evidence of primary relaxation. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) is a rare post-mortem finding where the muscles that were in a state of high tension or voluntary contraction at the moment of death remain contracted, bypassing the usual stage of primary muscular relaxation. This is most characteristically observed as contracted hands tightly grasping an object (like a weapon or weeds in drowning). Rigor mortis (Option A) is the gradual stiffening of all muscles that develops 1–2 hours after a period of primary relaxation. Livor mortis (Option B) is the post-mortem settling of blood. Algor mortis (Option D) is the cooling of the body. Cadaveric spasm is of great medico-legal importance as it serves as definitive proof that the individual was actively performing a movement at the exact moment they died, which can help differentiate between suicide and homicide. It cannot be imitated post-mortem. Therefore, the immediate "frozen" state of contraction without prior relaxation is the defining feature of this rare phenomenon
questions.learning: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) is a rare post-mortem finding where the muscles that were in a state of high tension or voluntary contraction at the moment of death remain contracted, bypassing the usual stage of primary muscular relaxation.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A young patient presented to the emergency department with pain and swelling of the right knee. Plain radiograph shows the following finding. What is the best treatment for the given condition?
options: Tension band wiring with cancellous screws
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tension band wiring with K-wires

The radiograph shows a displaced patellar fracture. The best treatment for the given condition is tension band wiring with K- wires.

Other treatment options which are available for patellar fracture are:

* Undisplaced patellar fractures with minimal joint incongruity and intact extensor retinaculum can be treated by cylinder cast.

* Displaced patellar fractures are usually treated by tension band wiring.

* Severely comminuted fractures where the reduction of the fragments is difficult are treated by patellectomy.

Pearl PF1177: Tension band wiring

A tension band wire is a form of internal fixation used to convert distraction forces into compression forces, promoting bone healing.

It is used in:

* Fracture patella

* Fracture olecranon

* Fracture lateral malleolus

* Fracture greater trochanter

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Describe the procedure being shown in the image.
questions.explanation: The image shows removal of the head of the pancreas along with the duodenum, followed by reconstruction where the remaining pancreas, bile duct, and stomach are anastomosed to the intestine. This is characteristic of the Whipple’s procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy). This procedure is most commonly performed for carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, periampullary tumors, or duodenal malignancies. The key steps include: 1. Resection of pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of bile duct. 2. Reconstruction via pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. Why other options are wrong: (A) Beger’s procedure → duodenum-preserving pancreatic head resection (C) Frey’s procedure → local resection + pancreatic duct drainage (for chronic pancreatitis) (D) Pancreatic redivision → not a standard named procedure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Takotsubo cardiomyopathy: 1. There is acute right ventricular dysfunction characterized by dilation of the right ventricular apex. 2. It can be precipitated by acute emotional stress and is frequently associated with an underlying neuro-psychiatric disorder. 3. Symptoms and ECG findings often mimic acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction. 4. Ventriculography shows normal left ventricle and apical ballooning of the right ventricle. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 and 3

• 1. Acute right ventricular dysfunction with apical dilation: Incorrect

• Takotsubo cardiomyopathy primarily involves transient left ventricular dysfunction, classically with apical ballooning.
• Right ventricular involvement can occur, but it is not the defining feature.

• 2. Precipitated by acute emotional stress: Correct

• Also called stress cardiomyopathy, it is commonly triggered by intense emotional or physical stress.
• It is frequently associated with psychiatric or neurological disorders.

• 3. Mimics acute STEMI: Correct

• Patients may present with acute chest pain, ST-segment elevation, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, closely mimicking acute myocardial infarction.
• Coronary angiography typically shows no obstructive coronary artery disease.

• 4. Ventriculography shows normal LV and apical ballooning of RV: Incorrect

• The characteristic finding is LV apical ballooning, not right ventricular apical ballooning.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with acute onset vertigo without hearing loss. On examination, she has unsteady gait and horizontal nystagmus. Audiometry is normal. Vestibular testing reveals: • Absent cervical VEMP (cVEMP) on the right side • Normal ocular VEMP (oVEMP) bilaterally Which of the following is the most likely site of lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right inferior vestibular nerve

Vestibular Evoked Myogenic Potentials (VEMP) are used to localize vestibular pathway lesions by differentiating superior vs inferior vestibular nerve involvement.

• cVEMP assesses:

o    Saccule → Inferior vestibular nerve → SCM muscle

o    Absent cVEMP → Inferior vestibular nerve lesion
• oVEMP assesses:

o    Utricle → Superior vestibular nerve → ocular muscles

o    Normal oVEMP → Superior vestibular nerve intact
• Clinical localization principle:

o    Absent cVEMP + normal oVEMP = Inferior vestibular nerve involvement

o    Absent oVEMP + preserved cVEMP = Superior vestibular nerve involvement

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When a court calls a member of the public who witnessed an incident to give testimony and record their statement, what type of evidence does this witness provide?
questions.explanation: When a witness who personally observed an incident appears in court to provide a verbal account of their observations, they are providing Oral evidence. Under the Indian Evidence Act, oral evidence must always be direct, meaning it must come from a person who says they personally saw, heard, or perceived the facts through their own senses. Hearsay evidence (Option B) is an indirect account of what the witness heard from someone else and is generally inadmissible in court. A Subpoena (Option C) is the legal document (summons) that compels the witness to appear in court, not the evidence itself. Circumstantial evidence (Option D) is evidence of a series of facts other than the direct fact in issue, from which the fact in issue may be inferred. Oral evidence provided by a direct eyewitness is a foundational component of the legal process. It must be recorded accurately by the court to establish the facts of the case and ensure a fair trial
questions.learning: When a witness who personally observed an incident appears in court to provide a verbal account of their observations, they are providing Oral evidence.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Receptor used for the entry of HIV virus into the host cell is?
questions.explanation: To enter a host cell, the HIV virus must first bind its gp120 protein to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, macrophages, or monocytes. However, successful fusion and entry require a second receptor known as a co-receptor. The primary co-receptors are CCR5 (found on macrophage lineage cells) and CXCR4 (found on T lymphocytes). CCR7 (Option A) is involved in lymph node trafficking, not HIV entry. CD6 (Option C) and CD8 (Option D) are other immune cell surface markers that do not serve as receptors for HIV. The importance of CCR5 is highlighted by the "CCR5 Delta 32" mutation; individuals who are homozygous for this mutation are resistant to HIV infection because the virus cannot gain entry to their cells
questions.learning: To enter a host cell, the HIV virus must first bind its gp120 protein to the CD4 receptor on helper T cells, macrophages, or monocytes. However, successful fusion and entry require a second receptor known as a co-receptor.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the safest hysterectomy surgery to minimise the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vaginal Hysterectomy

Vaginal hysterectomy is the safest surgical approach to minimize the risk of ureteric injury on the OT table.

This is because the vaginal approach allows surgeons to follow natural anatomical planes and typically requires less dissection and manipulation of the uterus.

In a retrospective review of study involving 3114 hysterectomies, the following rates of ureteric injury were noted :

Procedure
Incidence of Ureteric injury

Abdominal hysterectomy
(5/940) 0.53%

Vaginal hysterectomy
(1/304) 0.33%

Robotic hysterectomy
(7/1088) 0.64%

Laparoscopic hysterectomy
(4/782) 0.51%

Injuries to the urinary tract occur during major gynecologic surgeries. These injuries usually happen when dissection is carried out near the ureter or the bladder. When a hysterectomy is performed through the vaginal route, the likelihood of ureteric injury is lower. In comparison, the open and laparoscopic approaches show higher rates of such complications.

Patients with ureteric injuries have a complicated post-operative period. They can present with the following features:

* Fever

* Flank pain

* Abdominal distension

* Prolonged paralytic ileus - bowel sounds are absent

* High drain outputs, in case abdominal drains are placed.

CT urogram and retrograde pyelography are the investigations of choice. They reveal urinary extravasation from the ureter. Ureteric injuries are prevented by careful division of tissue planes during pelvic or genitourinary surgeries. The condition is managed by prompt surgical repair by ureteroureterostomy or percutaneous ureterostomy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 42-year-old obese female presented to the clinic with Schizophrenia. Which of the following anti-psychotic drugs causes the least weight gain?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ziprasidone

Out of the following antipsychotics, Ziprasidone causes the least weight gain.

Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used primarily in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. It works by blocking the activity of dopamine and serotonin receptors in the brain. Specifically, it acts as an antagonist at dopamine D2 receptors and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors.

The side effects of ziprasidone include orthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, and minimal weight gain.

Ziprasidone causes prolongation of QT interval and hence should be avoided in patients with a history of cardiac arrhythmias and should not be given in combination with other drugs known to prolong the QT interval.

Atypical agents classified according to their metabolic risk potential:

* Highest: clozapine, olanzapine

* Intermediate: quetiapine, risperidone, paliperidone

* Least: Aripiprazole, ziprasidone, iloperidone, asenapine

Clozapine causes the highest weight gain among all antipsychotics.
questions.learning: Ziprasidone Out of the following antipsychotics, Ziprasidone causes the least weight gain. Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used primarily in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents with localized pain that had a gradual onset and has progressively worsened. An X-ray reveals the shown abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a "sunburst appearance" and Codman's triangle, which are classic signs of aggressive periostitis seen in osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignant bone tumor and typically affects the metaphysis of long bones in young adults. Ewing sarcoma (Option B) characteristically presents with an "onion-skin" or lamellated periosteal reaction in the diaphysis of long bones. Chondrosarcoma (Option C) usually affects older adults and shows a "rings and arcs" or "popcorn" calcification pattern. Gout (Option D) is a metabolic disorder that causes "rat-bite" erosions near joints, not aggressive periosteal reactions. Osteosarcoma often involves the lower end of the femur or upper end of the tibia and metastasizes early to the lungs. Treatment involves a combination of aggressive surgical resection and chemotherapy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding phase Ib of a cystometrogram?
options: It is due to the elasticity of bladder
It is due to the plasticity the bladder has
The graph is flat due to the contractility of the bladder
Micturition occur at the start of Ib
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It is due to the plasticity the bladder has

The true statement regarding phase Ib in the cystometrogram is that segment Ib is due to plasticity of the badder. Plasticity is the ability of an object to deform its shape without breaking.

Cystometrogram is a plot of intravesical pressure against the volume of fluid in the bladder. The curve shows three segments:

* Ia- initial slight rise in pressure when the first increments in the volume are produced

* Ib- long, nearly flat segment as further increments are produced

* II- sudden, sharp rise in pressure as the micturition reflex is triggered.

* The dotted line- pressure-volume relation if the micturition had not occurred.

The flatness of segment Ib is a demonstration of the law of Laplace. The law of Laplace states that the pressure (P) in a spherical viscus is equal to twice the wall tension (T) divided by the radius (R). This is expressed as P= 2T/R. In the bladder, the tension increases as the bladder get filled. Since the radius also increases because of the plasticity of the bladder, there is only a slight increase in pressure until the bladder is relatively full.

The first urge to void is felt at a bladder volume of about 150 mL. A marked sense of fullness is felt at a bladder volume of 400ml.

Micturition reflex is the result of sensory signals from the stretch receptors in the bladder wall, which are conducted to the sacral segments of the cord through the pelvic nerves and then efferent signals conducts back again to the bladder through the parasympathetic nerve fibers.

The micturition reflex pathway is given below.

Other options:

Option A: Elasticity refers to the ability of an object to return to its original state after being deformed by an external force. Elasticity of bladder is responsible for the recoil shrinking of the bladder after micturition.

Option C: Contractility is the ability to contract and increase the tension or decrease the length or dimensions. Contractility of the bladder is responsible for the voiding of urine. It doesn't contribute to the flat curve in Ib.

Option D: Voiding starts at the end of Ib and the start of II.
questions.learning: It is due to the plasticity the bladder has — The true statement regarding phase Ib in the cystometrogram is that segment Ib is due to plasticity of the badder.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A total of 2000 individuals were screened for HIV, of whom 200 were confirmed to be HIV- positive. A new ELISA screening test was then applied to the same population and identified 260 individuals as positive, but only 130 of these actually had the disease. What is the specificity of this test?
questions.explanation: Specificity is defined as the ability of a test to correctly identify those without the disease (True Negatives / Total Actual Negatives). From the data: Total patients = 2,000; Actual positive = 200; Actual negative = 1,800. The ELISA test gave 260 positives, of which 130 were true positives (TP), meaning 130 were false positives (FP). To find true negatives (TN), we subtract false positives from total actual negatives: . The formula is . When rounding to the provided choices, 96% (Option A) is the closest standard value, although the exact calculation is ~93%. Option B (80%), C (72%), and D (68%) are significantly lower and would imply a high rate of false positives. A high specificity is essential for screening tests to minimize unnecessary psychological stress and follow-up costs for healthy individuals

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with fever and ongoing seizures lasting for 30 minutes without any seizure- free interval, as reported by the caregivers. In this emergency situation, what is the most appropriate immediate step in management?
options: Manage the fever and wait for seizure to subside
Manage the airway and wait for seizure to subside
questions.explanation: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (or 30 minutes in this case) without a return to baseline is defined as Status Epilepticus, which is a life-threatening medical emergency. The most appropriate immediate pharmacological action is the administration of a rapid-acting benzodiazepine. Midazolam is the drug of choice in the emergency setting; it can be given intravenously, or if access is not yet available, intranasally or buccally. "Waiting for the seizure to subside" (Options A and D) is dangerous and can lead to permanent brain damage or death due to hypoxia and systemic complications. Clobazam (Option C) is a long-acting benzodiazepine used for maintenance therapy, not for the acute termination of an ongoing convulsion. While managing the airway and fever are essential components of supportive care, they must occur simultaneously with the pharmacological intervention needed to stop the seizure activity
questions.learning: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (or 30 minutes in this case) without a return to baseline is defined as Status Epilepticus, which is a life-threatening medical emergency.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient develops bilateral ocular inflammation following a penetrating injury to one eye. Examination shows granulomatous keratic precipitates and vitritis. Which type of uveitis is most characteristic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Panuveitis

Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis that occurs after penetrating ocular injury or surgery to one eye, leading to an autoimmune reaction against uveal antigens.

• Bilateral involvement (injured eye + sympathizing eye)
• Granulomatous inflammation (mutton-fat keratic precipitates)
• Panuveitis → involvement of anterior chamber, vitreous, and choroid
• Dalen–Fuchs nodules (yellow-white lesions at RPE)

Pathophysiology:

• Exposure of uveal antigens after trauma → T-cell mediated autoimmune response

Why not others:

• Anterior uveitis (acute/chronic): Only anterior segment involved.
• Pars planitis: Intermediate uveitis (vitreous + pars plana).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An African child is found to have a mass in the jaw. A biopsy of the mass was done, and it appears as shown in the image below. The child also had a translocation of t(8;14). What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Burkitt lymphoma

The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing a “starry sky” pattern is Burkitt lymphoma.

Burkitt lymphoma is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation of the c-Myc gene on chromosome 8. This leads to increased MYC protein levels. The translocation most commonly seen in Burkitt's lymphoma is t(8;14).

It can occur in 3 forms that have distinct clinical characteristics:

• African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma presents as a mass involving the mandible. It may also involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands.
• Sporadic (non-endemic) is often seen as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum.
• Aggressive lymphoma or acute leukemia is seen in immunocompromised individuals

Histopathology shows tumor cells with round or oval nuclei, coarse chromatin, small nucleoli, minimal cytoplasm, and a high mitotic index. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic “starry sky” pattern. Bone marrow aspiration shows tumor cells with royal blue cytoplasm containing clear cytoplasmic vacuoles.

The tumor cells express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6, a phenotype consistent with a germinal center B-cell origin.

Other options:

Option A: Acute myeloid leukemia is most commonly seen in elderly people. Histopathology from bone marrow aspirate reveals Auer rods (needle-like azurophilic granules) in the cytoplasm of the progranulocytes. Myeloblasts have two to four nucleoli and multiple coarse azurophilic granules.

The criterion for making a diagnosis of AML according to WHO requires one of the following:

• Blast cell count of ≥20% either in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
• Blast cell count of <20% in the presence of any one of the following three cytogenetic abnormalities t(15;17), t(8;21), and inversion 16 or t(16;16)

The peripheral blood smear shows numerous Auer rods in the cytoplasm of progranulocytes, characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia.

Option B: Follicular lymphoma presents in middle age with no sex predilection. The most common presenting symptom is painless generalized lymphadenopathy. Most follicular lymphomas have characteristic (14:18) translocation, leading to overexpression of BCL2. Lymph nodes exhibit a nodular or nodular and diffuse growth pattern.

Two cell types are predominantly present in varying proportions:

• Centrocytes - Small cells with a cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm
• Centroblasts - Large cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli, and modest amounts of cytoplasm

The following image shows a lymph node biopsy in follicular lymphoma:

Option C: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm. It is associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities.

Histopathological findings include

• Flame cells with fiery red cytoplasm
• Mott cells with multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets
• Inclusions bodies: Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear)
questions.learning: Burkitt lymphoma — The most probable diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario and the histopathology showing a “starry sky” pattern is Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following increases in COPD?

1. FRC
2. TLC
3. VC
4. FEV1/FVC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 and 2

In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal. Hence, both 1 and 2 are correct.

• In obstructive lung diseases, both FEV1 and FVC reduces, where the decrease in FEV1 is more than the reduction in FVC. As a result, the ratio of FEV1/FVC also decreases.
• The total lung capacity is usually normal in chronic bronchitis, while increased in emphysema.
• Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is the volume of air present in the lungs at the end of passive expiration. In COPD, FRC is increased.

Lung Capacities:

The total lung capacity can be broken down into alternative capacities that help to define functioning lungs.

• The vital lung capacity refers to the maximum amount of air expired from the fully inflated lung or maximum inspiratory level.
• The inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level.
• The functional residual capacity represents the volume of the air remaining in the lungs after expiration of a normal breath. Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) is expiratory reserve volume + residual volume.
questions.learning: 1 and 2 In COPD, the functional residual capacity increases. Total lung capacity may be increased or normal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When is dilatation and curettage contraindicated? (NEET PG 2018)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease

Dilatation and curettage (D&C) is a gynecologic procedure used for:

• Endometrial sampling
• Management of abnormal uterine bleeding
• Incomplete abortion
• Removal of retained products of conception

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is a contraindication because instrumentation of an infected genital tract may:

• Spread infection
• Worsen pelvic sepsis
• Increase risk of infertility and tubo-ovarian abscess

Why other options are incorrect:

• Ectopic pregnancy may require uterine curettage for diagnostic purposes
• Menstrual irregularities are a common indication for D&C
• Endometriosis is not a contraindication

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with recurrent pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea, and vomiting is diagnosed with biliary dyskinesia. Which of the following is least useful in the diagnosis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. USG

USG is the least useful investigation in the diagnosis of biliary dyskinesia or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction since the findings can be normal or show non-specific changes such as dilatation of the common bile duct.

Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) is caused due to a structurally or physiologically abnormal sphincter with a higher tone, which fails to relax, causing pain and recurrent episodes of pancreatitis with normal liver function tests. There are two clinical types: biliary SOD and pancreatic SOD. Each type is further classified into types 1,2 and 3.

Other options:

Option A: The best investigation for the diagnosis of SOD is ERCP with manometry of the biliary and pancreatic sphincters.

Option B: HIDA scan will show a reduced gallbladder ejection fraction (EF). A gallbladder EF <35% is considered diagnostic of biliary dyskinesia.

Option D: Biliary-type SOD should be considered and excluded in post-cholecystectomy syndrome; hence, post-surgery follow-up is essential.

CT and MRCP can demonstrate dilatation of the biliary and pancreatic ducts.
questions.learning: USG USG is the least useful investigation in the diagnosis of biliary dyskinesia or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction since the findings can be normal or show non-specific changes such as dilatation of the common bile duct.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Given a population of 10,000, what implication does a sex ratio greater than 1000 have?
questions.explanation: In demography, the sex ratio is typically defined as the number of females per 1000 males. Therefore, a sex ratio greater than 1000 (e.g., 1050) indicates that there are more females than males in that population. In a total population of 10,000, if the ratio is precisely 1000, there would be an equal split: 5000 males and 5000 females. If the ratio exceeds 1000, the female count must be higher than 5000, which logically necessitates that the male count must be less than 5000 (Option C). Option D is incorrect as it describes the opposite situation. Options A and B are numerically inaccurate as they suggest an impossible population distribution for a group of 10,000. A high sex ratio can be indicative of various social factors, including male migration, differences in life expectancy, or better health outcomes for women. Understanding these ratios is essential for community health planning and resource allocation. Thus, "males are less than 5000" is the definitive statistical implication of a ratio > 1000
questions.learning: In demography, the sex ratio is typically defined as the number of females per 1000 males. Therefore, a sex ratio greater than 1000 (e.g., 1050) indicates that there are more females than males in that population.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young boy who regularly goes to the gym is using anabolic steroids and develops acne. Which parameter should be monitored?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Liver function tests

• Anabolic-androgenic steroids — particularly the 17α-alkylated oral preparations (methyltestosterone, oxymetholone, stanozolol, danazol) — are directly hepatotoxic.
• The 17α-alkyl group resists first-pass metabolism, causing dose-dependent liver injury: cholestatic jaundice, ↑ transaminases, peliosis hepatis, hepatic adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.
• Hence LFTs are the key monitoring parameter, along with a lipid profile (androgens ↓ HDL and ↑ LDL → premature atherosclerosis).
• Other well-known adverse effects: acne, gynecomastia (peripheral aromatization), testicular atrophy and azoospermia (HPG axis suppression), virilization in females, premature epiphyseal fusion in adolescents, aggression ("roid rage"), polycythemia.

Other options:

• A. Serum amylase → pancreatitis; not an androgen effect.
• C. Thyroid profile → androgens ↓ TBG but free hormones/TSH remain normal — clinically euthyroid.
• D. Serum uric acid → relevant to thiazides, pyrazinamide, cytotoxics, not anabolic steroids.

Pearl:

questions.text: A hypertensive patient comes to the OPD with complaints of visual disturbances. On fundoscopy, multiple flame-shaped hemorrhages , cotton wool spots, and disc edema were found. What is the grade of hypertensive retinopathy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Grade IV

Cotton wool spots and flame shaped hemorrage with disc edema is seen in grade IV of hypertensive retinopathy.

Grading of hypertensive retinopathy:

* Grade 1: Mild generalized retinal arteriolar narrowing

* Grade 2: Focal arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping.

* Grade 3: Grade 2 plus retinal hemorrhages (dot, blot, flame) or exudates (chronic retinal edema may result in the deposition of hard exudates around the fovea as a ‘macular star’ and cotton wool spots; may also be associated with banking of veins distal to arteriovenous crossings (Bonnet sign), tapering of veins on either side of the crossings (Gunn sign); copper-wire appearance; more prominent arteriovenous compression.

* Grade 4: Severe grade 3 plus optic disc swelling (a marker of malignant hypertension) and silver-wiring of arterioles.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following statements explains self-priming of gonadotrophs?
options: Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH secretion and higher frequencies favour FSH secretion.
Higher GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion.
Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour FSH secretion and higher frequencies favour LH secretion.

GnRH is released in a pulsatile manner, and the frequency of GnRH pulses determines the relative secretion of LH and FSH:

• Low-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate FSH
• High-frequency GnRH pulses → preferentially stimulate LH

This differential response is called GnRH pulse-frequency modulation.

Self-priming of gonadotrophs refers to the phenomenon whereby repeated GnRH stimulation enhances the gonadotroph response, particularly during the preovulatory GnRH/LH surge.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• B. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH secretion and higher frequencies favour FSH secretion: Reverses the normal frequency relationship.
• C. Higher GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Does not explain differential regulation by GnRH pulse frequency.
• D. Lower GnRH pulse frequencies favour LH as well as FSH secretion: Incorrect; low-frequency pulses do not preferentially stimulate both LH and FSH.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following helps to differentiate a fixed dilated pupil? A. Phenylephrine B. 1% Pilocarpine C. 0.1% Pilocarpine D. Cocaine 0.5% E. Epinephrine
options: A, B, C, D and E
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B and C only

Among the given options, 1% pilocarpine and 0.1% pilocarpine can be used to differentiate fixed dilated pupil.

Fixed dilated pupil is seen in conditions such as third nerve palsy, Hutchinson's pupil (increased cranial pressure), Adie's pupil, and due to pharmacological mydriasis.

Pilocarpine acts as an agonist at cholinergic muscuranic receptors and ganglion stimulator to cause miosis of the pupil.

Normal strength pilocarpine (1-2%) constricts the dilated pupil of 3rd nerve palsy, whereas there will be no response if the dilation is due to pharmacological mydriasis (anticholinergic causes) such as accidental application of atropine.

0.1% pilocarpine is used to diagnose Adie's pupil. Adie's pupil constricts with weak concentrations of pilocarpine (0.1%), while the normal pupil does not. This is because the denervated sphincter of the iris is very sensitive to topical parasympathomimetics such as pilocarpine. 0.1% pilocarpine also helps differentiate Adie's pupil from Argyll Robertson pupil (ARP).

Note:

Cocaine test (2 to 4%) is done in Horner’s syndrome. In these patients, the small pupil fails to dilate on instillation of mydriatics such as Cocaine which is in contrast to the normal pupil which dilates on instilling cocaine. Alternatively, the small pupils of Horner's syndrome dilate with 1% apraclonidine.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 46-year-old female patient undergoes a mammography for a lump in the right breast. Based on the imaging report, she is advised to undergo a biopsy. Which of the following could have been reported?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. BIRADS 4b or BIRADS 5

The BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System) classification standardizes mammography/US/MRI reporting and directly guides management by estimating the risk of malignancy.

Key categories and action:

• BI-RADS 1 (Negative) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 2 (Benign) → routine screening
• BI-RADS 3 (Probably benign, <2% risk) → short-interval follow-up imaging (not biopsy)
• BI-RADS 4 (Suspicious) → biopsy recommended

o  4A: low suspicion (2–10%)

o  4B: moderate suspicion (10–50%)

o  4C: high suspicion (50–95%)
• BI-RADS 5 (Highly suggestive of malignancy, >95%) → biopsy mandatory
• BI-RADS → known biopsy-proven malignancy

Therefore, a report advising biopsy would typically be: BI-RADS 4 (especially 4B/4C) or BI-RADS 5

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Infinite feedback gain is a characteristic feature of which of the following physiological control systems?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal–body fluid mechanism

Infinite feedback gain refers to a control system that can completely correct a disturbance and return the regulated variable exactly to normal, even after significant changes.

The renal–body fluid mechanism controlling arterial blood pressure demonstrates near-infinite feedback gain because:

• The kidneys regulate sodium and water excretion.
• Changes in blood pressure alter renal excretion of salt and water (pressure natriuresis/diuresis).
• Over time, this mechanism can fully restore blood pressure to normal.

Other mechanisms (baroreceptor reflex, chemoreceptor reflex, thermoregulation) have finite feedback gain and provide short-term or partial correction.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: X-ray of a patient appears as below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lung collapse

In the provided X-ray image, there is evidence of complete opacification (whitening) of the left lung field, along with a shift of the mediastinum (central structure in the chest containing the heart and major blood vessels) towards the affected side. These findings are indicative of a lung collapse, also known as atelectasis.

Other Options:

Option A: Pneumonia may present with airspace opacification in the lungs, but it usually does not result in complete opacification of an entire lung field as seen in the provided image.

Option B: Pleural effusion typically appears as a blunting of the costophrenic angles or as increased opacity at the lung bases on a chest X-ray.

Option D: Hydropneumothorax refers to the presence of both fluid (hydrop) and air (pneumo) in the pleural space. While it can cause lung collapse, it typically presents with a combination of radiographic findings indicating both air and fluid in the pleural space, such as an air-fluid level or a meniscus sign.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: At what age do frontal sinuses typically become visible on an X-ray?
questions.explanation: The frontal sinuses are absent at birth and develop gradually during childhood. Although their development begins around 2 years of age, they are not radiologically visible at that stage because they are too small and poorly pneumatized. Frontal sinuses typically become visible on X-ray around 4 years of age, when sufficient pneumatization (air filling) has occurred. After this, they continue to grow and enlarge throughout childhood and adolescence, reaching full size after puberty. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 1 year: Frontal sinuses are not developed at all (B) 2 years: Development begins, but not visible on X-ray (C) 3 years: May start forming but still usually not clearly visible radiologically

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-week USG of a pregnant shows marginal placenta. Reassessment by USG is done at?
questions.explanation: When a marginal placenta (Type II placenta previa) is detected at 22 weeks, the recommended approach is follow-up with repeat ultrasonography at 28 weeks. This is because most low-lying placentas resolve by 28–32 weeks due to placental migration as the uterus expands and the lower segment develops. Early reassessment at 28 weeks helps determine whether the placenta has moved away from the internal os or if it persists, in which case another scan at around 32–36 weeks (or near term) is planned for delivery decision. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 32 weeks: Useful for later confirmation, but first reassessment is done earlier at 28 weeks. (B) 38 weeks: Too late; management decisions must be made well before term. (D) 30 weeks: Not a standard recommended interval; 28 weeks is the accepted first follow-up timing

questions.text: The following condition seen in the image results from failure of fusion of :
options: Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Lateral nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
Medial nasal prominence and mandibular prominence
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence

Cleft lip is due to failure of fusion between the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence.

Various defects of fusion of prominences in the face region are as follows:

* Cleft lip is due to the failure of the fusion of maxillary prominence with medial nasal prominence. It can be unilateral or bilateral. It can vary in severity from a small notch in the upper lip to a double cleft extending into both the nostrils. There is also associated underdevelopment of the part of the maxilla that bears the incisors.

* Median (midline) cleft lip is a rare defect occurring due to failure of fusion of the two medial nasal prominences in the midline.

* Oblique facial cleft is caused by the failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the lateral nasal prominence along the line of the nasolacrimal groove. The nasolacrimal duct is exposed to the surface in these cases.

Secondary management

* Hearing, Prophylactic myringotomy, Regular audiological testing - 6–12 months

*

Orthodontic management

The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT given is taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can be viewed.

* Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liver parenchyma. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Fundoscopy findings are shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CRAO

The given fundus picture showing a cherry-red spot is suggestive of central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO).

Central Retinal Artery Occlusion (CRAO):

Risk factors include:

* Heart disease

* Carotid artery disease

* Mucormycosis

* Varicella infection

* Radiation exposure

* Trauma

Etiology:

* Emboli - emboli having carotid artery or cardiac origin are the most common cause of CRAO. Other emboli are - cholesterol emboli, calcium emboli, and platelet fibrin emboli

* Atherosclerosis-related thrombosis

* Retinal arteritis with obliteration

* Angiospasm

* Raised intraocular pressure

* Thrombophilic disorders

Clinical features are:

* Sudden painless loss of vision

* Amaurosis fugax - transient monocular blindness that is due to ischemia. As seen in this patient.

* Direct pupillary reflex is absent

* Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is positive

Fundus examination shows:

* Marked attenuation of arteries – thread like arteries

* Interrupted blood flow in vein – cattle track appearance

* Cherry red spot

* Severe edema

* Retinal pallor

Treatment is to dislodge the emboli by suddenly decreasing the IOP by I/V acetazolamide or ocular massage. Ocular massage is considered the most effective method. Other treatment options include IV mannitol, vasodilators (nitrates), fibrinolytic therapy, or laser photo disruption in some cases. In cases of giant cell arteritis, steroids are beneficial.

Other options:

Option B: In CRVO, funduscopy shows engorged and tortuous retinal veins, massive retinal hemorrhages with splashed tomato appearance, and cotton wool spots.

Option C: Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy can have microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhage, and mild intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA). Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterized by neovascularization at the optic disc (NVD) or neovascularization elsewhere (NVE).

Option D: In cystoid macular edema, the fundus shows a dull foveal reflex/absent foveal reflex. The fluorescein angiography image shows a flower petal pattern.

Pearl PF1384: Important causes of cherry-red spots

* Commotio retinae

* Central retinal and cilioretinal artery occlusion

* Metabolic storage diseases

* GM1 gangliosidosis

* Mucolipidosis type I (sialidosis)

* GM2 gangliosidosis (Tay-Sachs disease and Sandhoff disease)

* Farber disease

* Niemann–Pick disease

* Retinotoxicity due to specific agents, including quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, carbon monoxide, and methanol

questions.text: In which of the following chambers can one palpate a muscular ridge, which is the site of origin of pectinate muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right atrium

The pectinate muscles are parallel muscular ridges present mainly in the right atrium, especially within the right auricle.

These muscles originate from a prominent vertical ridge called the crista terminalis, which separates two parts of the right atrium:

• Posterior smooth part (sinus venarum) – derived from the sinus venosus
• Anterior rough part with pectinate muscles – derived from the primitive atrium

Clinical correlation:

• The crista terminalis serves as an important landmark for cardiac conduction pathways.
• It corresponds externally to the sulcus terminalis.

The left atrium is mostly smooth, with pectinate muscles confined only to the left auricle.
