questions.text: The image shows the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve plotted during different conditions. Which among the following conditions would result in curve D?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acidosis

The oxygen hemoglobin curve denoted by the curve D will be observed during Acidosis.

Conditions that cause a right shift (C->D) in the oxygen hemoglobin curve are: (Conditions with the increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

* Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - Metabolically active tissues utilize O2 and tissues produce CO2

* ↓ pH (Acidosis)- Secondary to increased CO2 production.

* ↑ in temperature, heat

* ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis

Conditions that cause a left shift (B <-C)  in the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve are:

* Decreased carbon dioxide (hypocarbia) (Option B)

* ↑ pH of the blood

* ↓ in the temperature of the body (hypothermia) (Option A)

* ↓ in 2,3-DPG (Option C)

* Fetal hemoglobin

Curve A represents the Myoglobin-O2 binding curve. It is a rectangular hyperbola (unlike a sigmoid curve of Oxy-hemoglobin curve). This is because it only has a single oxygen binding site. It is present in muscle in large amounts and can provide oxygen to muscles even at low blood oxygen levels.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a type 2 diabetes mellitus patient, serum insulin levels are found to be raised. He is advised to exercise to improve insulin resistance. Which of the following GLUT will help to improve insulin resistance after exercise ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. GLUT 4

There is an increase in the number of GLUT 4 receptors in response to exercise. This increases the insulin dependent glucose uptake into the cells, contributing to a decrease in insulin resistance.

GLUT-4 is an insulin-dependent GLUT. Other GLUTs are not insulin-sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane.

Insulin resistance is a condition in which the cells in muscles, fat, and liver are less responsive to insulin and have difficulty absorbing glucose from the blood. The pancreas then produces more insulin to facilitate the entry of glucose into the cells.

An arbitrary but clinically useful benchmark considers patients insulin resistant if they require greater than 1 unit/kilogram/day of exogenous insulin to maintain glycemic control. Patients requiring greater than 200 units of exogenous insulin per day are considered severely insulin resistant.

Other options

Option A:  GLUT 1 receptors are present in the red blood cell, brain, kidney, colon, retina, and placenta. It is responsible for glucose uptake.

Option B: GLUT-2 is found in the liver, pancreatic β cell, small intestine, and kidney. Its function is the rapid uptake or release of glucose.

Option C: GLUT-5 is present in the small intestine and is involved in the absorption of fructose.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 8-year-old child presents with eneuresis. The parents mention the child had a fall from bed once but has no other significant medical history. There are no signs of urinary tract infections or neurological deficits. What is the best next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Behavioural modification

Primary nocturnal enuresis in children is most often a benign, functional condition and is managed initially with non-pharmacological measures.

• Diagnosis is clinical after ruling out UTI, diabetes, and neurological causes
• Most children have normal bladder function and outgrow the condition

First-line management:

• Behavioral modification:
• Limit evening fluid intake
• Timed voiding before sleep
• Positive reinforcement (reward system)
• Enuresis alarm (most effective long-term)

Pharmacological therapy:

• Desmopressin or anticholinergics are reserved for refractory cases or specific indications

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A healthcare provider is evaluating the effectiveness of a new diagnostic test for early-stage pancreatic cancer. The test has been reported to have a sensitivity of 85% and a specificity of 95%. In a population where the prevalence of early-stage pancreatic cancer is 5%, what is the probability that a person who tests positive actually has the disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 47%

The probability that a person with a positive test actually has the disease is called the Positive Predictive Value (PPV). PPV depends on:

• Sensitivity
• Specificity
• Disease prevalence (very important)

Formula: PPV = True Positives / {True Positives + False Positives}

Using a hypothetical population of 1000:

• Prevalence = 5% → Diseased = 50, Non-diseased = 950
• Sensitivity = 85%

• True positives = 85% of 50 = 42.5
• False negatives = 7.5

• Specificity = 95%

• True negatives = 95% of 950 = 902.5
• False positives = 47.5

Now:

• PPV =  42.5 / ( 42.5 + 47.5) =  42.5 / 90 = approx 47%
• In low-prevalence diseases, even highly specific tests can have a relatively low PPV due to increased false positives. Increasing prevalence increases PPV and decreases NPV.

The image depicts cobalt blue filter, fluorescein dye and corneal ulcer.
Corneal ulcers can be detected with the help of fluorescein sodium dye and a cobalt blue filter. Fluorescein staining of the cornea is carried out with a disposable autoclaved filter paper strip impregnated with the dye. The denuded epithelial area seen in corneal abrasions or ulcers appears brilliant green when stained with fluorescein. The epithelial defect of the cornea appears opaque green with a cobalt blue filter.

Corneal epithelial lesions are visualised using vital dye staining techniques. Dyes used are:

1. Fluorescein - to delineate areas with epithelial damage. Fluorescein Staining is shown below.

2. Rose Bengal - Stain diseased and devitalised cells. Rose bengal staining is shown below.

3. Alcian Blue - Stains excess mucus selectively.
Other options :

Option C : Lissamine green dye is used to stain devitalized cells of the cornea and conjunctiva. It is used to diagnose ocular surface disorders, like dry eye.

Option D : Interstitial keratitis is a form of non ulcerative keratitis. It is a non suppurative inflammation of the corneal stroma without primary involvement of the epithelium or endothelium. It is characterized by cellular infiltration of the corneal stroma. Some causes of interstitial keratitis include herpes simplex virus, syphilis, cogan syndrome and rheumatoid arthritis.

Slit-lamp examination of the cornea and conjunctiva after rose bengal staining reveals punctuate corneal ulcerations and attached filaments of corneal epithelium in keratoconjunctivitis sicca. The image attached below sums up the various patterns of staining and their diagnostic utility.

questions.text: Patient presents with cough, stridor, and dyspnea. On examination, there was lymphadenopathy. Histopathological examination of the lymph node shows granulomas with giant cells and stellate concretions. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sarcoidosis

Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells containing stellate concretions (asteroid bodies) are characteristic of sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis commonly presents with lymphadenopathy and airway involvement causing cough, stridor, and dyspnea.

• Non-caseating granulomas
• Epithelioid histiocytes
• Inclusion bodies:

• ⭐ Asteroid bodies (stellate)
• Schaumann bodies (calcified)

Schaumann body

Asteroid bodies (stellate)

Tuberculosis shows caseating granulomas, while hypersensitivity pneumonitis and Churg–Strauss lack asteroid bodies.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young woman reports a history of unprotected intercourse four days ago and requests emergency contraception. Which option is most appropriate in this situation?
questions.explanation: For a woman requesting emergency contraception up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected intercourse, the most effective and suitable option is the insertion of a Copper Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD). The Copper T IUCD has a failure rate of less than 0.1% and provides the added benefit of ongoing, long-term reversible contraception. Levonorgestrel (LNG) (Option A) is very effective but its efficacy drops significantly if taken more than 72 hours after intercourse. OCPs (Option C) used in the "Yuzpe regimen" are less effective and cause more side effects than LNG or IUCD. Misoprostol (Option D) is used for medical abortion, not for emergency contraception. While oral medications like Ulipristal acetate are also effective up to 5 days, the IUCD remains the "gold standard" for efficacy regardless of the timing within the 5-day window or the patient's body mass index. Clinicians must offer the IUCD to all women seeking emergency contraception as it is the only method that offers near-perfect protection
questions.learning: For a woman requesting emergency contraception up to 5 days (120 hours) after unprotected intercourse, the most effective and suitable option is the insertion of a Copper Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD).

questions.explanation:

The above picture shows a red coloured bag which is used to dispose contaminated wastes (recyclable) such as tubing, bottles, intravenous tubes and sets, catheters, urine bags, syringes (without needles) and gloves.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which findings are suggestive of tubal pregnancy?
options: Ovarian mass with single layer of endometrium
Adnexal mass with empty uterus and fluid in pelvis
questions.explanation: A tubal (ectopic) pregnancy is suspected when a patient presents with abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test, but without an intrauterine gestational sac. The most suggestive ultrasound finding is an adnexal mass (the ectopic sac) in the presence of an empty uterus. The additional finding of fluid in the pelvis (Pouch of Douglas) significantly increases the suspicion of a ruptured tubal pregnancy or leakage, indicating hemoperitoneum. Regarding the distractors, an ovarian mass (Option A) often represents a corpus luteum cyst rather than an ectopic pregnancy. Option B is suggestive but less definitive than Option D, as pelvic fluid provides critical diagnostic weight. A trilayer endometrium (Option C) is a normal finding in the proliferative phase or early pregnancy and does not indicate an ectopic location. Thus, the combination in Option D is the most classic and serious diagnostic profile
questions.learning: A tubal (ectopic) pregnancy is suspected when a patient presents with abdominal pain and a positive pregnancy test, but without an intrauterine gestational sac.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida is being assessed for induction of labor. Her vaginal examination reveals a midline cervix soft in consistency, cervical length of 5cms, and dilation of 2cms. The head of the baby is at -2 station. What would be her modified Bishop's score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5-unfavorable

The Modified Bishop score in this patient is calculated to be 5, which is unfavourable.

The Bishop score is a scoring system used to assess labor induction outcomes. It is based on the station of the head, dilatation, effacement (or length), position, and consistency of the cervix noted by doing a vaginal examination. In the modified Bishop score (1991), the effacement is replaced by the cervical length in cm.

From the data given in the question:

* The position of the cervix is midline, hence score = 1

* Cervical length is 5 cm, hence score = 0

* Cervical dilatation is 2 cm, hence score = 1

* Consistency of cervix is soft, hence score = 2

* The station of the head is –2, hence score = 1

Hence, the Modified Bishop score is 1+0+1+2+1 = 5.

A score of 0–5 is considered unfavorable, while a score of 6–13 is regarded as favorable.

* According to Williams Obstetrics (26th edition), a score of 9 or more indicates a high likelihood of successful induction.

Pearl PF2186: Indications & contraindications for induction of labor

Indications:

* Uncontrolled maternal diabetes mellitus

* Gestational hypertension

* Pre-eclampsia

* Post-term pregnancy

* Abruption placentae

* Premature rupture of membranes

* Rh-isoimmunization

* Intra-uterine growth restriction (IUGR)

* Intra-uterine death (IUD)

* Oligohydramnios

Contraindications:

* Contracted/distorted pelvis and cephalopelvic disproportion

* Placenta previa or vasa previa

* Active genital herpes

* Pelvic tumor & carcinoma cervix

* Transverse lie or footling breech

* Appreciable macrosomia

* Severe hydrocephalus

* Umbilical cord prolapse

* High-risk pregnancy with fetal compromise

* Previous classical cesarean or hysterotomy

* Previous history of uterine rupture

* Pelvic surgeries like vesicovaginal fistula/rectovaginal fistula/pelvic floor repair (third or fourth-degree perineal tears repair)

* Previous 3 or more lower transverse cesarian sections.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with acute heart failure with pulmonary edema, severe breathlessness and bilateral basal crepitations. Which drug should be administered immediately?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Furosemide

• IV furosemide is the immediate drug of choice in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
• It has a dual benefit: within 5–10 minutes it causes venodilation → ↓ preload → ↓ pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, giving symptomatic relief even before diuresis begins; subsequently it inhibits the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ (NKCC2) cotransporter in the thick ascending limb → brisk diuresis → ↓ volume overload.
• Given IV because gut wall edema impairs oral absorption.

Other options:

• A. Digoxin: Is a positive inotrope with slow onset; useful only in HF with rapid AF — not for acute pulmonary edema rescue.
• C. Mannitol: Is an osmotic diuretic that first expands intravascular volume → will worsen pulmonary edema. Contraindicated here.
• D. Acetazolamide: Is a weak diuretic causing metabolic acidosis; upharsed in altitude sickness/glaucoma, not acute LVF.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with breathlessness and is diagnosed with a Pancoast tumor. Which of the following clinical features is least likely to be associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: A Pancoast tumor is an apical lung cancer that often invades the sympathetic chain, leading to Horner’s syndrome. Horner’s syndrome is characterized by a specific triad: miosis (constricted pupil), ptosis (drooping eyelid), and anhidrosis (loss of sweating) on the affected side. Enophthalmos (a recessed eye) is also frequently seen. Exophthalmos (Option D), which is the bulging or protrusion of the eyeball, is the opposite of enophthalmos and is typically associated with conditions like Graves' disease (thyroid eye disease) or orbital tumors, not sympathetic nerve damage. Anhidrosis (Option A) occurs specifically in preganglionic lesions like Pancoast tumors. Miosis (Option B) results from the loss of sympathetic innervation to the pupillary dilator muscle. Ptosis (Option C) occurs due to paralysis of the superior tarsal (Müller’s) muscle. Therefore, because exophthalmos represents a different pathological mechanism, it is not a finding associated with Pancoast tumor-induced Horner’s syndrome

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Ascites Chronic Diarrhoea
questions.text: Whipple’s disease is characterized by the infiltration of small intestinal mucosa by foamy macrophages. Which one of the following histological stains is characteristically used to stain them?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Periodic acid Schiff

Whipple disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption. The characteristic histopathological finding is the presence of foamy macrophages within the lamina propria that stain strongly positive with Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) due to the accumulation of glycoprotein-rich bacterial cell wall material.

Key points:

• Etiological agent: Tropheryma whipplei
• Histopathology: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant foamy macrophages in the small intestinal lamina propria
• Clinical features: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, weight loss, arthralgia, fever, and lymphadenopathy
• Diagnosis: Duodenal biopsy with PAS staining, confirmed by PCR when required
questions.learning: Periodic acid Schiff Whipple disease is a rare multisystem infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that primarily affects the small intestine, leading to malabsorption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following helps in the transport of fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carnitine

Carnitine is responsible for the transport of fatty acids or long-chain acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Fatty acids are oxidized in the mitochondria to produce acetyl-CoA to produce energy. They must first be converted to acyl-CoA (active fatty acid) before they can be catabolized.

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase - I (CPT- I) transports acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane only in the presence of carnitine. The acyl group of acyl-CoA is transferred to carnitine. The acylcarnitine so formed can penetrate the inner mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. This transporter transfers the acyl group back to CoA, restoring acyl-CoA and liberating carnitine, which is moved back to the intermembrane space. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase -II catalyzes this reaction. The deficiency of this enzyme is a common cause of recurrent myoglobinuria.

Carnitine deficiency can lead to hypoglycemia and restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy. It can also cause hepatic steatosis.

Other options:

Option A - Acyl carrier protein is a component of the fatty acid synthase complex involved in the biosynthesis of fatty acids. It has vitamin pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

Option C - Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is present in the plasma and plays an important role in the esterification of cholesterol. Deficiency leads to low levels of lysolecithin and cholesteryl esters.

Option D - The long-chain fatty acids are bound to albumin in the plasma. But albumin does not transport fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver. It is a carrier for acidic drugs.
questions.learning: Carnitine Carnitine is responsible for the transport of fatty acids or long-chain acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Fatty acids are oxidized in the mitochondria to produce acetyl-CoA to produce energy.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female patient presents to the outpatient department with recurrent, fever-associated lesions on the lips, as shown below. What is the characteristic feature observed on a Tzanck smear in this condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts recurrent vesicular lesions on the lip, characteristic of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) infection. A Tzanck smear, performed by scraping the base of a freshly opened vesicle, is a rapid bedside diagnostic test. The pathognomonic finding for herpetic infections (HSV or VZV) in a Tzanck smear is the presence of multinucleated giant cells with "molded" nuclei. Henderson-Patterson bodies (Option A) are intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in Molluscum contagiosum. Owl-eye appearance (Option C) refers to the intranuclear inclusions of Cytomegalovirus (CMV). Acantholytic cells (Option D), or Tzanck cells, are seen in Pemphigus vulgaris but are not multinucleated giant cells. While Tzanck smears cannot differentiate between HSV and VZV, the clinical location on the lip strongly favors HSV-1. These findings allow for the prompt initiation of antiviral therapy such as acyclovir to reduce the duration and severity of the outbreak
questions.learning: The image depicts recurrent vesicular lesions on the lip, characteristic of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV-1) infection. A Tzanck smear, performed by scraping the base of a freshly opened vesicle, is a rapid bedside diagnostic test.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a 70-year-old patient with schizophrenia who is being treated for drug-induced Parkinsonism, which medication is most likely responsible for anticholinergic side effects such as constipation, blurred vision, and dry mouth?
questions.explanation: Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a common side effect of traditional antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia. To manage these motor symptoms, clinicians often prescribe anticholinergic medications like Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) (Option C). These drugs block acetylcholine to restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia. However, they cause significant systemic anticholinergic side effects, including dry mouth (xerostomia), blurred vision (due to mydriasis/cycloplegia), and constipation. Lithium (Option A) causes polyuria and tremors. Pramipexole (Option B), a dopamine agonist, causes nausea and orthostatic hypotension. Selegiline (Option D), an MAO-B inhibitor, is less associated with this classic anticholinergic triad. Therefore, given the specific combination of symptoms—dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision—Benzhexol is the definitive medication responsible for the patient's distress. These side effects are particularly bothersome in elderly patients and can exacerbate pre-existing glaucoma or urinary retention. **************
questions.learning: Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a common side effect of traditional antipsychotic medications used for schizophrenia. To manage these motor symptoms, clinicians often prescribe anticholinergic medications like Benzhexol (Trihexyphenidyl) (Option C).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old woman, G1P1, presents with intermenstrual bleeding for the past 1.5 months. What is the initial investigation of choice?
questions.explanation: In any woman of reproductive age presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding, including intermenstrual bleeding, the absolute first step in management is to rule out pregnancy. A urine pregnancy test (UPT) is a rapid, cost-effective, and highly sensitive initial investigation that guides all subsequent diagnostic paths. Bleeding in a 28-year-old could be related to pregnancy complications such as a threatened abortion or ectopic pregnancy. Transvaginal ultrasound (Option B) is an excellent follow-up tool to visualize pelvic pathology like fibroids or polyps but is secondary to confirming pregnancy status. Abdominal ultrasound (Option A) is less sensitive for early gynecological issues than TVS. Endometrial biopsy (Option D) is generally reserved for women over 45 or those with significant risk factors for malignancy, which this patient lacks. Therefore, ruling out gestation remains the standard of care for the initial workup of abnormal bleeding
questions.learning: In any woman of reproductive age presenting with abnormal uterine bleeding, including intermenstrual bleeding, the absolute first step in management is to rule out pregnancy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a stab wound to the back. Neurologic exam shows loss of vibration and proprioception on the right side below the level of the umbilicus. She also has spastic weakness in the right leg and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side beginning two levels below the lesion. Which of the following best describes this spinal cord syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Brown-Séquard syndrome

The clinical picture is characteristic of Brown-Séquard syndrome, caused by hemisection of one side of the spinal cord (commonly due to penetrating trauma like stab injury).

Ipsilateral (same side as lesion):

• Loss of vibration & proprioception → dorsal column involvement
• Spastic paralysis/weakness → corticospinal tract involvement

Contralateral (opposite side):

• Loss of pain & temperature beginning 1–2 levels below lesion → due to crossing of spinothalamic tract

Tract-wise Understanding:

• Dorsal columns: ascend ipsilaterally → loss on same side
• Corticospinal tract: descends ipsilaterally → ipsilateral UMN signs
• Spinothalamic tract: crosses within 1–2 levels → contralateral loss
questions.learning: Brown-Séquard syndrome — The clinical picture is characteristic of Brown-Séquard syndrome, caused by hemisection of one side of the spinal cord (commonly due to penetrating trauma like stab injury).

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 28-year-old software professional presents with disturbed sleep, low mood, and stress persisting for the past three months, which he relates to ongoing workplace difficulties. He has no previous psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation fits the criteria for adjustment disorder. This condition involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor (work pressure) beginning within three months of the stressor's onset. The distress is often disproportionate to the stressor and causes functional impairment. Generalized anxiety disorder (Option B) requires a minimum of six months of excessive worry regarding multiple domains. Acute stress disorder (Option C) follows a "traumatic" event (e.g., natural disaster) and lasts less than one month. PTSD (Option D) also requires exposure to a life-threatening trauma and specific symptoms like re-experiencing and hyperarousal, which are absent here. As the symptoms are a direct response to common workplace stress and within the 3-month window, adjustment disorder is the diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation fits the criteria for adjustment disorder. This condition involves emotional or behavioral symptoms (low mood, stress) in response to an identifiable stressor (work pressure) beginning within three months of the stressor's onset.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A paradoxical carrier is defined as:
options: A person who sheds pathogens during incubation period
A carrier who acquired pathogen from another carrier
A person who acquired pathogen from patient
A patient who became a carrier
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A carrier who acquired pathogen from another carrier

A paradoxical carrier is a carrier that acquired a pathogen from another carrier.

Incubatory carriers are those who shed the infectious agents during the incubation period of the disease.

Convalescent carriers are those who continue to shed the disease agent during the period of convalescence.

Healthy carriers are those who had a subclinical infection and developed a carrier state without suffering from overt disease.
questions.learning: A carrier who acquired pathogen from another carrier A paradoxical carrier is a carrier that acquired a pathogen from another carrier. Incubatory carriers are those who shed the infectious agents during the incubation period of the disease.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the ratio of the incidence of the disease in the exposed to that of the non-exposed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Relative risk

The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).
questions.learning: Relative risk — The ratio of incidence of disease or death among exposed to that among the non-exposed is called relative risk (RR).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are true about Late Dumping Syndrome, except? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Diarrhea

Late dumping syndrome is a consequence of peptic ulcer surgery characterized by reactive hypoglycemia occurring typically 1-3 hours after meals. It develops when carbohydrate-rich food causes a rapid rise in blood glucose, triggering an excessive insulin response that leads to subsequent hypoglycemia. Diarrhea is typical of early dumping.
questions.learning: Diarrhea Late dumping syndrome is a consequence of peptic ulcer surgery characterized by reactive hypoglycemia occurring typically 1-3 hours after meals.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the most common site of an intra-abdominal abscess.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Among the marked parts, 4 represents the right subhepatic space. It is the most common site of an intra-abdominal abscess.

The right subhepatic space is a deep space situated in Rutherford Morison's pouch. It is located between the liver above and the transverse colon and the hepatic flexure below. The relations of the right subhepatic space are:

• the right lobe of the liver and diaphragm on the right side
• foramen of Winslow on the left
• duodenum below
• liver and the gall bladder in the front
• right kidney and the diaphragm behind.

Abscesses here usually arise from appendicitis, cholecystitis, perforated duodenal ulcer, or as sequelae of an upper abdominal surgery.

Intraperitoneal abscesses may develop following intraperitoneal sepsis in specific sites in the abdomen (intra-abdominal abscess) or pelvis (pelvic abscess). The intra-abdominal abscess may occur in subphrenic spaces, or the subhepatic spaces, on either the right or left side.

An intra-abdominal abscess is a localized collection of infected fluid within the abdominal cavity due to failure of the host's intra-abdominal defense mechanisms. Patients usually present with acute abdominal pain, fever, rigors, tachycardia, tachypnea, and leukocytosis. Other features such as nausea, anorexia, emesis, constipation, and diarrhea can occur.

CT scan with IV contrast is the imaging method of choice for an intra-abdominal abscess. Ultrasonography can also be useful.

Initial management is by early intravenous antibiotic therapy, drainage of the abscess, and fluid resuscitation with crystalloids. Vasopressors, inotropes, and packed red blood cell transfusion are given when needed.

Other measures include ultrasound or CT-guided percutaneous drainage (non-surgical) and operative drainage. Resection and debridement can also be done. It can be done through a minimally invasive technique or laparotomy.
questions.learning: 4 Among the marked parts, 4 represents the right subhepatic space. It is the most common site of an intra-abdominal abscess.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with complaints of palpitations and syncope. He has a history of inferior-wall myocardial infarction a year ago. Holter study was done and his 24 hour ECG strip obtained is given below. What is the long-term treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Permanent pacemaker

Based on his ECG findings, this patient is suffering from symptomatic (palpitations, syncope) Mobitz Type II AV block. The definitive long-term treatment is, therefore, a permanent pacemaker.

Mobitz Type II AV block is characterized by:

* a constant PR interval

* some P waves not be followed by QRS complexes

According to the rhythm strip (Lead II) of the ECG shown, the patient is experiencing a 3:2 AV block which is then progressing to a 2:1 AV block.

This patient is also suffering from a right bundle branch block (RBBB) as indicated by the wide QRS complexes in leads V1, V2, and V3 ('M'-shaped).

This patient with a history of ischemic heart disease (previous history of inferior-wall MI) and objective signs of Mobitz Type II AV block and RBBB will benefit most from a permanent pacemaker.

In the ECG below, the blue arrows show some P waves that were not followed by QRS complexes. The missed QRS complex is pointed by the red arrow. The red box indicates the wide QRS complexes in leads V1, V2, and V3:

Other options:

Option A - Amiodarone, a class III anti-arrhythmic agent, is the drug of choice in the acute treatment as well as prevention of ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. It is a rate-control medication.

Options B and D - Pharmacologic interventions such as atropine and isoproterenol serve as short-term supplementary treatment options until a pacemaker can be installed or if the AV block is transient in nature. Even in such instances, a temporary transcutaneous pacemaker is preferred until a permanent device is available.

Pearl PF1593: Indication for Pacemaker in AV Conduction Defects

• In any patient with symptomatic bradycardia

• Irreversible second- or third-degree AV bloc

• Pacing in patients with asymptomatic AV block should be individualized

With acquired CHB

Left ventricular dysfunction and

Waking heart rates 40 beats/min.

• Asymptomatic second-degree AV block of either type, if the block is demonstrated to be intra- or infra-His or is associated with a wide QRS complex

• Neuromuscular diseases having a predilection for the conduction system, such as myotonic dystrophy and other muscular dystrophies, and Kearns-Sayre syndrome

Pearl PF0353: Types of Heart block
questions.learning: Permanent pacemaker — Based on his ECG findings, this patient is suffering from symptomatic (palpitations, syncope) Mobitz Type II AV block. The definitive long-term treatment is, therefore, a permanent pacemaker.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child was brought to the hospital with a history of loose stools. No history of fever or blood in stools. The mother says he is irritable and eagerly drinks water if given. On examination, eyes are sunken and in the skin pinch test, the skin retracted within two seconds but not immediately. What treatment is advised for the child?
options: Give oral fluids and zinc supplementation only and ask mother to come back if danger sign develops.
Give oral fluids and ask mother to continue the same and visit again the next day.
Consider severe dehydration start IV fluids, IV antibiotics, and refer to higher centre.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give oral fluids and zinc supplementation only and ask mother to come back if danger sign develops.

In a child with diarrhea, thirst (eagerly drinks water), sunken eyes, restless and irritable behavior, and skin pinch showing slow retraction (<2 seconds) point towards some dehydration. Treatment includes oral rehydration therapy, zinc supplementation, and continued breastfeeding according to WHO integrated management of neonatal and childhood diseases (IMNCI) plan B.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a population study, the value of the mean is 200. If the standard deviation is 20, 68% of the population will lie between?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 180- 220

68% of the population will lie between 180- 220.

In a normal distribution curve, 68% of the values lie within the mean +/- 1 standard deviation and the mean=median=mode. Since the mean = 200 and the standard deviation = 20:

68% of population will lie between Mean +/- 1SD, that is, 200 +/- 20 = 180-220

95% of population lies between Mean+/-2SD, 200+/- 2*20 = 160- 240

99% of population lies between Mean+/-3SD, 200+/- 3*20 = 140- 260
questions.learning: 180- 220 68% of the population will lie between 180- 220. In a normal distribution curve, 68% of the values lie within the mean +/- 1 standard deviation and the mean=median=mode.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presented with a history of painless breast lump measuring 6.2 X 4.5 cm in the left upper outer quadrant and no axillary nodes. Core cut biopsy showed ductal carcinoma in situ. She underwent tumor resection with adequate margins and postoperative HPE showed DCIS with intermediate-grade necrosis and with 6-mm clearance on margins. What is the next step of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adjuvant radiotherapy

According to Silverstein Van Nuys prognostic index for DCIS, the total score is 9. Hence, the patient would require adjuvant radiotherapy.

Age: 42 years (score 2), size: 62mm (score 3), clearance margin: 6mm (score 2) with intermediate-grade necrotic features (score 2).

Treatment:

• Scores 4-6 with >3mm margin: Excision alone
• Score 7 with < 3 mm margin, score 8 with > 3mm margin, score 9 with >5mm margin: Excision with RT
• Score 9 with < 5mm margin & score 10-12: Mastectomy

If the patient is ER/PR+, adjuvant hormonal therapy with tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor is indicated. Current data does not support the use of HER-2-directed therapy in DCIS.

Indications for adjuvant radiotherapy in breast cancer:

• Locally advanced breast cancers (T3, T4, N1, N2, N3)
• Following breast conservation surgery
• After mastectomy if tumor size ≥5 cm, skin or chest wall involvement, lymphovascular invasion and axillary node-positive for metastasis.

Post-treatment surveillance after treatment for DCIS includes history, physical examination, and routine mammography (if applicable).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman with Rheumatoid arthritis is started on low-dose methotrexate therapy. After a few weeks, she develops oral ulcers and mild bone marrow suppression. Which of the following is most directly reduced due to this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymidine monophosphate (TMP)

Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that inhibits the enzyme dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

• Blocks conversion of dihydrofolate (DHF) → tetrahydrofolate (THF)
• THF is required for one-carbon transfer reactions
• Impaired synthesis of thymidylate (dTMP) from dUMP
• Leads to ↓ DNA synthesis, especially in rapidly dividing cells

Clinical relevance:

• Used in cancer chemotherapy, autoimmune diseases (RA)
• Causes megaloblastic anemia as a side effect

Why other options are incorrect:

• GMP, AMP: Purine synthesis also affected indirectly but main tested effect is dTMP inhibition
• CMP: Pyrimidine synthesis not directly dependent on folate in this step

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly diabetic male patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, a blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia. The most prevalent species is Rhizopus oryzae. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus and immunocompromised individuals.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common form of mucormycosis. It commonly occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus. The presenting features are facial pain, numbness, loosening of teeth, conjunctival swelling, congestion, and blurry vision. When the disease spreads to the orbit, proptosis can be present. It can later spread to the brain's frontal lobe and cavernous sinus.

The local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge is typically seen in invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discolouration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

A definitive diagnosis is done with a biopsy and histopathologic examination. It is the most sensitive and specific method. It reveals aseptate fungi with thick-walled, ribbon-like hyphae branching at right angles. Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick, cottony, and fluffy surface.

Among the imaging techniques used for diagnosis, MRI is more sensitive to detecting orbital and nervous involvement than CT. Contrast-enhanced MRI is the imaging technique of choice. The 1,3 beta D-glucan assay, which is helpful for the identification of most fungi, cannot be used for the diagnosis of mucormycosis.

Management: The underlying cause and risk factors should be addressed.

* Aggressive surgical debridement of involved tissues should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of any form of mucormycosis is suspected.

* Initial therapy with amphotericin B as the drug of choice.

* Posaconazole and isavuconazole are broad-spectrum azoles that can be used as step-down therapy after response to amphotericin B.

The benefit of hyperbaric oxygen has not been proven yet and is not considered a standard treatment.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is characterized by complications such as cavernous sinus thrombosis when advanced cases are encountered. Clinical features suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis are bilateral proptosis, chemosis, vision loss, and impairment of extraocular muscle function (ophthalmoplegia).

Other options:

Option A: Bacterial rhinosinusitis typically presents with purulent nasal discharge, pain, and fever, and the CT scan would show mucosal thickening without the characteristic hyperattenuation.

Option C: Allergic fungal sinusitis is an allergic reaction to the causative fungus. It is prevalent in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised hosts. There is no invasion of the sinus mucosa with fungus. It presents with sinonasal polyposis and mucin, which consists of eosinophils, Charcot-Leyden crystals, and fungal hyphae. A CT scan shows mucosal thickening with centrally hyperdense areas. (Double density sign) There is an expansion of the sinus or bone erosion due to pressure, but no fungal invasion.

Option D: Invasive aspergillosis tends to affect immunocompromised individuals and cause more aggressive symptoms like facial swelling, necrosis, and a more destructive pattern on CT.
questions.learning: Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic infection caused principally by species of Rhizopus, Mucor, and Lichtheimia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
In a town, there were 1000 live births in a period of 6 months. During the same period, 12 women died due to the following causes. What is the maternal mortality ratio?

Sepsis - 3

Road traffic accidents - 2

Obstructed labor - 2

Postpartum hemorrhage - 3

Snake bite - 2
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 800 per 100000 live births

This town's maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is 800 per 100,000 live births.

Maternal mortality refers to deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, from causes related to pregnancy. Excluding the deaths from traffic accidents and snake bite, the total number of maternal deaths is 8.

MMR = (Number of maternal deaths in a given year / Number of live births in the same area and year) x 1,00,000 (or 1000).

Hence, MMR = 8 x 100000/1000 = 800 per 100,000 live births.
questions.learning: 800 per 100000 live births This town's maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is 800 per 100,000 live births. Maternal mortality refers to deaths during pregnancy or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy, from causes related to pregnancy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A male patient with chronic kidney disease, age 58, comes in for a regular check-up. His blood pressure is 140/100 mmHg. Urine analysis reveals a significant proteinuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive medication for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Telmisartan

The antihypertensive that can be given in this case is telmisartan.

Management of hypertension in chronic kidney disease (CKD):

ACE inhibitors or ARBs are considered the first-line drugs in patients with proteinuria. These agents effectively reduce blood pressure and proteinuria and prevent kidney decline. Calcium channel blockers can be added if necessary.

For patients who do not have proteinuria, there is no established first-line therapy. One or two of the following drugs can be used:

* Thiazides/thiazide-like diuretics

* ACE inhibitors or ARBs

* Calcium channel blockers

In patients presenting with fluid retention or fluid overload, thiazide diuretics such as chlorthalidone and hydrochlorothiazide are recommended for management. In CKD stages 1 to 3 (GFR >= 30 ml/min), thiazides are recommended, while loop diuretics such as bumetanide and furosemide are used in stages 4-5 (GFR < 30 ml/min).

First-choice drugs used in the treatment of hypertension in patients without any comorbidities include:

* Thiazide diuretics: Chlorthalidone is usually preferred to hydrochlorothiazide.

* Calcium channel blockers: Extended-release, long-acting dihydropyridines are preferred.

* ACE inhibitors: Captopril is preferred for the initiation of therapy. Enalapril and ramipril twice daily may also be used.

In the presence of any associated conditions or comorbidities, the first-choice drugs for the treatment of hypertension would be as follows:

* Beta-blockers (Carvedilol, Metoprolol Succinate, Bisoprolol). These reduce mortality, improve left ventricular function, and prevent arrhythmias.
It should be initiated after euvolemia is achieved to avoid worsening congestion.

* Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone) are recommended for patients with EF ≤ 35% to reduce mortality and hospitalizations. Should be used with caution in patients with renal impairment or hyperkalemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: New A 55 yr old man is found to have hepatomegaly on physical examination. He also complains of having a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. His liver microscopy is given on the slide below. This patient most likely suffers from ________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemochromatosis

The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's prussian blue stain.

Hemochromatosis is an inherited or acquired metabolic disorder caused by excessive iron absorption. Iron overload leads to the accumulation of iron in parenchymal organs such as the liver and pancreas followed by heart, joints, and endocrine organs.

The characteristic triad of hemochromatosis includes:

* Micronodular cirrhosis

* Diabetes mellitus in 75% to 80% of patients

* Abnormal skin pigmentation in 75% to 80% of patients

Note: The total body iron pool ranges from 2 to 6 gm in normal adults. In hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm, more than one-third of which accumulates in the liver.
questions.learning: Hemochromatosis — The patient most likely suffers from hemochromatosis. Liver microscopy shows hepatocellular iron, which is stained blue with Perl's prussian blue stain.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which type of psoriasis is Von Zumbusch Disease associated with? (NEET PG 2017)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute Generalized Pustular Psoriasis

Von Zumbusch disease is the classic form of Acute Generalized Pustular Psoriasis (GPP), a rare but severe and potentially life-threatening variant of psoriasis.

Clinical Features:

• Sudden onset of widespread erythema
• Numerous sterile pustules over large areas of the body
• High fever and chills
• Malaise and toxicity
• Leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers

Triggers:

• Sudden withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids
• Infections
• Pregnancy
• Hypocalcemia
• Certain medications

Complications:

• Fluid and electrolyte imbalance
• Secondary infection
• Sepsis
• Multiorgan dysfunction

Why Other Options Are Incorrect:

Acute Localized Pustular Psoriasis: Usually limited to palms and soles (palmoplantar pustulosis).

Generalized Pustular Psoriasis of Pregnancy: Known as Impetigo Herpetiformis, a pregnancy-associated variant.

Generalized Annular Pustular Psoriasis: A less severe chronic variant with annular pustular lesions.
questions.learning: Acute Generalized Pustular Psoriasis Von Zumbusch disease is the classic form of Acute Generalized Pustular Psoriasis (GPP), a rare but severe and potentially life-threatening variant of psoriasis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presents with mucus and blood in the stool. Sigmoidoscopy shows inflammation mainly in the rectum, and biopsy reveals crypt abscesses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of blood and mucus in the stool combined with rectal inflammation (proctitis) and the pathognomonic histological finding of crypt abscesses is highly diagnostic of Ulcerative Colitis (UC) . UC is an inflammatory bowel disease that uniquely begins in the rectum and spreads proximally in a continuous fashion. Crohn’s disease (Option C) typically involves "skip lesions" anywhere in the GI tract (most often the terminal ileum) and is characterized by transmural inflammation and non-caseating granulomas rather than primary rectal crypt abscesses. Irritable bowel syndrome (Option B) is a functional disorder and would show a normal sigmoidoscopy and biopsy. Pseudomembranous colitis (Option D) is caused by C. difficile and shows characteristic yellowish plaques on endoscopy. Therefore, the specific combination of localized rectal disease and microscopic crypt abscesses confirms Ulcerative Colitis as the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, or immunosuppressants
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of blood and mucus in the stool combined with rectal inflammation (proctitis) and the pathognomonic histological finding of crypt abscesses is highly diagnostic of Ulcerative Colitis (UC) .

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with progressive memory impairment and confusion, and imaging reveals amyloid plaques along with neurofibrillary tangles. Accumulation of which specific protein is primarily responsible for the amyloid deposition seen in Alzheimer’s disease?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly and is pathologically characterized by the extracellular deposition of amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles. The primary protein component responsible for these amyloid plaques is the Amyloid-beta (Aβ) protein. Aβ is derived from the proteolytic cleavage of the larger Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP) by β-secretase and γ-secretase. In contrast, ATTR (Option B) refers to transthyretin amyloidosis, which typically affects the heart and nerves in familial or senile systemic amyloidosis. Amyloid beta-2 (Option C, -microglobulin) is associated with dialysis-related amyloidosis. Acal (Option D, Procalcitonin-derived) is found in medullary thyroid carcinoma. The accumulation of Aβ is thought to trigger a cascade of neurotoxicity, leading to the formation of tangles (composed of hyperphosphorylated tau protein) and subsequent neuronal death and cognitive decline. Understanding the specific Aβ protein is the target of modern research, including monoclonal antibody therapies designed to clear these plaques from the brain to slow disease progression
questions.learning: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia in the elderly and is pathologically characterized by the extracellular deposition of amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which enzyme acts as the primary glucose sensor in pancreatic β-cells and plays a key role in regulating insulin secretion?
questions.explanation: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells is triggered by rising blood glucose levels. The critical first step in this process is the phosphorylation of glucose, which is catalyzed by hexokinase IV, also known as glucokinase. Unlike Hexokinases I, II, and III (Options A, B, and C), which have a high affinity for glucose and are inhibited by their product (glucose-6-phosphate), hexokinase IV has a low affinity and is not inhibited by its product. This low affinity allows the enzyme to act as a "glucose sensor," ensuring that its activity increases linearly as blood glucose levels rise above normal fasting ranges. This metabolic rate-limiting step determines the rate of ATP production, which ultimately leads to the closing of K+ channels and the release of insulin. Therefore, hexokinase IV is the specific enzyme uniquely suited for glucose sensing and the regulation of insulin secretion
questions.learning: Insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells is triggered by rising blood glucose levels. The critical first step in this process is the phosphorylation of glucose, which is catalyzed by hexokinase IV, also known as glucokinase.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: An elderly male smoker presents with progressive hoarseness of voice and throat pain since 6 months. Examination reveals an irregular growth in the larynx and a single, ipsilateral, mobile cervical lymph node. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chemoradiotherapy

Recognize that locally advanced laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma with regional nodal involvement (N1) is best managed with concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which provides effective locoregional control while preserving laryngeal function. Treatment depends on the TNM stage, with organ-preserving CRT preferred for many advanced but resectable tumors.

Why not the other options?

• A. Radiotherapy: Appropriate for early-stage (T1–T2, N0) laryngeal cancers but insufficient when cervical nodal metastasis is present.
• C. Partial laryngectomy: Reserved for selected early, localized tumors where adequate oncologic margins and laryngeal function can be preserved.
• D. Total laryngectomy: Indicated for very advanced (T4), recurrent, or non-functional laryngeal tumors, or when organ-preservation strategies fail.

High-yield Pearl:

• Early laryngeal cancer (T1–T2, N0) → Radiotherapy or conservative surgery.
• Locally advanced disease (T3/T4 or N+) → Concurrent chemoradiotherapy (larynx preservation) or surgery in selected cases.
• Salvage total laryngectomy is performed for persistent or recurrent disease after chemoradiotherapy.
questions.learning: Chemoradiotherapy Recognize that locally advanced laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma with regional nodal involvement (N1) is best managed with concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CRT), which provides effective locoregional control while preserving laryngeal function.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: ABCDE rule applies for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malignant melanoma

ABCDE algorithm is used to diagnose melanoma.

It comprises of:

• Asymmetry
• Border irregularity
• Color variegation
• Diameter of more than 6 mm
• Evolution or change

Melanoma is a malignant tumor arising from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction. Though it represents only 4% of skin cancers, it accounts for 80% of deaths (high mortality rate). It presents as a pigmented lesion that has enlarged, ulcerated, or bled.

Histopathological confirmation is the gold standard in the diagnosis of melanoma. It is divided into four main types: nodular melanoma (NM), superficial spreading melanoma (SSM), lentigo maligna melanoma (LMM), and acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM).

The treatment consists of wide local excision of the tumor and follow-up to detect any local recurrence around the scar and excluding nodal spread.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Proton

The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in protons.

The proton is a heavy and charged particle that gradually loses its speed as it interacts with human tissue. It is easily controlled and delivers its maximum dose at a precise depth and can go as far as 32 cm. The absorbed dose increases very gradually with greater depth and lower speed, suddenly rising to a peak when the proton is ultimately stopped. This is known as the Bragg peak.

The behavior of the proton can be precisely determined, and the beam can be directed, allowing the Bragg peak to occur within the tumor site. Immediately following this burst of energy, the protons cease radiating and come to a complete stop. This property of proton therapy enables targeting tumors within the body, delivering radiation directly to the tumor while sparing the surrounding healthy cells, offering a much less invasive alternative to treat cancer.

The Bragg curve shown below plots the energy loss of ionizing radiation during its travel through matter.
questions.learning: Proton — The Bragg peak effect is pronounced in protons. The proton is a heavy and charged particle that gradually loses its speed as it interacts with human tissue.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 45-year-old female insists her face is deformed despite normal exam and demands surgery. What is the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. SSRI

This presentation is typical of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), where a person is preoccupied with an imagined or minimal defect in appearance despite a normal examination and may repeatedly seek cosmetic procedures.

Key features:

• Persistent belief that a body part (here, the face) is deformed or ugly
• Normal physical examination
• Repeated requests for cosmetic surgery
• Significant distress or impairment

Management:

• First-line treatment: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs) such as fluoxetine, sertraline, or escitalopram.
• Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) can also be helpful.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Insight-oriented behavioral therapy: Not the primary treatment of choice.
• Atypical antipsychotics: Used only if the belief becomes fixed and delusional or if SSRIs fail.
• Allowing surgery: Cosmetic procedures usually do not relieve symptoms and may worsen the disorder.

Therefore, the best management is SSRI therapy.
questions.learning: SSRI — This presentation is typical of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD), where a person is preoccupied with an imagined or minimal defect in appearance despite a normal examination and may repeatedly seek cosmetic procedures.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following suture material has the maximum tissue reaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Catgut

Natural sutures produce more tissue reaction than synthetic sutures. Among the options, catgut is a natural absorbable suture that is degraded by enzymatic proteolysis, leading to greater inflammation and tissue reaction. In contrast, synthetic absorbable sutures such as Vicryl (polyglactin), PDS (polydioxanone), and Monocryl (poliglecaprone) are broken down by hydrolysis, causing minimal tissue reaction.

Hence, catgut causes the maximum tissue reaction.
questions.learning: Catgut Natural sutures produce more tissue reaction than synthetic sutures. Among the options, catgut is a natural absorbable suture that is degraded by enzymatic proteolysis, leading to greater inflammation and tissue reaction.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 72-year-old patient, known to have diabetes mellitus, presents with a gradual decrease in vision one month after undergoing cataract surgery. Fundoscopic examination reveals a characteristic honeycomb or flower-petal pattern in the retina. This finding is suggestive of which condition?
questions.explanation: The "honeycomb appearance" or "flower petal pattern" observed during fluorescein angiography of the retina is the classic finding for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME). This pattern results from the accumulation of fluid in cystic spaces within the Henle's layer of the macula. CME is a common cause of vision decrease following cataract surgery (Irvine-Gass syndrome), and the risk is significantly higher in patients with Diabetes Mellitus (DM). Central serous retinopathy (Option B) involves a localized serous detachment of the neurosensory retina, usually showing a "smoke-stack" leak on angiography. Retinal detachment (Option C) is a separation of the retina from the pigment epithelium. Diabetic retinopathy (Option D) encompasses a range of findings including microaneurysms and hemorrhages, but the specific petaloid appearance refers to the resulting macular edema. Management of post-surgical CME typically involves topical NSAIDs and corticosteroids. In diabetic patients, ensuring stable blood sugar levels is also critical for resolution
questions.learning: The "honeycomb appearance" or "flower petal pattern" observed during fluorescein angiography of the retina is the classic finding for Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Reverse splitting of second heart sound is most commonly seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LBBB

Paradoxical (reverse) splitting of the second heart sound (S2) occurs when aortic valve closure (A2) is delayed, causing P2 to occur before A2. The split is heard during expiration and narrows or disappears during inspiration, which is the opposite of normal physiological splitting.

• Most common cause: Left bundle branch block (LBBB) due to delayed left ventricular depolarization and prolonged left ventricular ejection.
• Other causes:

• Severe aortic stenosis
• Left ventricular pacing
• Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)

Differentiate from other options:

• A. ASD: Fixed wide splitting of S2.
• B. Severe MR: Produces a pansystolic murmur; paradoxical splitting is not a typical finding.
• D. Pulmonary hypertension: Loud P2; splitting may become narrow but is not paradoxical.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a painless lump in her left breast. She describes it as freely mobile with a rubbery consistency. On examination, the mass is confirmed to be approximately the stated size. Based on these clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a painless, rubbery, and highly mobile breast mass in a young woman is the classic description of a Fibroadenoma. Due to its extreme mobility within the breast tissue, it is colloquially known as the "breast mouse." A breast abscess (Option A) would be intensely painful, red, and warm, often associated with fever. A Phyllodes tumor (Option B) is a differential but typically grows very rapidly to a much larger size and occurs in older women. Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option D) usually presents as a firm, fixed, hard mass with irregular borders in an older age group. Given the specific age of the patient and the "rubbery" texture and "highly movable" nature of the mass, fibroadenoma is the definitive and most common benign diagnosis. Management typically involves ultrasound confirmation and sometimes a fine-needle aspiration for cytology

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which Leopold's maneuver is done to assess the lie of the fetus?
questions.explanation: Leopold’s maneuvers are a systematic method of abdominal palpation used in obstetrics to assess the fetal lie, presentation, position, and engagement. Among these, Leopold’s first maneuver (fundal grip) is specifically used to determine the fetal lie. In this maneuver, the examiner palpates the uterine fundus using both hands to identify which fetal pole occupies the upper part of the uterus. If the head is felt in the fundus, the fetus is in a breech presentation, while if the breech is felt, it suggests a cephalic presentation, both indicating a longitudinal lie. If neither pole is clearly identified, it may indicate a transverse or oblique lie. Leopold’s second maneuver assesses fetal position by locating the back and limbs. Leopold’s third maneuver identifies the presenting part above the pelvic inlet, and Leopold’s fourth maneuver evaluates engagement of the presenting part. Therefore, the first maneuver is most important for determining the fetal lie
questions.learning: Leopold’s maneuvers are a systematic method of abdominal palpation used in obstetrics to assess the fetal lie, presentation, position, and engagement.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What kind of sanitation facilities should be arranged for soldiers returning from a war zone?
questions.explanation: In temporary camps or emergency field situations, such as for soldiers returning from war, the most appropriate and rapid sanitation solution is the trench latrine. Trench latrines (either shallow or deep) are specifically designed for short-term use in situations where permanent infrastructure is unavailable. They involve digging a trench of specific dimensions and providing privacy screens. Shallow trenches are used for very brief stays, while deep trenches are suitable for longer periods. The Pit method (Option A) refers to more permanent rural latrines. The Dumping method (Option B) is an unhygienic practice for waste disposal that is never recommended. An Aqua privy (Option D) is a more complex septic-style system not suitable for rapid field deployment. Proper sanitation is critical in military or refugee settings to prevent the outbreak of waterborne diseases like cholera and dysentery. Trench latrines must be located at a safe distance from water sources and should be covered daily with soil to minimize fly breeding and odors
questions.learning: In temporary camps or emergency field situations, such as for soldiers returning from war, the most appropriate and rapid sanitation solution is the trench latrine.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
What is the mechanism of action of methotrexate in osteosarcoma?

UMP- Uridine monophosphate

DHFR- Dihydrofolate reductase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Competitive inhibitor of DHFR

The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs. The antifolate action of the drug is responsible for its anti-cancer properties.

Mechanism of action:

It is a folic acid analog and binds to the active catalytic site of dihydrofolate reductase(DHFR). This would inhibit the formation of tetrahydrofolate(THF) which is needed for purine nucleotides, thymidylate, and the amino acids serine and methionine. This would interfere with the production of DNA, RNA, and important cellular proteins.

Low doses of methotrexate are used in the management of rheumatic diseases. It is due to the inhibition of amino-imidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and thymidylate synthetase. This results in increased levels of adenosine that inhibits inflammation.

Adverse effects:

Common side effects are nausea and mucosal ulcers. Others include anemia, leukopenia, stomatitis, GI ulcerations, and alopecia. Dose-related hepatotoxicity is also seen. The GI effects and hepatotoxicity can be reduced by the use of leucovorin or folinic acid.
questions.learning: Competitive inhibitor of DHFR — The anticancer activity of methotrexate is by inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Methotrexate belongs to the antimetabolite class of anticancer drugs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In rural areas, one ASHA worker is assigned to a population of ___ people.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1000

In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA.

An Accredited Social Health Activist (ASHA) does not procure ORS, contraceptives, IFA tablets, etc. from the CHC for her community.

An ASHA acts as a depot holder for these essential supplies, hence making them readily available to her community. These include Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORS), Iron Folic Acid tablets (IFA), chloroquine, Disposable Delivery Kits (DDK), Oral Pills & Condoms, etc.

General norm:

* Must be a woman - married/divorced/widow (age group 25-45 years)

* Must be a resident of that village

* Formal education of up to 10th standard

* At least 1 ASHA for a population of 1000.

Relaxations in the general norm:

* If no candidate is available with a qualification of 10th standard, the requirement can be relaxed to 8th standard.

* In tribal, hilly, and desert areas, the norm can be relaxed to 1 ASHA per habitation.

Note: The States have been given the flexibility to relax the population norms as well as the educational qualifications on a case-to-case basis, depending on the local conditions as far as her recruitment is concerned. However, these are exceptions and not the general norm.

Pearl PF0294: ASHA

ASHA is an Accredited Social Health Activist.

An ASHA must be a woman, a resident of the village, 25 to 45 years old and have a formal education till 10th standard preferably if they are in good numbers. This may be relaxed upto 8th standard only if no suitable person with this qualification is available. She is part of the primary health care at the village level.

National norm: In rural areas, a population of 1000 should have at least 1 ASHA, but in remote areas, one ASHA per habitation is the norm. In urban areas, 1 ASHA worker is assigned to a population of 1000-2500. This norm is also mandated by each state, differently, according to their requirements.

Responsibilities of ASHA:

* Health education and awareness

* Reproductive and child health and family planning

* Facilitate the access to health services

* Promotion of sanitation and household toilet construction

* Provision of primary medical care for minor ailments

* Provider of DOTS

* Depot holder of essentials like ORS, iron and folic acid tablets, condoms, disposable delivery kits, etc.

* Dispersal of health information on her community to higher centres

* Some responsibilities are integrated with Anganwadi workers and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Testosterone helps in the development of various organs in the fetus. Which of the following stimulates its production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. hCG from placenta

hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) from placenta stimulates the production of testosterone in the male fetus.

hCG released from the placenta is the initial stimulus for testosterone production in the male fetus. Later by the eighth week of gestation, fetal pituitary LH (luteinizing hormone) stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone.

Sex differentiation of the embryo depends on the Y chromosome, which contains the testis-determining gene called the SRY (sex-determining region on Y) gene. In a genetically male embryo (46, XY), the gonad is converted into testis under the influence of this gene. Female development occurs in the absence of this gene.

Testosterone released from the Leydig cells acts on the Wolffian duct to develop vas deferens, epididymis, and seminal vesicles. Testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) with the help of 5-alpha-reductase which helps in the differentiation of male external genitalia.

The Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules of testes secrete antimüllerian hormone (AMH)/Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) by 7 weeks of gestation. It causes regression of the Mullerian duct and prevents the development of the uterus, fallopian tube, and upper vagina.

Other options:

Option A: It is LH from the fetal pituitary, and not the maternal pituitary that stimulates testosterone production in the male fetus.

Option C: Inhibin A is produced by the corpus luteum and inhibin B is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovary. They inhibit FSH secretion.
questions.learning: hCG from placenta hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) from placenta stimulates the production of testosterone in the male fetus. hCG released from the placenta is the initial stimulus for testosterone production in the male fetus.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He gets an urge to micturate but is unable to urinate. On examination, blood was seen at the tip of the urethra, and swelling of the penis and scrotum was seen. What is the site of injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bulbar urethra injury

The given clinical scenario with a history of a blow to the perineum, blood at the tip of the meatus, swelling of the penis and scrotum is suggestive of an injury to the bulbar urethra.

Urethral injuries can be classified into:

Type
Proximal urethral injury
Distal urethral injury

Site of injury

• Prostatic urethra
• Membranous urethra

• Bulbar urethra
• Penile urethra

Mechanism
Secondary to pelvic fracture

Occurs due to a blow to the perineum by:

• Straddle injury
• Loose manhole covering
• Gymnasium accidents

Clinical features

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• High-riding prostate on digital rectal examination (Vermooten sign)
• Deep perineal hematoma

• Urinary retention
• Blood at the urethral meatus
• Perineal hematoma (butterfly hematoma)

Note: Urinary bladder rupture occurs due to an injury to the suprapubic region. Extraperitoneal bladder rupture is more common and associated with pelvic fracture. Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is caused by a blow or a fall on a distended bladder. It manifests as sudden severe pain in the hypogastrium and syncope.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A person who had dinner at 8 pm the previous night, tested his blood glucose levels at 7 am the next morning. What is the source of blood glucose in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hepatic glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a person fasting overnight for 11 hours (8 pm to 7 am) is hepatic glycogenolysis.

First stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.
Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

• Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and
• Glycerol from adipose tissue

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

• Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon:insulin ratio.
• Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol.
• Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA.
• In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon:insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon:insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

1. It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.
2. It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependant on glucose in the fasting state.
3. Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

Metabolic process
Fasting state
Fed state

Glucagon: insulin
Increased
Decreased

Gluconeogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogenolysis
Increased
Decreased

Ketogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogen storage
Decreased
Increased

Other options:

Option C: Muscle glycogen cannot contribute directly to plasma glucose, since muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase. So glycogen cannot be converted to glucose to be used as fuel during starvation.

Option D: In the well-fed state/ absorptive state of two to four hours after a meal, dietary glucose is the main source of fuel.
