questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Steroidal contraceptives available in the basket of contraceptive choice from Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India are:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monophasic

The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India provides monophasic combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) in the national family planning programme.

The commonly supplied pill is Mala-N/Mala-D, which contains a fixed dose of estrogen and progestin in all 21 active tablets, making it a monophasic preparation.

• A. Monophasic ✓: Correct. The estrogen and progestin dose remains constant throughout the cycle.
• B. Biphasic ✗: Hormone doses vary in two phases; not supplied under the national programme.
• C. Triphasic ✗: Hormone doses vary in three phases; not part of the Government of India’s contraceptive basket.
• D. Estrogen-only pills ✗: Estrogen-only contraceptive pills are not used because of the high risk of endometrial hyperplasia and other adverse effects.
questions.learning: Monophasic — The Ministry of Health & Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India provides monophasic combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) in the national family planning programme.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with pregnancy-induced hypertension and requires pharmacological treatment. Which of the following drugs is considered safe for managing this condition during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Managing hypertension in pregnancy requires drugs that are effective for the mother while being non-teratogenic for the fetus. Alpha-methyldopa (Option C) is the gold-standard, first-line antihypertensive in this setting. It is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist with a long-established safety profile and no known adverse effects on fetal development. Lisinopril (Option A), an ACE inhibitor, and Losartan (Option D), an ARB, are strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy as they are highly teratogenic, causing fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and skull ossification defects. Propranolol (Option B) is generally avoided as it may be associated with intrauterine growth restriction and neonatal hypoglycemia. Labatalol and Nifedipine are other common alternatives, but among the choices provided, Alpha-methyldopa is the classic and definitive safe choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension management
questions.learning: Managing hypertension in pregnancy requires drugs that are effective for the mother while being non-teratogenic for the fetus. Alpha-methyldopa (Option C) is the gold-standard, first-line antihypertensive in this setting.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
options: Most common clinical presentation is pain and tenderness in calf
Some cases may directly present as pulmonary thromboembolism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mostly bilateral

Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

DVT refers to thrombosis of the deep venous system.

Caused by:

• Postoperative thrombosis (most common cause)
• Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
• After childbirth
• Immobility

Sites:

• Pelvic veins—common
• Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (common on the left side).

Fever is the earliest symptom, which is also most commonly accompanied by pain and tenderness in the calf and thigh (option C).

The following signs could be elicited:

• Positive Homan's sign: Resistance of calf muscles on passive foreceful dorsiflexion of the foot.

• Mose's sign: Gentle squeezing of the lower part of the calf from side to side is painful.
• Neuhof's sign: Thickening and deep tenderness seen on deep palpation of the calf muscles.

Sometimes, the thrombus may get dislodged and present as pulmonary thromboembolism (option D) with features of dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and chest pain.

Clinical features are unreliable for making a definitive diagnosis (option A), and a venous Doppler is the best modality for confirming DVT. It reveals a non-compressible dilated vein. The likelihood of pulmonary embolism can be predicted using modified Wells criteria.

Patients with DVT should be immediately started with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). If contraindicated due to renal insufficiency or thrombocytopenia-related conditions, they should be started on fondaparinux (indirect factor Xa inhibitor) or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor). Anticoagulants should be administered for a minimum period of 3 months. Vena cava filters are used in patients with bleeding risks (like hemophilia).
questions.learning: Mostly bilateral Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient who was diagnosed with prostate cancer is being investigated. The bone scan is reported as a super scan with increased uptake in the bones and reduced activity in the kidney and soft tissue. What is the reason for this super scan appearance?
options: Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis
Decreased uptake by adrenal glands and kidney
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis

The super scan appearance is due to increased uptake due to diffuse metastasis.

Diffuse osteoblastic metastatic diseases such as carcinoma breast and prostate carcinoma lead to a generalized increase in the skeletal uptake relative to soft tissue and absent or faint renal activity on a bone scan. This is known as a super scan. It may also be seen in generalized bone diseases such as hyperparathyroidism.

Carcinoma of the prostate is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements. Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in decreasing order of frequency.

Prognosis and staging: The Gleason grading system correlates with the pathological stage, spread, and prognosis. Measurement of serum PSA levels may be useful to assist with the diagnosis and management.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Arrange the following anesthetic agents on the basis of their potency.

Nitrous oxide

Halothane

Isoflurane

Methoxyflurane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide

The potency of the inhaled anesthetics given above can be arranged as methoxyflurane> halothane> isoflurane> nitrous oxide. It is due to the change in the agents' minimum alveolar concentration (MAC).

The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an inhaled anesthetic is the lowest concentration required to prevent movement in response to a defined noxious stimulus in 50% of subjects. It is a measure of the potency of inhalational anesthetics. So, the lower the MAC value, the lower the concentration of anesthetic drug required, implying the drug is more potent.

MAC values (expressed as a '%' of 1 atmosphere) of some anesthetic agents:

• Nitrous oxide with a MAC value of 104 is the least potent inhaled anesthetic
• Methoxyflurane – MAC- 0.2 (most potent)
• Desflurane: 6.0
• Sevoflurane– 2.05
• Isoflurane – 1.28
• Halothane – 0.75
questions.learning: Methoxyflurane> Halothane> Isoflurane> Nitrous oxide The potency of the inhaled anesthetics given above can be arranged as methoxyflurane> halothane> isoflurane> nitrous oxide.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most appropriate treatment option for an 8 cm endometrial cyst?
questions.explanation: An 8 cm endometrial cyst (endometrioma or "chocolate cyst") is a large lesion that warrants active surgical intervention. The most appropriate and standard treatment is surgical cystectomy (Option B), usually performed laparoscopically. Cystectomy involves excising the cyst wall, which provides higher relief of symptoms and a lower rate of recurrence compared to other methods. Needle aspiration (Option A) carries an extremely high risk of recurrence and potential spillage of irritant contents, making it less preferred. Medical management with GnRH agonists (Option C) can shrink the cyst temporarily and improve pelvic pain but will not resolve a large 8 cm collection. Conservative management (Option D) is generally only for very small ( cm) cysts; a large 8 cm cyst is at high risk for ovarian torsion or rupture. Therefore, laparoscopic excision is the definitive clinical standard
questions.learning: An 8 cm endometrial cyst (endometrioma or "chocolate cyst") is a large lesion that warrants active surgical intervention. The most appropriate and standard treatment is surgical cystectomy (Option B), usually performed laparoscopically.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 17-year-old male presents with a painless swelling on the lateral aspect of his left knee. Based on the image shown, what is the most likely diagnosis among the following options?
questions.explanation: The X-ray finding of a bony, pedunculated outgrowth (exostosis) pointing away from the nearby joint is pathognomonic for an osteochondroma. It is the most common benign bone tumor and typically occurs in adolescents around the growth plates of long bones, like the distal femur. These lesions are usually painless unless they interfere with surrounding tendons or nerves. Ewing’s sarcoma (Option B) would show an "onion-skin" periosteal reaction and look highly aggressive. Giant cell tumor (Option D) is an expansile "soap-bubble" lesion that is located in the epiphysis (reaching the joint surface), not on a stalk projecting away. Enchondroma (Option A) is a benign cartilaginous tumor located inside the medullary cavity, often in the small bones of the hands. Therefore, the classic "stalk" or pedunculated appearance confirms the diagnosis of osteochondroma

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Liver synthesizes all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Immunoglobulins

Immunoglobulins are not synthesized by the liver. They are produced by plasma cells.

Plasma proteins synthesized by the liver are:

• Albumin
• Coagulation/clotting factors
• Acute-phase proteins
• Steroid binding and other hormone-binding proteins

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the first line of treatment of mastitis in a lactating mother?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dicloxacillin

Dicloxacillin is the first line of treatment for mastitis in lactating mothers and should be taken for 10-14 days.

Mastitis refers to the infection of the breast parenchymal tissue. The most common organism causing breast infection is Staphylococcus aureus. It is common in new mothers at the beginning of lactation who are inexperienced with breastfeeding or during weaning when nipple trauma occurs due to the infant's growing teeth.

Clinical features of mastitis include:

• Fever and malaise
• Localized pain and tenderness
• Purulent nipple discharge
• Redness and swelling of the affected breast
• Positive fluctuation test

A culture from nipple discharge or test-needle aspiration of the cellulitic area is done to confirm the organism and its antibiotic sensitivity. An ultrasonogram of the involved breast is done to exclude abscess. They are treated with antibiotics and adequate breast support. Choice of antibiotics in lactational mastitis:

1. Dicloxacillin 500 mg 4 times a day is to be started empirically.
2. Erythromycin is given to women who are penicillin-sensitive.
3. If the infection is caused by resistant, penicillinase-producing Staphylococcus species then vancomycin, clindamycin, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is given for at least 10 days.
questions.learning: Dicloxacillin Dicloxacillin is the first line of treatment for mastitis in lactating mothers and should be taken for 10-14 days. Mastitis refers to the infection of the breast parenchymal tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-year-old child has a history of biting his lips and fingers. On evaluation, you notice lip lacerations, missing sections of his fingers, and developmental delay. Lab reports reveal hyperuricemia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase

The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. It occurs due to the complete deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) involved in the salvage pathway.

Purines produced in the body or introduced through diet can be converted to nucleoside triphosphates to be reused by the body. This pathway is called the salvage pathway for purines as shown in the image below.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the HGPRT enzyme. This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine resulting in increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) and decreased levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and guanosine monophosphate (GMP). An increase in guanine and hypoxanthine eventually gets converted into uric acid, There is increased de novo purine synthesis.

The clinical features include compulsive self-mutilation, intellectual disability, delayed milestones, dystonic movements, and hyperuricemia. The excess uric acid can form kidney stones (urolithiasis) or deposits in joints as urate crystals (gouty arthritis).

The treatment of this condition includes:

* Allopurinol or febuxostat for hyperuricemia

* Behavioural management using restraints for self-mutilation

* High fluid intake, reduced fructose and purine intake

Partial deficiency of HGPRT leads to Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency leads to severe T-cell deficiency with normal B-cell function. Patients present with autoimmune diseases and opportunistic infections.

Option C: Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) is another enzyme along with HGPRT to be involved in the salvage of purine bases to nucleotides.

Option D: Adenosine deaminase deficiency leads to sparse or defective T cells and B cells. Patients suffer from severe immunodeficiency and often succumb to fatal infections.

Pearl PF1567: Purine salvage deficiencies: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Adenosine deaminase deficiency(SCID)

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency(SCID):

Adenosine deaminase enzyme deficiency is one of the major cause of SCID. It is also called as Glanzmann–Riniker syndrome.

SCID patients are usually affected by severe bacterial, viral, or fungal infections early in life and often present with interstitial lung disease, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome:

It is due to deficiency of the enzyme Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase(HGPRT). It is an X-linked recessive disease.

Clinical features:

* Intellectual disability

* Self-mutilation

* Aggression

* Hyperuricemia

* Gout

Treatment:

* Allopurinol

* Febuxostat

Pearl PF0701: Enzymes and Steps Involved in Purine Degradation

Enzymes

Reaction

AMP deaminase

AMP to IMP

Adenosine deaminase

Adenosine to Inosine

5'-nucleotidase

IMP & GMP to Inosine & Guanosine respectively

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase

Inosine & Guanosine to Hypoxanthine & guanine respectively

Xanthine oxidase

Hypoxanthine to Xanthine & Xanthine to uric acid
questions.learning: Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase — The given clinical scenario of self-mutilating behavior, delayed developmental milestones and hyperuricemia is highly suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following antiretroviral drugs is not used in HIV & hepatitis B co-infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Abacavir

Abacavir is not used in HIV and hepatitis-B co-infection. It is used in the first-line ART regimen for patients with abnormal serum creatinine values.

Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) drugs like lamivudine, its closely related drug emtricitabine, and the nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) tenofovir have activity against hepatitis B virus. These drugs are preferred in combination with other antiretrovirals for the treatment of HIV & HBV co-infections.
questions.learning: Abacavir Abacavir is not used in HIV and hepatitis-B co-infection. It is used in the first-line ART regimen for patients with abnormal serum creatinine values.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Out of the following areas of brain, which area is most commonly affected on brain imaging in Wilson’s disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Basal ganglia

Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation. The basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, are the most commonly affected structures on brain MRI, explaining the characteristic movement disorders seen in the disease.

• Basal ganglia, especially the putamen, show the most frequent MRI abnormalities.
• MRI may demonstrate:

• Bilateral symmetric T2 hyperintensities in the putamen
• Globus pallidus involvement
• Caudate nucleus involvement
• Thalamic and brainstem involvement in advanced disease
• “Face of the giant panda” sign in the midbrain (classic MRI finding).

Why not the other options?

• A. Cerebellum – May be involved in advanced disease but is not the most commonly affected area.
• B. Sub-cortex – White matter involvement is less common than basal ganglia involvement.
• C. Thalamus – Can be affected but less frequently than the basal ganglia.
questions.learning: Basal ganglia Wilson’s disease (hepatolenticular degeneration) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and excessive copper accumulation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the cornerstone of treatment for a patient of dengue with warning signs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IV Fluids

The primary modality of treatment in patients with dengue with warning signs is IV fluids.

The main pathology in dengue is plasma leakage resulting in intravascular volume depletion and thereby shock. Warning signs in dengue include:

• Abdominal pain or tenderness
• Persistent vomiting
• Clinical fluid accumulation (ascites, pleural effusion)
• Mucosal bleeding
• Lethargy or restlessness
• Hepatomegaly >2 cm
• Increase in hematocrit concurrent with a rapid decrease in platelet count

Inpatient management is advised to all patients of dengue with warning signs. The management of dengue includes:

• IV crystalloids - mainstay of treatment
• Platelet transfusion - severe thrombocytopenia (<10,000/mm3) and active bleeding

FFP and cryoglobulins are not the preferred for treatment in dengue.
questions.learning: IV Fluids — The primary modality of treatment in patients with dengue with warning signs is IV fluids. The main pathology in dengue is plasma leakage resulting in intravascular volume depletion and thereby shock.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a causality triage scenario, following a road traffic accident, whom would you treat first?
options: 60-year-old conscious patient with pants covered in blood
40-year-old female who is unconscious with laboured breathing
20-year-old female who is agitated with anxiety and increased breathing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 40-year-old female who is unconscious with laboured breathing

In triage, priority is given based on immediacy of life-threatening conditions, following the ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) principle.

An unconscious patient with laboured breathing has a compromised airway and respiration, which are immediately life-threatening and require urgent intervention.

Patients who are conscious, crying, anxious, or bleeding but stable can be managed after stabilization of airway and breathing–threatened cases.
questions.learning: 40-year-old female who is unconscious with laboured breathing In triage, priority is given based on immediacy of life-threatening conditions, following the ABCDE (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) principle.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents for a routine well- child visit. Examination reveals a systolic murmur and a widely split second heart sound that is fixed and does not vary with respiration. There is no family history of heart disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The physical finding of a widely split second heart sound (S2) that does not vary with respiration (fixed split S2) is pathognomonic for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option C) . This occurs because the left-to-right shunt causes a constant volume overload of the right ventricle, delaying the closure of the pulmonic valve regardless of the phase of breathing. The associated systolic murmur is usually due to increased flow across the pulmonic valve. Ventricular septal defect (Option B) typically presents with a loud pansystolic murmur and a variable S2. Pulmonic stenosis (Option D) features a mid-systolic click and a widely split S2, but the split usually does vary with respiration. TAPVC (Option A) is a more severe cyanotic lesion that would present earlier with significant distress. Because the "fixed split S2" is the quintessential physical hallmark of an ASD, it is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The physical finding of a widely split second heart sound (S2) that does not vary with respiration (fixed split S2) is pathognomonic for an Atrial Septal Defect (ASD) (Option C) .

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 2-year-old child presented to OPD of a PHC Watery diarrhoea having severe dehydration. Most likely causative agent underlying would be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rota virus

In children below 5 years, rotavirus is the most common cause of acute watery diarrhoea and is frequently associated with severe dehydration due to profuse fluid loss.

Rotavirus infects the enterocytes of the small intestine which causes destruction of intestinal epithelial cells, reduced absorption of fluids and increased intestinal secretion that results in Profuse watery diarrhoea.

Bacterial causes like Shigella and Salmonella typically produce inflammatory or dysenteric diarrhoea, while E. coli O157:H7 is more often linked to bloody diarrhoea and HUS rather than severe watery diarrhoea.

Rotavirus infection can be prevented by vaccination.

India includes the Rotavirus vaccine in the Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).
questions.learning: Rota virus — In children below 5 years, rotavirus is the most common cause of acute watery diarrhoea and is frequently associated with severe dehydration due to profuse fluid loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome?
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), which leads to massive gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease. The primary medical management objective is the profound suppression of acid production. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) like Omeprazole (Option B) are the first-line and most effective treatment for this purpose. PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase pump, providing more potent and longer-lasting acid suppression than H2-receptor antagonists like Cimetidine (Option A). Misoprostol (Option C) is a prostaglandin analog used to prevent NSAID-induced ulcers but is insufficient for ZES hypersecretion. Aluminum hydroxide (Option D) is a simple antacid that only provides transient relief. While surgical resection of the gastrinoma is the definitive cure, high-dose PPI therapy is mandatory to manage symptoms and prevent life-threatening complications like perforation or bleeding. Therefore, Omeprazole is the gold standard for pharmacological management
questions.learning: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), which leads to massive gastric acid hypersecretion and severe peptic ulcer disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent episodes of severe generalized pain, often triggered by vigorous physical activity. Blood examination reveals anemia and elongated, sickle-shaped red blood cells instead of the normal biconcave shape, confirming a diagnosis of sickle cell anemia. Which specific amino acid substitution is responsible for this condition?
options: Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 6th position
Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position
Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 5th position
Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 5th position
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease caused by a single point mutation in the -globin gene. Specifically, it involves the substitution of the amino acid glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position of the -polypeptide chain. This change from a polar, hydrophilic amino acid (glutamate) to a non-polar, hydrophobic one (valine) creates a "sticky" patch on the hemoglobin molecule. When oxygen levels are low (e.g., during vigorous exercise), these hemoglobin S (HbS) molecules polymerize into long fibers, distorting the red blood cell into a sickle shape. Options A, C, and D describe incorrect substitutions or positions. The sickle cells are rigid and block small blood vessels, leading to the "excruciating pain" of a vaso-occlusive crisis. This specific biochemical detail is a hallmark of genetic medicine, illustrating how a minute change in a protein's primary structure can lead to profound systemic illness and anemia
questions.learning: Sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease caused by a single point mutation in the -globin gene. Specifically, it involves the substitution of the amino acid glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position of the -polypeptide chain.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 66 breaths per minute, chest indrawing, nasal flaring, and poor feeding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Severe pneumonia

The clinical presentation of a 4-month-old child with fast breathing (>50 beats/min for 2-12 months), chest indrawaing along with the presence of a danger sign(poor feeding) strongly points towards the diagnosis of severe pneumonia. The treatment for severe pneumonia is to administer IV antibiotics and refer to a higher centre.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

* Pneumonia: with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

Age of child

Fast breathing RR

<2 months

>60 breaths/min

2-12 months

>50 breaths/min

1-5 years

>40 breaths/min

* Severe pneumonia: Pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs of pneumonia in children include:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

If a child has only a fever, cough or cold, it is categorised as no pneumonia.
questions.learning: Severe pneumonia — The clinical presentation of a 4-month-old child with fast breathing (>50 beats/min for 2-12 months), chest indrawaing along with the presence of a danger sign(poor feeding) strongly points towards the diagnosis of severe pneumonia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 2-year-old child was eating peanuts when he suddenly developed respiratory distress, cough, and was unable to speak. What is the initial treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Perform Heimlich maneuver

In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts.

The rescuer should stand or kneel behind the patient and wrap his arms around the patient’s waist. A fist is made with one hand and using the other hand, the fist is driven into the patient’s abdomen with a rapid, forceful upward thrust so as to dislodge the foreign body. This is continued until the foreign body is expelled or if the patient becomes unresponsive.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

In a choking infant who is responsive, 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades and 5 downward thrusts on the chest are given in order to dislodge the foreign body.

If the patient becomes unresponsive, immediately start CPR.

Other Options:

Option A: The blind finger sweep should be avoided in infants to avoid pushing the object further inside the airway. However, it can be done for unresponsive adults with complete FBAO. With the patient's face up, the mouth is opened by grasping both the tongue and lower jaw and lifting the mandible. The index finger is inserted along the inside of the cheek and using a hooking action, the foreign body is dislodged and removed.

Option B: Endoscopic removal is wrong as an initial treatment because it's not an immediate life-saving measure and requires time to set up and organize. It can be attempted once the airway is stabilized.

Option C: Immediate X-ray is wrong as initial treatment because it delays essential life-saving intervention. Not all foreign bodies are radio-opaque (especially peanuts) and the patient needs immediate intervention for respiratory distress.
questions.learning: Perform Heimlich maneuver — In a choking child (more than 1 year old) or an adult, the first step to be done is to perform Heimlich maneuver, which involves delivering abdominal thrusts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 34-year-old man presents with a painless right groin lump extending into the scrotum. On examination, a cough impulse is noted when pressing with the index finger on the swelling, and the swelling can be fully reduced through the deep inguinal ring with an audible gurgling sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of a groin lump extending into the scrotum that is reducible through the deep inguinal ring definitively identifies an Indirect Inguinal Hernia . Indirect hernias enter the inguinal canal through the internal (deep) ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and often follow the path of the spermatic cord into the scrotum. The "gurgling sound" noted during reduction is a classic sign indicating that the hernia sac contains loops of bowel. Direct inguinal hernias (Option B) occur through a weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach’s triangle) and do not typically enter the scrotum or reduce through the deep ring. Femoral hernias (Option A) are found below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and are more common in females. Umbilical hernias (Option D) occur at the navel. Because the defect is specifically associated with the deep inguinal ring and reaches the scrotum, indirect inguinal hernia is the correct anatomical diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical findings of a groin lump extending into the scrotum that is reducible through the deep inguinal ring definitively identifies an Indirect Inguinal Hernia .

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enhances iron absorption?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin C

Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C.

Vitamin C reduces the ferric iron to its ferrous form, thereby helping in the process of absorption of dietary iron from the intestine.

Vitamin C deficiency causes

• Decreased absorption of iron leading to microcytic-hypochromic anemia
• Decreased hydroxylation of proline and lysine, which results in defective collagen synthesis and bleeding manifestations.

Conversely, vitamin C toxicity (>2000 mg/ day) can lead to iron overloaded states.

Note: Alcohol and fructose also enhance iron absorption. However, the absorption of both inorganic and heme iron is impaired by calcium. So, a glass of milk with a meal significantly reduces iron availability.
questions.learning: Vitamin C Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C. Vitamin C reduces the ferric iron to its ferrous form, thereby helping in the process of absorption of dietary iron from the intestine.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which structure does the anterior ethmoidal sinus drain into?
questions.explanation: The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity through specific meatuses located beneath the nasal turbinates. The anterior ethmoidal sinuses, along with the frontal and maxillary sinuses, drain into the middle meatus, primarily via the hiatus semilunaris or ethmoid infundibulum. The inferior meatus (Option B) is exclusively the drainage site for the nasolacrimal duct. The superior meatus (Option C) receives drainage from the posterior ethmoidal sinuses. The sphenoethmoidal recess (Option D), located posterior and superior to the superior turbinate, receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus. Understanding these anatomical drainage pathways is clinically essential for diagnosing sinusitis and for planning Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS). Obstruction of the "osteomeatal complex" in the middle meatus is the most frequent cause of chronic rhinosinusitis. Thus, the middle meatus serves as the primary drainage hub for the most commonly affected anterior sinuses
questions.learning: The paranasal sinuses drain into the nasal cavity through specific meatuses located beneath the nasal turbinates. The anterior ethmoidal sinuses, along with the frontal and maxillary sinuses, drain into the middle meatus, primarily via the hiatus…

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A term neonate weighing 2 kg, delivered to a primigravida mother through vaginal route and through clear liquor, is found having gasping respiratory efforts after performing the initial steps in the delivery room. The next step in resuscitation is:
options: Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using 30% oxygen
Intubate and initiate positive pressure ventilation using 30% oxygen
Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using room air
Intubate and initiate positive pressure ventilation using room air
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using room air

• The neonate has gasping respirations after the initial steps of newborn resuscitation. Gasping is considered ineffective breathing, so positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) must be initiated immediately.
• For a term neonate, PPV is started with room air (21% oxygen).

Why not the other options?

• A. PPV with 30% oxygen: Incorrect. For term/late-preterm neonates, initial PPV is generally started with 21% oxygen.
• B. Intubation + 30% oxygen: Intubation is not routinely required as the first step; begin with bag-mask PPV.
• D. Intubation + room air: Although room air is appropriate initially, immediate intubation is not required unless bag-mask ventilation is ineffective or specific indications for intubation are present.
questions.learning: Initiate positive pressure ventilation with bag and mask using room air • The neonate has gasping respirations after the initial steps of newborn resuscitation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Supravital stains are used in the identification of all except ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Copper in tissue

In the following options all except copper can be visualised by supravital stains like methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue.

Reticulocytes have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA which can be stained by supravital stains.Reticulocytosis indicates effective erythropoiesis, which refers to a good bone marrow response to anemia which is seen hemolytic anemias and acute blood loss.

Heinz bodies are seen in G6PD deficiency where the RBCs are exposed to high levels of oxidants causing the cross-linking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains. The globin chains become denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates known as Heinz bodies which can cause intravascular hemolysis. These can be detected by supravital staining.

Histology of non-hodgkin lymphoma in an elderly male, showing reticulocytosis and spherocytosis:

Note:

To visualize the copper in tissues e.g in Wilson's disease, liver biopsy samples are stained using rubeanic acid/rhodanine stain to visualize the cytoplasmic copper.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 46-year-old male presented with chronic back pain and neck stiffness. X-ray cervical spine is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

The given clinical scenario and the radiograph showing ossification of the anterior longitudinal ligament, in front of the C2 to C7 cervical vertebral bodies, point towards a diagnosis of Diffuse Idiopathic Skeletal Hyperostosis (DISH). It is also referred to as Forestier disease.

DISH is a common disorder characterized by bone and calcium formation at the sites of ligamentous insertions. It occurs in the middle-aged or elderly. The radiograph shows calcification of anterior and sometimes posterior longitudinal ligaments appearing as flowing or dripping-like candle wax. It is usually asymptomatic but the calcification might cause compression of the spinal cord and can be better visualized on CT and MRI. In contrast to ankylosing spondylitis, the sacroiliac joints are usually spared.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 3-day-old neonate presented with recurrent bilious vomiting. An X-ray erect abdomen is given below. What is the next best step in managing this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gastrograffin follow-through

Explanation:

The given clinical history with an x-ray showing a triple bubble sign is suggestive of jejunal atresia. The next best step is to perform a contrast study to localize the site of obstruction.

Small bowel atresias present with intestinal obstruction soon after birth.

• Bilious vomiting is the dominant feature in jejunal atresia
• Abdominal distension is more prominent in ileal atresia

A small amount of pale meconium may be passed, despite the atresia.

Plain abdomen radiographs in a jejunal/ileal atresia case will show multiple air-fluid levels and dilated loops. They don't reliably distinguish small and large bowels in neonates and hence contrast studies are often required to localize the obstruction.

Water-soluble enemas (Gastrogaffin, Hypaque) are particularly useful in differentiating atresia from meconium ileus and Hirschsprung disease. Contrast studies also help to rule out distal intestinal obstruction and occasionally may act therapeutically to relieve obstructions.

In most cases of jejunal/ileal atresia, the distal end of the dilated proximal small bowel is resected and a primary end-to-end anastomosis is done. If the proximal bowel is extremely dilated, it may need to be tapered to the distal bowel before anastomosis.

Other options:

Option A:  CT is not recommended for neonates owing to the harmful effects of radiation.

Option C: USG abdomen does not help to localize the site of obstruction and is more useful in the diagnosis of intussusception, where there is an abdominal mass.

Option D: Explorative laparotomy is not done for diagnosing intestinal atresias.
questions.learning: Gastrograffin follow-through Explanation: — The given clinical history with an x-ray showing a triple bubble sign is suggestive of jejunal atresia. The next best step is to perform a contrast study to localize the site of obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presents with amenorrhea for the past three months. Ultrasound examination reveals the following findings: [details]. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these ultrasound results?
options: Multiple renal cysts in the fetus
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays a classic "snowstorm" or "honeycomb" appearance within the uterine cavity, characterized by a mass of multiple small, translucent vesicles . Combined with the clinical history of amenorrhea (3 months) in a young woman, this finding is pathognomonic for a Hydatidiform mole (gestational trophoblastic disease). Ectopic pregnancy (Option A) would show an empty uterus and a gestational sac elsewhere, typically in the fallopian tube. Renal cysts (Option C) and oligohydramnios (Option D) are fetal anomalies that would require the presence of a distinct fetus, which is absent in a complete mole. Molar pregnancies are associated with extremely high levels of serum beta-hCG and risk of choriocarcinoma. Therefore, based on the definitive "snowstorm" visual and the clinical context of pregnancy-related symptoms without a visible embryo, Hydatidiform mole is the correct diagnosis. Management involves urgent suction and evacuation of the uterus
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays a classic "snowstorm" or "honeycomb" appearance within the uterine cavity, characterized by a mass of multiple small, translucent vesicles .

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which macrovascular complication typically occurs in the later stages of diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation: Chronic complications of diabetes mellitus are broadly categorized into microvascular and macrovascular groups. Macrovascular complications result from damage to large blood vessels due to accelerated atherosclerosis. Coronary artery disease (Option A) is the primary macrovascular complication, leading to myocardial infarction and heart failure. Other macrovascular diseases include stroke (cerebrovascular disease) and peripheral artery disease. Nephropathy (Option C) and retinopathy (Option D) are microvascular complications, meaning they involve the damage of small capillaries in the kidneys and eyes, respectively. A foot ulcer (Option B) is a complex complication usually resulting from a combination of microvascular neuropathy and macrovascular peripheral artery disease, but it is not classified purely as a macrovascular disease. Because CAD involves the major arteries of the heart, it is the classic example of diabetic macrovascular pathology
questions.learning: Chronic complications of diabetes mellitus are broadly categorized into microvascular and macrovascular groups. Macrovascular complications result from damage to large blood vessels due to accelerated atherosclerosis.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The given chest X-ray is suggestive of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot

The given chest X-ray shows a boot-shaped cardiac silhouette which is suggestive of the Tetralogy of Fallot.

The boot-shaped (coeur en sabot) cardiac silhouette is seen due to the right ventricular hypertrophy and upward shift of the cardiac apex. The hilar areas and lung fields appear relatively clear due to reduced pulmonary blood flow or the small size of the pulmonary arteries, or both.

In Ebsteins's anomaly (Option D) box-shaped heart is seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The female patient comes to the ER with palpitations and syncopal attacks following exercise. She has had similar episodes in the past. An ECG was done as follows. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia

The ECG provided shows epsilon waves and T wave inversions, which is a hallmark finding suggestive of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD).

The clinical presentation of young females with palpitations and syncope, especially post-exercise, are common in ARVD due to ventricular arrhythmias.

The changes marked in ECG show a notched deflection at the end of the QRS complex due to delayed ventricular activation known as an epsilon wave. It is commonly seen in patients with ARVD.

ARVD is autosomal dominant cardiomyopathy characterized by fibrofatty replacement in the myocardium of the ventricles. It most commonly affects the right ventricle. It is due to mutations in the gene encoding desmosome-associated protein plakophilin 2. This leads to defective cell-adhesion proteins in the desmosomes that link adjacent cardiac myocytes.

The patients usually present with rhythm disturbances, right-sided heart failure, and sudden cardiac death. ARVD is associated with Naxos syndrome. This syndrome is characterised by arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and hyperkeratosis of the palmar and the plantar surfaces.

Morphology shows severe thinning of the right ventricular wall due to loss of myocytes, accompanied by extensive fatty infiltration and fibrosis. In ARVD, there is T inversion and delayed ventricular activation manifesting as epsilon waves. This reflects the involvement of the right ventricular myocardium.

Other options

Option A: Uhl’s disease is rare and typically associated with the absence of RV muscle. It does not have specific ECG patterns like those in ARVD.

Option C: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) usually shows LV hypertrophy with left-axis deviation and repolarization abnormalities, particularly in lateral leads.

Option D: Brugada syndrome is characterized by coved-type ST elevation in leads V1-V3, not T wave inversions as seen here.
questions.learning: Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia — The ECG provided shows epsilon waves and T wave inversions, which is a hallmark finding suggestive of Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia (ARVD).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following acts as a major intracellular antioxidant and helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species?
questions.explanation: Glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant responsible for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine. Glutathione detoxifies ROS by donating electrons, converting harmful radicals into less reactive compounds, and is also essential for regenerating other antioxidants like vitamins C and E. While other enzymes are involved in the antioxidant defense, they have more specific roles: Superoxide dismutase (Option C) specifically converts superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide. Catalase (Option B) then converts that hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Peroxidase (Option D) breaks down peroxides using reducing agents, often utilizing glutathione as a donor. Because glutathione acts as the central hub for electron donation and cellular redox balance, it is classified as the major intracellular antioxidant
questions.learning: Glutathione is the primary intracellular antioxidant responsible for neutralizing reactive oxygen species (ROS). It is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Endometrial sampling for diagnosis of ovulation is done on which day of menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 21st–23rd day

Endometrial biopsy to assess ovulation is performed during the late secretory (premenstrual) phase, typically on days 21–23 of a 28-day menstrual cycle. The presence of secretory endometrium confirms that ovulation has occurred.

Why not the other options?

• A. 8th–10th day: Early proliferative phase.
• B. 12th day: Late proliferative phase, before ovulation.
• C. 14th day: Around the time of ovulation; secretory changes have not yet developed.
questions.learning: 21st–23rd day Endometrial biopsy to assess ovulation is performed during the late secretory (premenstrual) phase, typically on days 21–23 of a 28-day menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All the following conditions are manifestations of IgG4RD except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Crescentic glomerulonephritis

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a chronic fibroinflammatory disorder characterized by:

• Dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration
• Storiform fibrosis
• Obliterative phlebitis
• Often elevated serum IgG4 levels
• Commonly affects multiple organs and produces tumefactive (mass-like) lesions.

Common manifestations of IgG4-RD:

• Autoimmune pancreatitis (most classic)
• IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis
• Orbital pseudotumor / dacryoadenitis
• Retroperitoneal fibrosis
• Lymphoplasmacytic aortitis
• Salivary & lacrimal gland enlargement (Mikulicz disease)
• Tubulointerstitial nephritis (most common renal involvement)

Why crescentic glomerulonephritis is NOT seen:

• IgG4-RD typically causes tubulointerstitial nephritis, not primary glomerular disease
• Crescentic GN is characteristic of:

o    ANCA-associated vasculitis

o    Anti-GBM disease

o    Immune complex GN

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Please provide an evaluation of the placement of the pacemaker lead.
questions.explanation: In a standard chest X-ray evaluation of a single-chamber permanent pacemaker, the lead is typically visualized passing through the superior vena cava, into the right atrium, and terminating in the apex of the right ventricle. The right ventricle is the most common site for lead placement because it is easily accessible via the venous system and provides reliable ventricular pacing. Placement in the left atrium (Option B) or left ventricle (Option C) would usually require a more complex approach (such as via the coronary sinus for biventricular pacing) and is not the standard location for a primary lead. The superior vena cava (Option D) is a conduit for the lead but not its final functional position. Radiologists check for proper lead tip positioning, absence of perforation, and lead integrity to ensure the device functions correctly
questions.learning: In a standard chest X-ray evaluation of a single-chamber permanent pacemaker, the lead is typically visualized passing through the superior vena cava, into the right atrium, and terminating in the apex of the right ventricle.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false about the umbilical cord?
options: It has one artery and two veins
It contains a gelatinous substance called Wharton's jelly
Presence of a single umbilical artery is associated with congenital anomalies
Normal average umbilical cord length is 50-60 cms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It has one artery and two veins

The umbilical cord normally has two arteries and one vein. The presence of a single umbilical artery is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord. It is associated with congenital anomalies such as genitourinary and cardiac anomalies.

The umbilical cord is a tube that connects the fetus to the placenta. It contains umbilical vessels and an obliterated allantois duct, all surrounded by Wharton's jelly and contained within an outer layer of amnion. Maternal blood enters the fetus through the umbilical vein, and blood exits the fetus via the two umbilical arteries. Wharton's jelly is a gelatinous mucopolysaccharide that protects the umbilical vessels. Local collections of Wharton's jelly produce false knots in the cord.

The average length of the umbilical cord is between 40-70 cm at term. A long cord can form a loop around the fetus' neck and can cause asphyxia. A short cord can result in cord rupture during labor.
questions.learning: It has one artery and two veins — The umbilical cord normally has two arteries and one vein. The presence of a single umbilical artery is the most common vascular anomaly of the cord.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. She is diagnosed with endometriosis and undergoes diagnostic laparoscopy, which reveals extensive pelvic adhesions, with the intestines adherent to the upper uterus and the ovaries fused together forming cystic masses. Following these findings, what should be the next appropriate step in her management?
options: Gestrinone to decrease the LH surge
questions.explanation: For a 30-year-old patient who wishes to conceive (infertility) but has extensive stage IV endometriosis, the goal of management is to restore normal pelvic anatomy and preserve fertility. The most appropriate subsequent course of action during laparoscopy is cystectomy of the ovarian endometriomas and extensive adhesiolysis (Option C). This procedure aims to free the ovaries and intestines and excise the cystic disease to improve the chances of spontaneous conception or success with assisted reproduction. LUNA (Option A) is an older procedure for pain that does not address fertility or adhesions. Gestrinone (Option B) is a medical therapy that suppresses the cycle but will not clear established adhesions or large cysts. Hysterectomy and oophorectomy (Option D) are "definitive" but radical treatments that would result in permanent surgical menopause and total loss of fertility, which is inappropriate for this young woman
questions.learning: For a 30-year-old patient who wishes to conceive (infertility) but has extensive stage IV endometriosis, the goal of management is to restore normal pelvic anatomy and preserve fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a patient diagnosed with unilateral breast cancer, what potential risk should be considered when initiating treatment with tamoxifen?
options: Breast cancer in the opposite breast
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. While it acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast, it acts as an estrogen agonist (stimulator) in the uterus. This stimulatory effect on the uterine lining significantly increases the potential risk of developing endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer (Option B). This is a well-documented long-term side effect that requires regular gynecological monitoring for any abnormal bleeding. Paradoxically, tamoxifen actually reduces the risk of cancer in the opposite (contralateral) breast (Option C), which is one of its primary therapeutic benefits. It is not associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer (Option A) or cervical cancer (Option D). Therefore, the tissue-specific estrogenic action on the endometrium is the primary oncological risk associated with its use
questions.learning: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. While it acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast, it acts as an estrogen agonist (stimulator) in the uterus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Our body was built to identify toxic substance by the recognition of bitter taste. Which of the following substances is responsible for the bitter taste?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alkalaoids

Alkaloids cause an intensely bitter taste, that causes the rejection of the food.

Bitter taste sensations are caused by two particular classes of substances:

• Long-chain organic substances that contain nitrogen.
• Alkaloids

Alkaloids cause an intensely bitter taste, leading to the rejection of certain foods. They are found in many medicinal drugs such as quinine, caffeine, strychnine, and nicotine. The bitter taste sensation in many deadly toxins found in poisonous plants is often caused by alkaloids. This helps the person or animal to reject the food.

Sweet taste is caused by chemicals such as sugars, glycols, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, amides, esters, some amino acids, some small proteins, sulfonic acids, halogenated acids, and inorganic salts of lead and beryllium.

Sour taste is caused by acids (Hydrogen ion concentration). The sour taste is directly proportional to the strength of the acid.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: During inspiration, the systolic blood pressure decreases due to:
options: Increased venous return to the right heart transiently reduces LV filling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Increased venous return to the right heart transiently reduces LV filling

During inspiration, intrathoracic pressure becomes more negative.

This has two major cardiovascular consequences:

1️⃣ Increased venous return to the right heart

Negative intrathoracic pressure pulls more blood from systemic veins into the right atrium and right ventricle.

2️⃣ Interventricular septal shift

Because the RV fills more, the RV expands and pushes the interventricular septum toward the LV.

This causes:

• Reduced LV filling
• Reduced LV stroke volume
• Transient fall in systolic BP

Hence systolic BP normally falls by about 5 mmHg during inspiration.

Mechanism Flow- Inspiration → ↓ Intrathoracic pressure → ↑ Venous return to RV → RV dilation → Septum shifts left → ↓ LV filling → ↓ Stroke volume → ↓ Systolic BP

Interventricular Dependence- Both ventricles share the pericardial space. When RV filling increases suddenly:

• RV expands
• LV chamber size decreases temporarily
• LV stroke volume falls

This phenomenon is called ventricular interdependence.

A) Decreased pulmonary compliance- Pulmonary compliance affects lung mechanics, not the primary mechanism of inspiratory BP drop.

B) Increased peripheral vascular resistance- Peripheral resistance does not increase during inspiration and is unrelated to the transient BP fall.

C) Increased left ventricular filling-This is the opposite of what happens.

Inspiration → LV filling decreases due to septal shift.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 36-year- old farmer presenting with a one-week history of cough and chest pain, along with persistent fatigue for the past month and abnormal findings on chest X-ray?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray displays a classic Hydatid Cyst, caused by the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus. A characteristic radiological sign seen in pulmonary hydatid disease is the "Water-lily sign" (Camelot sign), which occurs when the endocyst ruptures and its membranes float on the surface of the remaining fluid. Anthrax (Option B) usually presents as a severe pneumonia with widened mediastinum. Silicosis (Option C) shows small, nodular opacities in the upper lobes with hilar "eggshell" calcification. Byssinosis (Option D) is an occupational lung disease from cotton dust and typically does not show large discrete cysts. Hydatid cysts are common in farmers and people in contact with dogs and sheep (the definitive and intermediate hosts). Given the patient's occupation and the pathognomonic radiological appearance of a large, well-defined pulmonary cyst, Hydatid cyst is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old patient with a long history of tobacco chewing presents with a persistent whitish lesion in the gingivobuccal sulcus for the past seven months, raising suspicion of malignancy. What is the appropriate line of management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of a persistent whitish lesion (leukoplakia) in the gingivobuccal sulcus, especially in a chronic tobacco user, is a classic precancerous presentation that necessitates definitive diagnosis. The correct management is an incisional or excisional biopsy to rule out squamous cell carcinoma or varying grades of dysplasia. "Wait and watch" (Option B) is dangerous and inappropriate, as a biopsy is the only way to confirm if malignancy is already present. Steroidal injections (Option C) are used for inflammatory conditions like lichen planus but would be ineffective and potentially mask the progression of a cancer. Sclerotherapy (Option D) is used for vascular malformations or varicose veins and has no role in the management of oral mucosal lesions. Therefore, given the high correlation between tobacco chewing and oral cancer, immediate biopsy via local excision is the only safe and professional course of action to ensure early detection and treatment
questions.learning: The presence of a persistent whitish lesion (leukoplakia) in the gingivobuccal sulcus, especially in a chronic tobacco user, is a classic precancerous presentation that necessitates definitive diagnosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 15-year-old boy presents with tremors, dysarthria, and behavioral changes. Examination reveals hepatomegaly and a golden-brown Kayser–Fleischer ring at the corneal limbus, raising suspicion of Wilson’s disease. Which investigation is best to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Wilson's Disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and systemic copper accumulation. While low serum ceruloplasmin (Option A) and high urinary copper (Option D) are important screening tools, the gold standard for definitive diagnosis is a liver biopsy with quantitative copper estimation. This directly measures the pathological buildup of the metal in the tissue. Serum copper (Option C) is generally low in these patients because most copper in the blood is normally bound to ceruloplasmin, which is deficient. The presence of a Kayser-Fleischer ring (Option B) is highly suggestive of neurological involvement, but the tissue biopsy remains the most accurate confirmatory test. Management involves long-term chelation therapy or zinc supplements to inhibit further copper absorption
questions.learning: Wilson's Disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, leading to impaired biliary copper excretion and systemic copper accumulation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. On examination, a bluish hue is seen in vagina. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Imperforate Hymen

Imperforate Hymen is the most common obstructive cause of primary amenorrhea.

Pathophysiology

The hymenal membrane fails to perforate during fetal development, blocking menstrual outflow.

When menstruation begins:

• Blood accumulates in the vagina (hematocolpos)
• May extend to uterus (hematometra)

This causes the classic bluish bulging hymen.

Accumulation of menstrual blood behind the obstruction leads to:

• Hematocolpos → blood in vagina
• Hematometra → blood in uterus

Symptoms include:

• Pelvic pain
• Urinary retention
• Constipation (due to pelvic pressure)

Treatment:-

Cruciate incision of hymen (hymenotomy) to allow drainage of retained blood.

Small incision made in hymen --> Evacuation of retained menstrual blood --> Hymenal edges sutured

B) Transverse Vaginal Septum

• Congenital obstruction within the vagina, not at hymen.
• Usually no bluish bulging hymen.

C) Mayer–Rokitansky–Küster–Hauser (MRKH) Syndrome

Features:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Absent uterus and upper vagina
• Normal secondary sexual characters

There is no bluish bulge.

D) OHVIRA Syndrome

Features:

• Uterus didelphys
• Obstructed hemivagina
• Ipsilateral renal agenesis

Usually presents with pelvic pain and mass, not the typical bluish hymenal bulge.
questions.learning: Imperforate Hymen Imperforate Hymen is the most common obstructive cause of primary amenorrhea. Pathophysiology The hymenal membrane fails to perforate during fetal development, blocking menstrual outflow.

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. NaF and K oxalate

Since it contains sodium fluoride, the fluoride will inhibit the glycolytic enzyme enolase. Potassium oxalate binds to calcium and inhibits coagulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient who is on treatment for angina, presents to you with erectile dysfunction. You decide against prescribing sildenafil because the patient is being treated with _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nitrates

The patient would be on nitrates for angina and thus should not be prescribed sildenafil as sildenafil causes dangerous potentiation of nitrate action resulting in severe hypotension.

The combination of the two drugs has a synergistic action on the intracellular cGMP levels that can result in uninhibited vasodilation and a precipitous fall in blood pressure. Hence, the use of sildenafil is a contraindication when on nitrates.
questions.learning: Nitrates — The patient would be on nitrates for angina and thus should not be prescribed sildenafil as sildenafil causes dangerous potentiation of nitrate action resulting in severe hypotension.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 39 year old patient presents to the OPD with complaints of pain over his ear lobule. He also complains of difficulty in eating food and the inability to close his eyes completely. On examination, there is a swelling below his ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve

The clinical scenario of pain over the ear lobule, inability to close eyes, and difficulty in eating point toward an injury to the facial nerve. The swelling could possibly be a parotid swelling injuring the facial nerve. The course of facial nerve is given below

Nerve supply of external ear

Pinna

* Greater/Great auricular nerve - medial surface and posterior part of lateral surface (lobule, posterior part of helix and anti helix).

* Lesser occipital nerve - upper part of medial surface.

* Auriculotemporal nerve - tragus, crus of helix and adjacent part of helix.

* Auricular branch of vagus (Arnold's nerve or Alderman's nerve) - concha on the lateral surface and post auricular groove medially.

* Facial nerve - concha and post auricular groove along with Arnold's nerve.

External Auditory Canal

* Auriculotemporal nerve - anterior wall and roof

* Auricular branch of vagus - posterior wall and floor

* Facial nerve - sensory supply to the posterior wall through the vagus

Tympanic Membrane

* Auriculotemporal nerve - anterior half of lateral surface

* Auricular branch of vagus - posterior half of lateral surface

* Tympanic branch of Glossopharyngeal - medial surface
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The clinical scenario of pain over the ear lobule, inability to close eyes, and difficulty in eating point toward an injury to the facial nerve.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: When a doctor is summoned to court to give evidence, the nature of the testimony depends on the doctor’s professional knowledge and the circumstances of the case. Which statement correctly describes the role or type of witness in this situation?
questions.explanation: In legal proceedings, a doctor typically testifies as an "expert witness." Unlike a common witness (Option B), who can only testify to facts they personally perceived through their senses (what they saw or heard), an expert witness is permitted to provide opinions based on their specialized training, skill, and experience. For example, a doctor can testify not just that a wound existed, but also offer an expert opinion on the type of weapon used or the cause of death. Oral evidence (Option A) refers to the medium of delivery rather than the status of the witness. A hostile witness (Option D) is someone who shows bias against the party that called them, leading the court to allow cross-examination by that same party. While a doctor's testimony is a form of oral evidence, their primary legal classification in a professional capacity is that of an expert, whose role is to assist the court in understanding complex medical facts

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which infection contracted in pregnancy won't be teratogenic?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HSV 2

Herpes simplex virus type 2 usually causes neonatal infection during delivery, not congenital malformations. Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 mainly causes neonatal herpes infection during delivery through contact with infected genital lesions. Certain infections during pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause congenital anomalies in the fetus. These are classically remembered under TORCH Infections. Common teratogenic infections

| Infection | Fetal effects

| --------- | -------------

| Rubella | Cataracts, PDA, deafness
Classic triad:

• Cataracts
• Patent ductus arteriosus
• Sensorineural deafness

| CMV | Microcephaly, periventricular calcification, Hearing loss

| Varicella (Chickenpox) | Limb hypoplasia, skin scarring, Neurological defects

| Toxoplasmosis | Hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis
questions.learning: HSV 2 Herpes simplex virus type 2 usually causes neonatal infection during delivery, not congenital malformations. Herpes Simplex Virus Type 2 mainly causes neonatal herpes infection during delivery through contact with infected genital lesions.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a patient diagnosed with dysgerminoma of the ovary, which tumor marker is most likely to be elevated? (NEET PG 2015)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)

Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant germ cell tumor of the ovary and is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma in males. The tumor marker most commonly elevated in dysgerminoma is Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)

Important tumor marker associations:

• Dysgerminoma → LDH (sometimes β-hCG mildly elevated)
• Yolk sac tumor → AFP
• Choriocarcinoma → β-hCG
• Epithelial ovarian tumors → CA-125

Clinical features of dysgerminoma:

• Occurs in adolescents and young women
• Rapidly enlarging pelvic mass
• Highly radiosensitive and chemosensitive
• Excellent prognosis with treatment
questions.learning: Serum Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) Dysgerminoma is the most common malignant germ cell tumor of the ovary and is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma in males.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman reports headaches for the past nine months that worsen on lying down and gradually improve during the day. She has a history of oral contraceptive use, and fundoscopic examination shows papilledema without any focal neurological deficits. What is the most likely cause of her headaches?0 0000000
questions.explanation: Pseudotumor cerebri, also known as Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), is a condition characterized by increased intracranial pressure without an identifiable cause like a tumor or infection. It typically affects young, obese females, and its development is strongly associated with the use of oral contraceptives, Vitamin A toxicity, or tetracyclines. The headache is classically worse when lying down (due to further increases in intracranial pressure) and may improve when upright. The hallmark finding is bilateral "papilledema" on fundus examination, which reflects the high pressure being transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths. Crucially, the neurological exam remains normal otherwise. Myasthenia gravis (Option A) causes fatigable muscle weakness, not headaches. Temporal arteritis (Option B) affects older adults and presents with scalp tenderness and high ESR. Chronic migraine (Option C) does not cause papilledema. Therefore, given the demographic, oral contraceptive use, and papilledema without focal deficits, Pseudotumor cerebri is the most likely diagnosis. Management includes weight loss, acetazolamide, and monitoring vision
questions.learning: Pseudotumor cerebri, also known as Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH), is a condition characterized by increased intracranial pressure without an identifiable cause like a tumor or infection.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male presents with 2 weeks of cough, fever and night sweats. Investigations reveal a CD4 count of 100 /μL. Which of the following infections is most likely to be seen in him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mycobacterium avium complex

The clinical vignette suggests opportunistic infection in HIV patients. The most common opportunistic infection when CD4 counts falls below 100 is disseminated mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections

Mycobacterium avium complex, or Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare complex, is a group of slow-growing, nonchromogenic non-tuberculous mycobacteria. The infections occur in both immunocompetent and immunosuppressed patients. It is the most frequent organism affecting HIV and immunosuppressed patients, although about 40% of pulmonary infections occur in immunocompetent patients. Cervical lymphadenitis is the most common presentation in young children of age <5 years. Other manifestations include skin, and soft tissue infections, musculoskeletal infections, and disseminated disease

Treatment with either clarithromycin or azithromycin plus ethambutol is a preferred initial therapy along with starting anti-retroviral therapy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Barium swallow

The given image shows a barium swallow. It is a type of imaging where the patient ingests barium, a contrast agent, to visualize the esophagus and detect abnormalities. The described indentations in the esophageal lumen caused by anterior osteophytes (bony outgrowths) are characteristic findings that can be seen with a barium swallow.

Fluoroscopy (option A) is a technique that provides real-time X-ray images and is often used during procedures like a barium swallow, but the term is more general. X-ray of alkali ingestion (Option B) and X-ray of acid ingestion (option D) might show damage to the esophagus in barium swallow which is not seen in the image.
