questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A P1L1 lady after 4 hours of delivery is suffering from persistent, severe pain in the perineal region, rectal tenesmus, bearing down feeling and retention of urine. The probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vulval hematoma

Vulval hematoma is a postpartum complication caused by injury to the branches of the pudendal artery or vulval veins during vaginal delivery, episiotomy, or perineal tears. Blood collects in the loose connective tissue of the vulva, causing a tense, painful swelling. Since the bleeding is concealed, significant blood loss may occur without obvious external bleeding. The classical presentation is:

• Severe perineal pain out of proportion to examination findings
• Perineal swelling
• Rectal tenesmus
• Bearing-down sensation
• Urinary retention due to compression of the urethra and bladder neck.

Why not the other options?

• A. Cervical tear: Presents with persistent postpartum hemorrhage despite a well-contracted uterus, not severe perineal pain.
• C. Supralevator hematoma: Usually presents with pelvic pain and shock, with minimal visible vulval swelling.
• D. Complete perineal tear: Presents immediately after delivery with disruption of the anal sphincter and rectal mucosa, not as a delayed painful swelling with urinary retention.
questions.learning: Vulval hematoma Vulval hematoma is a postpartum complication caused by injury to the branches of the pudendal artery or vulval veins during vaginal delivery, episiotomy, or perineal tears.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are probable sites for Ectopic pancreas? 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum 2. Liver 3. Small bowel mesentery 4. Splenic hilum Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Ectopic (heterotopic) pancreas is pancreatic tissue located outside the normal pancreas without any anatomical or vascular continuity. It is most commonly found in the upper gastrointestinal tract but may occur at several other sites.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Submucosa of the stomach and duodenum ✔️: Correct. Most common site (also jejunum).
• 2. Liver ✔️: Correct. Rare but reported site.
• 3. Small bowel mesentery ✔️: Correct. Rare site.
• 4. Splenic hilum ❌: Incorrect. Not a recognized site of ectopic pancreas.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Ectopic (heterotopic) pancreas is pancreatic tissue located outside the normal pancreas without any anatomical or vascular continuity. It is most commonly found in the upper gastrointestinal tract but may occur at several other sites.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the obstetric grip performed in the picture.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic grip

The obstetric grip shown in the picture is a pelvic grip.

Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head. They are as follows:

* Fundal grip (first Leopold): Assesses the uterine fundus.

* Helps in the identification of fetal lie and determination of fetal pole at the fundus.

* The breech is felt as a large, irregular mass. The head feels hard and round and is more mobile.

* Lateral grip (second Leopold):  Assesses fetal orientation.

* The palms are placed on either side of the maternal abdomen, and gentle but deep pressure is exerted.

* The back is felt on one side as a hard, resistant structure. The fetal extremities are felt on the other side as numerous small, irregular, mobile parts.

* Pawlik's grip/ 1st pelvic grip (third Leopold): Assesses the presenting part.

* The thumb and fingers of one hand grasp the lower portion of the maternal abdomen just above the symphysis pubis.

* If the presenting part is not engaged, a movable mass will be felt, usually the head.

* Deep pelvic grip/ 2nd pelvic grip (fourth Leopold): Assesses the engagement and attitude of the fetal head.

* The examiner faces the mother's feet, and the fingertips of both hands are positioned on either side of the presenting part.

* They exert inward pressure and then slide along the axis of the pelvic outlet.
questions.learning: Pelvic grip — The obstetric grip shown in the picture is a pelvic grip. Leopold's manoeuvres help assess the fetal pole, lie, presenting part, engagement, and attitude of the fetal head.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with short stature, muscle weakness, and learning difficulties. Chromosomal analysis shows a deletion on the short arm of chromosome 15 (15p) inherited from the paternal side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS) is a classic example of genomic imprinting, caused by a deletion on the paternal chromosome 15q11-q13. Clinically, it presents with neonatal hypotonia (muscle weakness), short stature, intellectual disability, and a characteristic insatiable hunger leading to obesity. Regarding the distractors, Angelman syndrome (Option A) involves a deletion at the same chromosomal locus but on the maternal side; it presents differently with frequent laughter and severe ataxia. Cri du chat syndrome (Option C) is caused by a deletion on chromosome 5p and is marked by a distinctive high-pitched cat-like cry. Rett syndrome (Option D) is an X-linked disorder typically seen in females, characterized by developmental regression and hand-wringing behaviors. Therefore, because the genetic defect originates from the paternal allele on chromosome 15, Prader-Willi is the correct diagnosis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child can ride a tricycle, copies a circle, knows name and gender. The developmental age of this child is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 years

Developmental milestones are assessed in four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social skills. The combination of riding a tricycle, copying a circle, and knowing one’s name and gender are classic milestones of a 3-year-old child.

Why is B correct?

The child demonstrates the following 3-year milestones:

• Rides a tricycle ✔ (Gross motor)
• Copies a circle ✔ (Fine motor)
• Knows own name and gender ✔ (Language/Personal-social)

These milestones correspond to a developmental age of 3 years.

Why not the other options?

• A. 2 years ✘

• Runs well
• Climbs stairs with both feet on each step
• Tower of 6 blocks
• Uses 2-word sentences
• Vocabulary >50 words

• C. 4 years ✘

• Hops on one foot
• Copies a cross
• Draws a person with 3 parts
• Knows 4 colors

• D. 5 years ✘

• Skips
• Copies a triangle
• Draws a person with 6 parts
• Knows full address and can count to 10
questions.learning: 3 years Developmental milestones are assessed in four domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, and personal-social skills. The combination of riding a tricycle, copying a circle, and knowing one’s name and gender are classic milestones of a 3-year-old…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following carbapenems has increased risk of causing seizures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Imipenem

Imipenem is the carbapenem that is associated with an increased risk of causing seizures, especially when high doses are given to patients with CNS lesions.

Excretion of imipenem is mainly renal and dosage modification is required to avoid seizures in renal failure patients.
questions.learning: Imipenem Imipenem is the carbapenem that is associated with an increased risk of causing seizures, especially when high doses are given to patients with CNS lesions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child is brought to the outpatient department with irritability, poor academic performance, and a history of recurrent ear infections. Otoscopic examination reveals a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid visible behind it, without any blood clot in the ear. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The findings of a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid accumulation in the absence of acute inflammatory signs like purulence or a bulging membrane are characteristic of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as "glue ear". This condition is common in school-aged children and often results from Eustachian tube dysfunction, frequently caused by adenoid hyperplasia. Acute otitis media (Option A) would present with sudden ear pain, fever, and a red, bulging membrane. Otitis externa (Option B) involves infection of the outer ear canal, typically causing pain when the tragus is moved. Cholesteatoma (Option D) involves a keratinizing epithelial growth in the middle ear, often presenting with foul discharge and a retraction pocket. Thus, the clinical picture specifically describes non-purulent middle ear effusion. ОРТНALMOLOGY
questions.learning: The findings of a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with fluid accumulation in the absence of acute inflammatory signs like purulence or a bulging membrane are characteristic of Otitis Media with Effusion (OME), also known as "glue ear".

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old male patient presents with decreased hearing in higher frequencies. It was noted that the basilar membrane was affected. Which of the following structures lie near the affected structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Oval window

The affected structure in high-frequency hearing loss is the basal turn of the cochlea. Among the given options, the structure that lies near it is the oval window.

The traveling wave theory of von Bekesy states that a sound wave, depending on its frequency, reaches maximum amplitude at a segment on the basilar membrane and stimulates that segment. The high frequencies are represented in the basal turn of the cochlea and the progressively lower ones towards the apex.

The cochlea has a bony core called the modiolus, and a spiral canal that runs around it. At the base of the canal, the two main openings are the oval window and the round window. The footplate of stapes rests against the oval window. The base of the modiolus transmits nerves and vessels to the cochlea. (option A)

The inner ear consists of a bony labyrinth and a membranous labyrinth. The bony labyrinth consists of the vestibule, semicircular canals, and the cochlea. The membranous labyrinth consists of the cochlear duct, the utricle and saccule, semicircular ducts, and the endolymphatic duct and sac.

The cochlear duct has three walls- the basilar membrane, Reissner's membrane, and the stria vascularis. The basilar membrane supports the organ of Corti, which is the sensory hearing epithelium. The length of the basilar membrane increases from the base to the apex. As a result of this, higher frequency sound is heard at the basal coil while lower frequencies are heard at the apex.

The stria vascularis is involved in the secretion of endolymph and contains vascular epithelium. (Option B)

The helicotrema (option D) is an opening at the apex of the cochlea, at which the scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate. The scala vestibuli, tympani, and media are three compartments of the bony cochlea.
questions.learning: Oval window — The affected structure in high-frequency hearing loss is the basal turn of the cochlea. Among the given options, the structure that lies near it is the oval window.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with diabetes asks for dietary advice, and you recommend foods with a low glycemic index. Which of the following options would be most appropriate to suggest?
questions.explanation: The glycemic index (GI) measures how quickly a food raises blood glucose levels. For diabetic patients, low GI foods (<55) are preferred because they cause a slow, gradual rise in blood sugar, helping maintain better glycemic control. Among the given options, papaya has a low to moderate GI and is rich in fiber, vitamins, and antioxidants, which help slow glucose absorption and improve overall metabolic health. Hence, it is the most appropriate choice. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Corn flakes : Very high GI (~80–85) → causes rapid spike in blood glucose (B) Brown rice : Moderate GI (~65–70) → better than white rice but not low GI (C) Sucrose : Simple sugar with high GI (~65) → quickly raises blood glucose
questions.learning: The glycemic index (GI) measures how quickly a food raises blood glucose levels. For diabetic patients, low GI foods (<55) are preferred because they cause a slow, gradual rise in blood sugar, helping maintain better glycemic control.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the nuclear family life cycle, which stage begins when the family has its first child?
questions.explanation: The developmental cycle of a nuclear family consists of several predictable stages. The stage of Extension (Option A) begins with the birth of the first child . This phase is characterized by the expansion of the family size and the increasing responsibilities of child-rearing. Complete extension (Option B) refers to the point when the family has reached its maximum size (all children are born). The phase of Contraction (Option C) begins when the first child leaves home (often for work or marriage), and the family starts to shrink. Completed contraction (Option D) occurs when all children have left, and the original couple is alone again (the "empty nest" stage). Therefore, because the family is just beginning to grow with its first new member, they are entering the phase of Extension
questions.learning: The developmental cycle of a nuclear family consists of several predictable stages. The stage of Extension (Option A) begins with the birth of the first child .

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A drug was given IV at a rate of 1.6mg/min. The clearance of the drug is 640ml/min. The half life of the drug is 1.8 hour. Calculate the plasma concentration of the drug at steady state.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 0.002mg/ml

Plasma steady-state concentration is achieved when the amount of drug being administered equals the amount of drug being excreted from the body.

The amount of drug being administered = 1.6mg/min

Amount of drug being excreted = Clearance (CL) x Plasma concentration of the drug (C)

Clearance = 640ml/min

Therefore,

1.6mg/min = 640ml /min ( clearance) x Plasma concentration of the drug

Hence,

Plasma concentration of the drug = 1.6 mg/min / 640 ml/min = 0.002 mg/ml.
questions.learning: 0.002mg/ml Plasma steady-state concentration is achieved when the amount of drug being administered equals the amount of drug being excreted from the body.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Where is Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy used?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical cancer

Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy is used for cervical cancer.

Ovoid and tandem brachytherapy is a combination technique where a tandem applicator and ovoid applicators are used for radiation treatment.
A tandem is a narrow tube, that is inserted through the cervix into the uterus, while the ovoids are placed in the upper part of the vagina. Once in place, a radioactive source is introduced into both the tandem and ovoids, ensuring precise radiation delivery to the cancerous tissues.

Both ovoid and tandem brachytherapy are designed to deliver targeted radiation therapy, maximising the dose to the tumor while minimizing side effects to adjacent healthy structures.

Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which the radiation source is placed close to the tumour. It can be either a low-dose or high-dose rate system. High-dose brachytherapy is safe and effective.
Dosage is calculated with respect to the amount of radiation received at two arbitrary points A and B (Image below).

Different techniques of brachytherapy:

Techniques
Device
No. of application
Duration

Stockholm

Intrauterine tandem

One vaginal plaque

Three
24 hours each week

Paris

Intrauterine tandem

Three vaginal ovoids

One
120 hours

Manchester

Two vaginal ovoids

Two
72 hours each weekly

Radiation dose in surrounding normal tissue is less due to inverse square law (Inverse square law - the intensity of radiation is inversely proportional to squared distance from the source of radiation). This method is unsuitable for large tumours and has potential risks of radiation exposure to medical staff.

Note: After loading technique by remote control is the recent development of brachytherapy. It protects the staff from radiation exposure.
questions.learning: Cervical cancer Ovoid and tandem radiotherapy is used for cervical cancer. Ovoid and tandem brachytherapy is a combination technique where a tandem applicator and ovoid applicators are used for radiation treatment.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the primary underlying factor responsible for mortality in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.explanation: This question repeats the critical clinical point that "cerebral edema" is the leading cause of mortality in patients suffering from Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), particularly among pediatric and young adult populations. DKA is a complex metabolic state of profound dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and acidosis. While sepsis (Option A) can be a trigger for DKA, and severe dehydration (Option B) or hypokalemia (Option C) are major complications that must be addressed, it is the rapid swelling of the brain that most frequently leads to coma and death. The exact mechanism of cerebral edema in DKA is not fully understood but is thought to be related to the rapid drop in serum glucose and osmolality during treatment, leading to an osmotic shift of water into brain cells. Clinical signs include headache, declining consciousness, and bradycardia. To minimize this risk, clinicians must lower blood glucose gradually and avoid the over-aggressive use of hypotonic fluids or bicarbonate. Thus, preventing and managing cerebral edema is the highest priority in DKA care
questions.learning: This question repeats the critical clinical point that "cerebral edema" is the leading cause of mortality in patients suffering from Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA), particularly among pediatric and young adult populations.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: You suspect dengue in a patient who presented with a 3-day history of fever, headache, and retro-orbital pain. Blood investigations revealed Hb=14 g/dl, WBC= 4000 cells/ mm3 and platelet count = 8900 cells/mm3. Which of the following tests will not be useful in confirming the diagnosis of this condition?
options: Viral culture and isolation in aedes albopticus c6/36 cell line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IgM ELISA

In a suspected case of dengue, where a patient presented with a 3-day history of symptoms like fever, headache, and retro-orbital pain, all the above investigations can be done except for IgM-ELISA, which is used to identify antibodies against the dengue virus.

Dengue viruses belong to flaviviruses and present with sudden onset of fever (saddleback type), frontal headache, retro-orbital pain, back pain, and severe myalgias. It is transmitted from person to person by the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

The virus can be found in serum, plasma, circulating blood cells, and other tissues for 4-5 days following the onset of the illness. Virus isolation, nucleic acid detection, or antigen detection can be used to diagnose the infection in its early stages. Serology is the preferred method of diagnosis at the end of the acute phase of infection.

Before day 5 of illness, during the febrile period, diagnosis can be made by the following tests:

• Virus isolation can be done during the period of viremia i.e. usually before day 5. The mosquito cell line C6/36 (cloned from Aedes albopictus) or AP61 are the host cells of choice for routine isolation of the dengue virus.
• RT-PCR - They have higher sensitivity than virus isolation and a much faster turnaround time.
• NS1 antigen can be detected up to 7-10 days after the onset of illness.

After day 5, dengue viruses and antigens disappear from the blood with the appearance of specific antibodies. The presence of IgM antibody or rising titres of IgG antibody on ELISA is used for detecting and distinguishing primary and secondary dengue infections.
questions.learning: IgM ELISA — In a suspected case of dengue, where a patient presented with a 3-day history of symptoms like fever, headache, and retro-orbital pain, all the above investigations can be done except for IgM-ELISA, which is used to identify antibodies against…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which test is being performed to detect fixed flexion deformity at hip?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thomas test

Thomas test is used to detect fixed flexion deformity of the hip.

Flexion deformity is seen in the initial stages of the disease. The patient keeps the hip in flexion as this is the position of ease and maximum joint capacity. Soft tissue contractures convert this into a fixed flexion deformity, making locomotion impossible.

In an effort to bring the limb on the ground and to make locomotion possible, the lumbar spine undergoes exaggerated lordosis and thus conceals the fixed flexion deformity. This is revealed by the Thomas test. The easy passage of the examiner's hand between the bed and the back of the patient is considered as a positive test as normally this is not possible.

Other options:

* Trendelenburg test is used to assess the weakness or paralysis of gluteus medius muscle.

* Telescopy test: To asses the stability of the hip joint. Positive telescopy test indicates hip dislocations or fracture neck of femur.

* Ober's test is used in physical examination to identify the tightness of the iliotibial band.
questions.learning: Thomas test Thomas test is used to detect fixed flexion deformity of the hip. Flexion deformity is seen in the initial stages of the disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most common cause of post-menopausal bleeding all over the world is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Senile endometrial atrophy

The most frequent cause of post menopausal bleeding globally is senile endometrial atrophy.

Hypoestrogenism in a menopausal woman causes atrophy of the endometrium and vagina. In the uterus, the atrophic endometrial surfaces contain little or no fluid to prevent intracavitary friction. This results in microerosions of the surface epithelium and a subsequent chronic inflammatory reaction, which is prone to light bleeding or spotting.

Other Options :

* Cervical cancer : Cervical cancer is the most common cause of post menopausal bleeding in India, and not over the world.

* Endometrial cancer : Endometrial cancer is the most common cause of postmenopausal bleeding in developed countries, and not over the world.

* Hormone replacement therapy : Hormone replacement therapy is the second most common cause of post-menopausal bleeding all over the world.

Note: Endometrial cancer accounts for 10% of cases of post-menopausal bleeding. Unexpected post-menopausal bleeding should be assessed for endometrial carcinoma. Remember, no cancer is as prevalent as hypoestrogenism in a postmenopausal woman, and this is why senile endometrial atrophy is the most common cause of bleeding in them, and not any cancer.
questions.learning: Senile endometrial atrophy — The most frequent cause of post menopausal bleeding globally is senile endometrial atrophy. Hypoestrogenism in a menopausal woman causes atrophy of the endometrium and vagina.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What type of fracture is caused by a hammer?
questions.explanation: A hammer is a heavy, blunt object with a relatively small impact surface. When it strikes the skull with significant force, it typically causes a depressed fracture. In this type of injury, bone fragments are pushed inward toward the brain, often creating an indentation that may even mirror the shape of the hammer's head. Regarding other options, a linear or fissured fracture (Option A) is caused by impact against broad surfaces, like a fall onto a flat floor, and shows cracks without bone displacement. A hinge fracture (Option (C) is a transverse fracture at the skull base often seen in side impacts or motorcyclist accidents. A ring fracture (Option D) circles the foramen magnum and is usually caused by vertical force transmitted through the spine, such as falling from a height and landing on the feet. Therefore, the focused, high-energy impact of a hammer uniquely leads to a localized depression of the skull vault
questions.learning: A hammer is a heavy, blunt object with a relatively small impact surface. When it strikes the skull with significant force, it typically causes a depressed fracture.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of hypocalcemia in a child? I. Hypomagnesemia II. Hypophosphatemia III. Metabolic acidosis IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and IV

Hypocalcemia is defined as a low serum ionized calcium or total serum calcium (after correction for albumin). It commonly presents with neuromuscular irritability, including tetany, seizures, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval on ECG.

Among the important causes in children are hypomagnesemia and pseudohypoparathyroidism.

Why is D correct?

• I. Hypomagnesemia ✔

• Correct.
• Magnesium deficiency impairs parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and causes PTH resistance, leading to hypocalcemia.
• Hypocalcemia due to hypomagnesemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

• II. Hypophosphatemia ✘

• Incorrect.
• Hypophosphatemia is usually associated with increased calcium levels or normal calcium.
• Hyperphosphatemia, not hypophosphatemia, commonly causes hypocalcemia.

• III. Metabolic acidosis ✘

• Incorrect.
• Acidosis reduces calcium binding to albumin, thereby increasing ionized (physiologically active) calcium.
• Alkalosis, not acidosis, precipitates symptomatic hypocalcemia by decreasing ionized calcium.

• IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism ✔

• Correct.
• It is caused by end-organ resistance to PTH, resulting in:

• Hypocalcemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Elevated PTH levels
questions.learning: I and IV Hypocalcemia is defined as a low serum ionized calcium or total serum calcium (after correction for albumin). It commonly presents with neuromuscular irritability, including tetany, seizures, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval…

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the site of lesion in internuclear ophthalmoplegia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus

In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) the lesion is at the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).

In INO, there is impaired adduction on the ipsilateral side of the lesion, and nystagmus on abduction on the contralateral side. When the gaze is initiated in the motor cortex, the horizontal gaze center or the paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) generates the eye movements.

The PPRF has two outputs. The first is to the ipsilateral 6th cranial nerve nucleus which causes abduction of the ipsilateral eye. The second output is to the contralateral MLF which sends an impulse to the contralateral 3rd cranial nerve nucleus causing contralateral adduction. These two outputs from PPRF lead to conjugate movement of the eyes to the same side.

Therefore, a lesion in the right MLF leads to failure of the right eye adduction. The left eye, however, abducts normally. This is called internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

The following image shows the pathway for horizontal eye movements as described above.
questions.learning: Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus — In internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) the lesion is at the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). In INO, there is impaired adduction on the ipsilateral side of the lesion, and nystagmus on abduction on the contralateral side.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A child came for DPT vaccination at 10 weeks. He has a history of fever of more than 40°C and an inconsolable cry at 6 weeks of age following vaccination. What should be done next?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Give DPT vaccine

The next step for this patient should be to administer DPT vaccine.

Events such as persistent inconsolable crying (more than 3 hours in duration), hyperpyrexia (fever > 40°C), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes within 48 hours of DTwP administration, and seizures, with or without fever, within 72 hours DTwP administration are considered precautions but not contraindications to future doses of DTwP. These events don't recur with the next dose and have been shown to have no permanent sequelae.

Absolute contraindications to any pertussis vaccination are a history of anaphylaxis or development of encephalopathy within 7 days following previous DTwP vaccination. In case of anaphylaxis, further immunization with diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis vaccines are contraindicated as it cannot be said with certainty which component caused anaphylaxis. For patients with a history of encephalopathy following vaccination, any pertussis vaccine is contraindicated, and only diphtheria and tetanus vaccines may be used.

Note: This answer might be controversial. The above answer is as per the IAP Guidebook on Immunization.
questions.learning: Give DPT vaccine — The next step for this patient should be to administer DPT vaccine. Events such as persistent inconsolable crying (more than 3 hours in duration), hyperpyrexia (fever > 40°C), hypotonic-hyporesponsive episodes within 48 hours of DTwP…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who has sustained electrical burns and has stable vital signs, the urine appears red in color. Which abnormal finding is most likely to be detected on serological (blood) investigation?
questions.explanation: In patients with electrical burns, deep tissue injury commonly leads to rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by extensive skeletal muscle breakdown. Damaged muscle cells release large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream, most notably myoglobin and potassium (K⁺). The presence of red-colored urine in this setting is due to myoglobinuria, not hematuria. Therefore, RBCs in urine (Option A) are typically absent or minimal, as the discoloration is pigment-related rather than due to bleeding. A critical and early serological abnormality in rhabdomyolysis is hyperkalemia, caused by the massive release of potassium from injured muscle cells. Hyperkalemia is potentially life-threatening, as it can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias, making it the most important immediate laboratory finding to monitor. Creatinine levels (Option B) may rise later due to acute kidney injury from myoglobin-induced nephrotoxicity, but this is not the earliest or most characteristic finding. Hemoglobin levels (Option C) are usually unaffected unless there is significant associated blood loss. Thus, in a stable patient with electrical burns and red urine, increased serum potassium is the most likely and clinically urgent serological finding
questions.learning: In patients with electrical burns, deep tissue injury commonly leads to rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by extensive skeletal muscle breakdown.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids for the past six months. She also complains of intermittent regurgitation of undigested food and a feeling of food getting stuck in the chest after meals. A barium swallow study has been performed and is shown below. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hypertensive lower (A) Achalasia cardia The barium swallow image displays the classic "bird's beak" sign—a dilated proximal esophagus with smooth, symmetric tapering at the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). This is diagnostic of "Achalasia Cardia," a motility disorder caused by the loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus, leading to a failure of the LES to relax and an absence of esophageal peristalsis. The clinical history of "progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids" is highly characteristic of achalasia, distinguishing it from mechanical obstructions like cancer which initially cause dysphagia only for solids. Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option B) shows a "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow. Nutcracker esophagus (Option C) and hypertensive LES (Option D) typically require esophageal manometry for diagnosis and do not show this degree of proximal dilation and distal tapering. Treatment options for achalasia include pneumatic dilation, botulinum toxin injection, or surgical Heller myotomy.
questions.explanation: Ankylosing spondylitis. The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy. The provided X-ray provides the definitive diagnosis, showing vertical syndesmophytes fusing the vertebral bodies, creating the classic "bamboo spine" appearance of Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option C). Pott’s spine (Option A) is spinal tuberculosis, which causes vertebral destruction and angulation (gibbus) rather than smooth fusion. Psoriatic arthritis (Option B) can cause sacroiliitis but usually presents with asymmetric large syndesmophytes. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) primarily affects the small joints of the hands and the cervical spine, not the lumbar spine in this manner. Therefore, the inspiratory efforts against a closed glottis, a high negative intrathoracic pressure is generated. This pressure draws fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli, leading to rapid onset "desaturation and crepitations". ARDS (Option A) takes longer to develop and is associated with sepsis or major trauma. Pleural effusion (Option B) is a slower accumulation of fluid. Atelectasis (Option D) is common post-operatively but usually causes localized findings rather than diffuse acute pulmonary edema symptoms. NPPE is a medical emergency but usually resolves quickly with supplemental oxygen, CPAP, or brief mechanical ventilation once the airway obstruction is relieved. Clinicians must be vigilant for laryngospasm to prevent this sudden respiratory deterioration. What is the standard treatment for empyema thoracis? (A) Antibiotics alone (B) Chest tube drainage and antibiotics (C) Intercostal drain (ICD) alone (D) Wait and watch
questions.learning: The combination of chronic inflammatory back pain (worse in the morning, improves with exercise) and a history of inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis) is highly suggestive of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the first investigation in newborn for audiological assessment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions)

Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the first-line screening test for hearing assessment in newborns.

·  Measures sound waves generated by outer hair cells of cochlea

·  A small probe in the ear canal records these emissions

Screening protocol:

·   Step 1: OAE screening

·   Step 2 (if abnormal): BERA/ABR for confirmation

Why other options are incorrect:

·    BERA: Confirmatory test, not initial screening

·    PTA: Requires cooperation (not suitable for newborns)

·    Impedance audiometry: Assesses middle ear, not primary screening
questions.learning: OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions) Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) is the first-line screening test for hearing assessment in newborns. · Measures sound waves generated by outer hair cells of cochlea · A small probe in the ear canal records these emissions Screening…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The deepest part of perineal body injury, which causes cystocoele, enterocoele and urethral descent is ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pubococcygeous

Pubococcygeus is the deepest part of the levator ani muscle. Injury to it can cause enterocele, cystocele, and urethral descent.

Levator ani muscles are the most important muscles in the pelvic floor and maintain a constant state of contraction. They provide a stable floor and support the weight of the abdominopelvic contents against intra-abdominal forces. Weakening of levator ani and pelvic fascia from stretching or tearing during childbirth, may decrease support for the vagina, bladder, uterus, or rectum or alter the position of the neck of the bladder and urethra.

The levator ani muscle is a complex unit, which consists of 3 muscle components namely

• Pubococcygeus (anterior fibers)

• Pubovaginalis - elevates the urethra and hence contributes to urinary continence
• Puboperinealis - draws the perineal body towards the pubic symphysis
• Puboanalis - elevates the anus and keeps the urogenital hiatus narrowed

• Puborectalis (intermediate fibers)
• Iliococcygeus (posterior fibers)

Origin: The levator ani muscle has a linear origin from the pelvic surface of the body of the pubis, a tendinous arch of obturator fascia, and the pelvic surface of the ischial spine.

Insertion:

• The anterior fibres form a sling around the prostate (levator prostatae) or vagina (sphincter vaginae) and are inserted into the perineal body (a mass of fibrous tissue) in front of the anal canal.
• The intermediate fibres (puborectalis) form a sling around the anorectal junction to be inserted into the anococcygeal raphe (a fibrous raphe which extends from the anorectal junction to the tip of the coccyx).
• The posterior fibres (iliococcygeus) are inserted into the anococcygeal raphe and the coccyx.

Nerve supply:

• perineal branch of 4th sacral nerve (S4) from its pelvic surface.
• perineal branch of the pudendal nerve (S2, S3) from its perineal surface.

Actions:

• The levator ani muscles of two sides together support the pelvic viscera and resist the intra-abdominal pressure during straining and expulsive efforts of the anterior abdominal wall muscles.
• They also subserve a sphincteric action on the anorectal junction to maintain the continence of faeces in both sexes and vagina in females.

questions.learning: Pubococcygeous Pubococcygeus is the deepest part of the levator ani muscle. Injury to it can cause enterocele, cystocele, and urethral descent.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with nasal obstruction, loss of smell (anosmia), and a foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On clinical examination, the findings shown below are observed. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of nasal obstruction (paradoxically, despite a spacious cavity), anosmia (loss of smell), and ozaena (a repulsive foul smell that the patient themselves cannot perceive) is the classic presentation of Atrophic rhinitis. On examination, as shown in the image, the nasal mucosa is thin and atrophied, and the cavity is filled with characteristic greenish-black crusts. Rhinitis sicca (Option B) involves dry mucosa without the severe atrophy and foul crusting. Rhinitis medicamentosa (Option C) is a rebound congestion following the overuse of topical decongestants. Allergic rhinitis (Option D) presents with sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, and pale, boggy turbinates. Atrophic rhinitis often affects young or middle-aged women and may be primary or secondary to surgery. Management focuses on nasal douching with alkaline solutions to remove crusts and maintain hygiene. In severe, refractory cases, surgical procedures like Young's operation (closing the nostrils) may be performed to allow the mucosa to heal in a humid environment
questions.learning: The clinical triad of nasal obstruction (paradoxically, despite a spacious cavity), anosmia (loss of smell), and ozaena (a repulsive foul smell that the patient themselves cannot perceive) is the classic presentation of Atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: GCS of a patient who had a road-traffic accident is 10. Using the GCS scoring system, the head injury of this patient is classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Moderate traumatic brain injury

Using the Glasgow Coma Scale score(GCS) , the head injury of this patient with a GCS 10 is classified as moderate.

GCS is used in the assessment of patients with a head injury. The maximum GCS score is 15 (E4 V5 M6).

Based on the GCS score, the head injury sustained can be classified as follows:

GCS Score

* 13-15 represent mild injury

* 9-12 represent moderate injury

* ≤8 represent severe injury

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following adverse effects is NOT commonly associated with long-term lithium therapy?
questions.explanation: Lithium is a cornerstone therapy for bipolar disorder, but it is associated with several important long-term adverse effects. Tardive dyskinesia (Option D) is not caused by lithium; it is a potentially irreversible movement disorder classically associated with long-term use of dopamine receptor–blocking antipsychotics. Therefore, attributing tardive dyskinesia to lithium is incorrect. Lithium commonly causes hypothyroidism (Option A) by interfering with thyroid hormone synthesis and release, making regular TSH monitoring essential. Another well-recognized adverse effect is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (Option C), which results from reduced renal responsiveness to antidiuretic hormone and presents with polyuria and polydipsia. Fine tremors (Option B) are a frequent, dose-related side effect and may worsen with toxicity. Additional long-term effects of lithium include weight gain, acne, edema, and chronic interstitial nephropathy, which may lead to progressive renal impairment over years. Because lithium has a narrow therapeutic index (approximately 0.6–1.2 mEq/L), regular serum level monitoring is mandatory. Lithium toxicity presents with coarse tremors, ataxia, dysarthria, and confusion, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and drug interaction awareness

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the structure marked in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Genioglossus

The structure marked 'A' in the image is the Genioglossus muscle.

Genioglossus is one of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue which brings about the forward traction of the tongue to protrude its apex from the mouth. Hence, it is also called the safety muscle of the tongue.

Acting bilaterally, the two muscles depress the central part of the tongue, making it concave from side to side. Acting unilaterally, the tongue diverges to the opposite side.

Other options:

Hyoglossus: Depresses and retracts the tongue, pulling it downward and backward.

Styloglossus: Elevates and retracts the tongue, drawing it upward and backward.

Palatoglossus: Elevates the posterior portion of the tongue and narrows the fauces during swallowing.

Note:

* All the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus (cranial accessory nerve through pharyngeal plexus) are supplied by hypoglossal nerve.

* All the muscles of pharynx except stylopharyngeus (glossopharyngeal nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of soft palate except tensor veli palatini (nerve to medial pterygoid from mandibular nerve) are supplied by pharyngeal plexus.

* All muscles of larynx except cricothyroid (external laryngeal nerve) are supplied by recurrent laryngeal nerve.

All intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of tongue are derived from occipital myotomes, hence innervated by hypoglossal nerve, except palatoglossus which is derived from the pharyngeal arch and is supplied by vago-accessory nerve.
questions.learning: Genioglossus — The structure marked 'A' in the image is the Genioglossus muscle. Genioglossus is one of the extrinsic muscles of the tongue which brings about the forward traction of the tongue to protrude its apex from the mouth.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 34-year-old man undergoes an open appendectomy for acute appendicitis using a McBurney’s incision. A few days after surgery, he develops pain and a bulge in the right lower quadrant and is diagnosed with an indirect inguinal hernia. Injury to which nerve during the appendectomy is most likely responsible for this complication?
questions.explanation: Injury to the ilioinguinal nerve is a known complication of an appendectomy, particularly when using a McBurney's incision. This nerve supplies the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles; its damage can weaken the abdominal wall, leading to the later development of an indirect inguinal hernia. The femoral nerve (Option B) supplies the anterior thigh and is located deeper and more laterally, making it an unlikely target during standard appendectomy. The genitofemoral nerve (Option C) and pudendal nerve (Option D) supply the genital region and perineum and are not typically at risk during this superficial right lower quadrant dissection. While wound infection is the most common early complication, nerve injury is a significant cause of long-term morbidity. Careful surgical technique is required to identify and preserve the ilioinguinal nerve within the muscle layers

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following factors are involved in maintaining and regulating calcium levels in the blood?
questions.explanation: Blood calcium homeostasis is a tightly regulated process involving three primary hormones. Parathormone (PTH), secreted by the parathyroid glands, is the most important regulator for "increasing" blood calcium; it stimulates bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and the activation of Vitamin D. Vitamin D (Option C), specifically its active form calcitriol, increases calcium levels by promoting its absorption from the small intestine. Calcitonin (Option A), secreted by the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid, acts as a physiological antagonist to PTH by "decreasing" blood calcium through the inhibition of bone-resorbing osteoclasts. While calcitonin plays a smaller role in daily human calcium regulation compared to PTH, it is still a recognized component of the regulatory system. Together, these substances ensure that ionized calcium remains within a narrow physiological range, which is critical for muscle contraction, nerve conduction, and blood coagulation. Therefore, the combination of all three factors (Option D) constitutes the complete regulatory machinery for serum calcium

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Gibbs free energy curve of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is given by
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A

Among the given graphs, the Gibbs free energy change of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction is shown by graph A (Option B).

Graph B (Option A) cannot represent the Gibbs free energy of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, as the energy state of an intermediate cannot be lower than the product. A lower energy state of the intermediate implies that the enzyme-intermediate complex is stable and such a complex will usually not further form a product.

During any chemical reaction, the product is formed by the breaking of substrate bonds and the conformational change of the substrate into a highly unstable transition state. This transition state is denoted by the peak of the graph. The Gibbs free energy curve of an enzyme-catalyzed reaction (with no intermediate state) is shown in the image given below:

The below graph shows the normal intermediate formation with an energy state still higher than that of the product:

All the reactions have a transition state, but not all reactions have an intermediate state. Every intermediate state is again always followed by another transition state.

Activation energy is the energy difference between the free energy of the substrates and that of the transition state. Because of the high activation energy, the rates of uncatalyzed chemical reactions are often slow.

In an enzyme-catalyzed reaction, the activation energy is reduced by forming a relatively stable intermediate-enzyme complex. Enzymes provide attachment sites for the substrate and speed up the rate of reaction. They don't change the energy state of either the substrate or the product. The Gibbs free energy change remains the same.

Graph C: Free energy change cannot be a straight line. Every reaction passes through a high-energy intermediate transition state.

Graph D: The activation energy of any reaction is never lower than the free energy of the product.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 48-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling. Investigations for testicular tumours revealed that LDH was raised but AFP was within normal limits. Following orchidectomy, the following histological picture was observed. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Seminoma

The clinical scenario, high LDH with normal AFP levels, and the given histology picture showing fried egg appearance are highly suggestive of testicular seminoma.

In yolk sac tumors and embryonal carcinoma, AFP is elevated whereas in teratoma LDH is normal.

Seminoma is the most common testicular tumour. It is common in men between 20-40 years of age.

The patients usually present with a painless testicular lump. If a testicular tumour is suspected, blood samples are taken from the patient for the evaluation of the tumour markers (hCG, LDH, and AFP), and a high inguinal orchidectomy is performed for diagnosis.

Further treatment of seminoma depends on the stage of the tumor. Stage I tumors, whose levels of tumor markers decline after orchidectomy may not require further treatment. Stage II-IV tumors require radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The chemotherapeutic agents used are bleomycin, etoposide, and platin-based agents (BEP).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A man is abducted from his home, and his son later claims rights over his father’s property. According to Section 111 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), until what period is the son not legally entitled to claim inheritance?
questions.explanation: Under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), a person who has been missing and not heard of by those who would naturally have heard from them is legally presumed dead only after a period of 7 years. Until this statutory seven-year period is complete, the individual is considered alive in the eyes of the law, and legal heirs are not entitled to claim inheritance or take possession of the estate. The burden of proving that the individual is missing for this duration lies with the person claiming the inheritance. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because they do not align with the specific time requirement mandated by Indian law for the presumption of death. Therefore, the son must wait for exactly seven years of the father being missing before any legal claim to the property can be validated
questions.learning: Under Section 111 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), a person who has been missing and not heard of by those who would naturally have heard from them is legally presumed dead only after a period of 7 years.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden- onset, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, accompanied by breathlessness and nausea. CT imaging of the chest suggests an aortic dissection. What is the most appropriate management strategy for this patient?
questions.explanation: Aortic dissection is a critical emergency where a tear in the inner layer of the aorta allows blood to flow between the layers of the aortic wall. The classic presentation is "tearing" or "ripping" chest pain that radiates to the back. Management depends on the location. For Stanford Type A dissections (involving the ascending aorta), the risk of catastrophic rupture, aortic regurgitation, or coronary involvement is extremely high. The standard of care is immediate heart rate and blood pressure control, typically with intravenous Labetalol (an alpha and beta-blocker), to reduce the "shear stress" on the aortic wall. This is followed by "urgent surgical repair." Urgent surgery alone (Option B) without medical stabilization is dangerous. A "wait and watch" approach (Option C) is only considered for some stable Type B (descending) dissections. Blood transfusion (Option D) is not a primary treatment unless there is overt hemorrhage or rupture. Therefore, the combination of pharmacological control and surgical intervention is the life-saving protocol for suspected Type A aortic dissection
questions.learning: Aortic dissection is a critical emergency where a tear in the inner layer of the aorta allows blood to flow between the layers of the aortic wall. The classic presentation is "tearing" or "ripping" chest pain that radiates to the back.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe headache unlike any previous episodes, accompanied by elevated blood pressure and nuchal rigidity on examination. Based on this presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient's description of a "worst headache of their life" (thunderclap headache) combined with nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) is the classic clinical presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH). The accompanying NCCT brain image provides definitive evidence, showing hyperdense (bright white) areas in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, and sulci, representing acute blood in the subarachnoid space. Cluster headache (Option A) causes excruciating unilateral orbital pain but would not cause nuchal rigidity or CT findings. Encephalitis (Option C) and Meningitis (Option D) can cause headache and nuchal rigidity (signs of meningism), but they would typically be accompanied by fever and would not show acute intracranial blood on a CT scan. SAH is most commonly caused by a ruptured berry aneurysm and is a neurosurgical emergency. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic "thunderclap" history and the bright blood visible on CT, SAH is the diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient's description of a "worst headache of their life" (thunderclap headache) combined with nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) is the classic clinical presentation of a Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Match the following stages with their relevant descriptions.

1. Pre-pathogenesis
a. Normal course without any intervention

2. Pathogenesis
b. Appearance of clinical signs and symptoms

3. Natural  history of a disease
c. Reaching normalcy with the help of the community

4. Rehabilitation
d. Period before the onset of the disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c

The correct match is 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, and 4-c.

Natural history of disease refers to the progression of a disease in an individual over time, in the absence of treatment. It has two phases, a period of pre-pathogenesis and a period of pathogenesis.

The period of pre-pathogenesis is before the onset of disease in humans. An interaction between the agent, host and the environment occurs in this phase before the pathogenesis. It starts with appropriate exposure to or accumulation of factors sufficient for the disease process to begin in a susceptible host. The exposure is a microorganism in an infectious disease. For lung cancer, it is any factor that initiates the process, such as asbestos fibres or components in tobacco smoke. Primary prevention (health promotion and specific protection) is applicable in this period.

The period of pathogenesis starts after the disease process has been triggered and pathological changes occur without the individual being aware of it. It begins with the entry of the organism till recovery, death, or disability. The subclinical or asymptomatic period between exposure and onset of symptoms is called the incubation period for infectious diseases, and the latency period for chronic diseases. The onset of clinical symptoms is the beginning of the clinical stage of the disease. Secondary (halting of the disease process) and tertiary prevention (measures to limit disability) are applicable in this period.

Rehabilitation has been defined as the use of medical, social, educational, and vocational measures for training the individual to the highest possible level of functional ability. It is a part of tertiary prevention like providing callipers for walking patients and arranging schooling after being affected by polio.
questions.learning: 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c The correct match is 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, and 4-c. Natural history of disease refers to the progression of a disease in an individual over time, in the absence of treatment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following best describes the control of enzyme activity by phosphorylation or dephosphorylation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Covalent modification

The control of enzyme activity by phosphorylation or dephosphorylation is best explained by covalent modification.

Covalent modification is a key regulatory mechanism in which enzymes or proteins undergo chemical changes through the addition or removal of functional groups, altering their activity, stability, or interactions. One of the most common types is phosphorylation, where a phosphate group is added to a protein, typically by a kinase, leading to activation or inhibition of the target enzyme.

Conversely, dephosphorylation, catalyzed by phosphatases, removes the phosphate group, reversing the effect. This dynamic process plays a crucial role in cell signalling, metabolism, and gene regulation. For example, in glycogen metabolism, glycogen phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation to promote glycogen breakdown, while glycogen synthase is inactivated by phosphorylation to stop glycogen synthesis. These modifications ensure rapid and reversible control of cellular functions in response to physiological needs.

A few enzyme covalent modifications that regulate enzyme kinetics include:

* Partial proteolysis

* Acetylation

* Methylation

* ADP-ribosylation

* Phosphorylation

Other options:

Option A: Competitive inhibition is a type of inhibition that occurs when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the same site that the substrate would normally occupy. It, therefore, competes with the substrate for binding to the enzyme active site. The effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the concentration of the substrate. Km is increased, but Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition.

Option B: Allosteric inhibition occurs when a molecule binds to a site on an enzyme other than the active site, causing a conformational change that reduces the enzyme's activity. This regulatory mechanism is crucial for feedback control in metabolic pathways.

Option C: Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

* Non-Competitive inhibitors

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following events could be caused or precipitated by an active component of vaccine? 1. Anaphylaxis after measles vaccine 2. Encephalopathy after DPT vaccine 3. Adenitis following BCG vaccine 4. Gastroenteritis following MMR vaccine Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Vaccine product-related reactions are adverse events caused by the active component (antigen/live organism) of the vaccine. These include:

• Encephalopathy (rarely) after pertussis-containing (DPT) vaccine.
• BCG adenitis due to replication of the live attenuated BCG bacilli.
• Mild gastroenteritis may occur after live viral vaccines such as MMR, although it is uncommon.

Why not statement 1?

• Anaphylaxis after measles vaccine is usually due to vaccine excipients (e.g., gelatin or neomycin), not the active viral component.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 19-year-old female comes to the OPD with complaints of weakness, amenorrhea, and fatigue. Upon eliciting history, she reveals that she is always worried about gaining weight. Her mother complains that she doesn't eat well. Her BMI is 15.8. Laboratory findings in this patient will show which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hypersecretion of corticotrophin-releasing hormone

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of anorexia nervosa. Hypersecretion of corticotrophin-releasing hormone is seen in a patient with anorexia nervosa.

Anorexia nervosa is a type of eating disorder that is characterized by self-induced starvation to a significant degree, drive for thinness or a morbid fear of fatness, and the presence of medical signs and symptoms resulting from starvation.

Investigations in anorexia nervosa:

* Complete blood count: Leukopenia with a relative lymphocytosis

* Serum electrolyte: Hypokalemic alkalosis (Purging)

* Fasting serum glucose: Often low (emaciated phase) (Option D)

* Serum salivary amylase: Often elevated (if the patient is vomiting)

* ECG: ST segment and T-wave changes (secondary to electrolyte disturbances)

* Hypotension and bradycardia

* High serum cholesterol level (Option A)

* Endocrine changes (caused by the underweight):

* Amenorrhea

* Hypothyroidism (Option B)

* Hypersecretion of corticotrophin-releasing hormone
questions.learning: Hypersecretion of corticotrophin-releasing hormone — The given clinical vignette is suggestive of anorexia nervosa. Hypersecretion of corticotrophin-releasing hormone is seen in a patient with anorexia nervosa.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: cGMP is the second messenger of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. NO (nitric oxide)

Vasodilatory actions of NO are mediated by cGMP.

NO is a hormone derived from the amino acid arginine. It activates guanylyl cyclases in vascular smooth muscle cells resulting in the conversion of cGTP to cGMP (2nd messenger). cGMP activates cGMP dependent protein kinase, which causes blood vessels to relax.

cGMP is the second messenger for nitric oxide and atrial natriuretic factor.
questions.learning: NO (nitric oxide) Vasodilatory actions of NO are mediated by cGMP. NO is a hormone derived from the amino acid arginine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is not required to be a part of the consent for surgery in a patient who has an obstetric score of G6L1A3 with a history of two previous LSCS?
options: Risk of bladder injury during surgery due to PAS
Risk of bowel injury during surgery due to PAS
Possible need for hysterectomy during surgery due to PAS
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Risk of bowel injury during surgery due to PAS

A patient with a history of two previous caesarean deliveries would be at a high risk of having a morbidly adherent placenta or placenta accreta spectrum (PAS). However, bowel injury is an unlikely complication of placenta accreta spectrum (PAS) and hence may not be required as part of the consent for surgery in such a patient.

The placenta accreta spectrum is characterized by abnormally implanted, invasive, or adhered placenta. This occurs due to partial or complete absence of the decidua basalis and imperfect development of the Nitabuch layer. The major risk factors include associated placenta previa and previous cesarean delivery as seen in this patient.

There are three variants of this condition based on the depth of trophoblastic growth.

• Placenta accreta, the villi are attached to the myometrium.
• Placenta increta, the villi invade into the myometrium.
• Placenta percreta, the villi penetrate the myometrium into the serosa, with possible adherence to the bladder wall

PAS can be diagnosed in the antepartum period by ultrasound which will reveal loss of normal hypoechoic retroplacental zone between the placenta and uterus, placental vascular lacunae, bridging vessels, and placental bulging leading to distortion of the contour of the uterus. MRI can be performed when the ultrasound is inconclusive. However, ultrasound remains the modality of choice for diagnosis.

Patients with PAS have a significant risk of haemorrhage and shock. Management of this condition therefore involves appropriate multidisciplinary efforts with adequate surgical, anesthetic, intensive care, and blood banking capabilities. Patients are recommended scheduled delivery between 34 0/7 to 35 6/7 weeks of gestation and the risk of hemorrhage necessitating paripartum hysterectomy and blood transufsion, or bladder injury in percreta must be properly communicated.
questions.learning: Risk of bowel injury during surgery due to PAS — A patient with a history of two previous caesarean deliveries would be at a high risk of having a morbidly adherent placenta or placenta accreta spectrum (PAS).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) who shows no improvement on inhaled salmeterol alone, which additional medication can be added to the treatment regimen?
questions.explanation: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is currently taking Salmeterol, which is a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA). The most appropriate and standard "next step" is to add an anticholinergic agent, such as Ipratropium (a short-acting muscarinic antagonist) or Tiotropium (a LAMA) . These drugs provide synergistic bronchodilation by blocking parasympathetic-mediated airway constriction. Theophylline (Option A) is an oral bronchodilator with a narrow therapeutic window and more side effects, typically used as a third-line agent. Azithromycin (Option B) is used for its anti-inflammatory properties in patients with frequent exacerbations but is not a primary bronchodilator. Oral glucocorticoids (Option C) are reserved for managing acute exacerbations rather than daily maintenance due to systemic side effects. Therefore, adding an inhaled muscarinic antagonist like Ipratropium to the existing LABA is the definitive and recommended clinical strategy to improve symptoms
questions.learning: In the management of stable COPD, therapy is escalated by combining different classes of bronchodilators. The patient is currently taking Salmeterol, which is a Long-Acting Beta-Agonist (LABA).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The school health programs are managed by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary health center

The school health programs are managed by the primary health centre (PHC).

The School Health Committee (1961) in India recommended that the school health services should be a part of the general health services. Since the general health services are administered through PHCs, school health programs are also managed by the PHCs under their jurisdiction.

The School Health Committee advocated the formation of school health committees at the village level, block level, district level, state level, and national level. The National School Health Council will be an advisory and coordinating body.

PHCs provide the following school health services:

* Screening of general health assessment of anemia/nutritional status, visual acuity, hearing problem, dental check-up, physical disabilities, learning disorders, and behavior problems, etc.

* Basic medicines for common ailments

* Immunization

* Micronutrient (Vitamin A, iron, and folic acid) management

* Deworming

* Mid-day meal

Note: National Programme for Mid-Day Meal in Schools has recently been renamed Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN).

Pearl PF1580: Primary Health Centres-PHC

* One PHC per 30,000 population in plain areas and 20,000 in remote areas with a minimum of 6 beds.

* Types:

* Type A: PHC with less than 20 deliveries per month.

* Type B: PHC with 20 or more deliveries per month.

* Functions:

* Medical care: OPD, emergencies, referrals and in-patient services.

* Maternal and child health care, family planning and MTP

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Double bleb sign seen in early pregnancy is due to _______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yolk sac and amniotic sac

The double bleb sign is due to the yolk sac and amniotic sac.

On ultrasonographic examination, a gestational sac may contain the yolk sac and amniotic sac, appearing like two small bubbles. This is known as the double bleb sign. The embryonic disc is located between the yolk sac and the amniotic sac. It is an important feature of an intrauterine pregnancy.

Other options:

In a twin pregnancy, the chorionicity of the placenta is best diagnosed with the help of an ultrasound examination.

• In dichorionic gestation, the twins are separated by amniotic membranes and an intervening chorion. So, a thicker twin peak sign or lambda (λ) sign is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta.

• In monochorionic diamniotic gestation, the twins are separated only by the two amniotic membranes with no intervening chorion. So, a thin T sign is formed at the point at which the amnions meet the placenta.

Heterotopic pregnancy is a condition in which a normal uterine pregnancy co-exists with an extrauterine (ectopic) pregnancy. Although heterotopic pregnancy can occur spontaneously, it is more likely after artificial reproductive technology (ART) and ovulation induction.

The below image shows heterotopic pregnancy with 2 sacs, one inside the uterus (white arrow) and the other in the cervix (black arrows).
questions.learning: Yolk sac and amniotic sac — The double bleb sign is due to the yolk sac and amniotic sac. On ultrasonographic examination, a gestational sac may contain the yolk sac and amniotic sac, appearing like two small bubbles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Cranial nerve X carries multiple functional components. Which nucleus or functional group does not contribute fibers to the vagus nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GSE

The correct answer is GSE (General Somatic Efferent).

The vagus nerve (CN X) carries GVE (parasympathetic) fibres from the dorsal motor nucleus, GVA fibres from thoracoabdominal viscera, and GSA fibres from the external auditory canal and dura.

Its motor fibres are branchial efferent (SVE) to muscles of pharynx and larynx, not true GSE, which supply extraocular and tongue muscles only.
questions.learning: GSE — The correct answer is GSE (General Somatic Efferent). The vagus nerve (CN X) carries GVE (parasympathetic) fibres from the dorsal motor nucleus, GVA fibres from thoracoabdominal viscera, and GSA fibres from the external auditory canal and dura.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old patient presents to the outpatient department with a history of prolonged topical steroid use for a skin disorder. The patient reports an enlarging rash that has become less itchy and less erythematous after steroid application. On examination, well-defined, mildly raised plaques with central clearing and a scaly margin are seen over multiple body sites. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: Tinea incognito is a fungal infection (dermatophytosis) that has had its classic clinical appearance altered by the inappropriate application of topical or systemic corticosteroids. Ordinarily, tinea presents with highly inflammatory, itchy, and well-defined scaly borders. Steroids suppress this local inflammation, making the rash appear "less red and itchy," but they simultaneously impair the local immune response, allowing the fungus to proliferate more extensively into deeper layers of the skin. This often results in a less well-defined, widespread, and "bizarre" looking rash. Tinea corporis (Option B) refers to a standard ringworm infection of the body without steroid modification. Tinea cruris (Option C) is specific to the groin area, and tinea pedis (Option D) is athlete's foot. The patient’s specific history of using steroids followed by an "expanding" but less symptomatic rash is the hallmark of tinea incognito, requiring cessation of steroids and initiation of proper antifungal therapy for resolution
questions.learning: Tinea incognito is a fungal infection (dermatophytosis) that has had its classic clinical appearance altered by the inappropriate application of topical or systemic corticosteroids.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PT

Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation.

PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin). This indicates the overall efficiency of the extrinsic clotting system.

Causes of prolonged PT:

• Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs - vitamin K antagonists
• Liver disease - obstructive jaundice
• Vitamin K deficiency
• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect (rare)

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) measures the clotting time of plasma after the activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and CaCl2, but without added tissue thromboplastin. It indicates the overall efficiency of the intrinsic pathway.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

• Disseminated intravascular coagulation
• Liver disease
• Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
• Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
• A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
• Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII
• Intake of oral anticoagulant drugs
• Vitamin K deficiency
questions.learning: PT Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies_______.
options: Between the internal oblique and external oblique
Between the internal oblique and rectus abdominis
Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis

The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis in the anterior abdominal wall.

The plane contains:

* Lower 6 thoracic nerves (T7-12)

* Iliohypogastric nerves

* Posterior intercostal and subcostal vessels

* Anastomosis between superior and inferior epigastric arteries.
questions.learning: Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis The neurovascular plane of the abdominal wall lies between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis in the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is a component of the neuromuscular criteria for maturity according to the expanded New Ballard score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Scarf sign

Scarf sign is a component of the neuromuscular criteria for maturity according to the expanded new Ballard score.

Scarf sign: If the infant's arm is pulled medially across the chest (as shown in the image below),

• In a hypotonic infant, the elbow will cross the midline.
• In a term infant with a normal tone, the elbow will not reach the midline.

Neuromuscular criteria for maturity (according to the expanded New Ballard score) include:

1. Posture
2. Square window (wrist)
3. Arm recoil
4. Popliteal angle
5. Scarf sign
6. Heel to ear

Physical criteria for maturity (according to the expanded New Ballard score) include:

1. Skin
2. Lanugo
3. Eye/ear
4. Plantar crease
5. Breast
6. Genitals

The expanded new Ballard score is used to assess the physical and neuromuscular maturity of the newborn by scoring six criteria and thereby calculating the gestational age. It is accurate between 20 to 44 weeks.

The lowest score on the expanded New Ballard Score is -10, which corresponds to 20 weeks gestational age, and the highest score is 50, which corresponds to 44 weeks gestational age. An increase in the score by 5 points corresponds to an increase of 2 weeks gestational age
